multiple_choice_quizzes.explanation: Double apostrophes indicates separate ownership; an apostraphe only after the second name indicates joint ownership.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was their 23th wedding anniversary.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It was their 23rd wedding anniversary.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use -th when the word for the number ends with '-th': '6th May'(= sixth), '18th May'(= eighteenth). Do not use -th with (numbers ending) 1, 2, 3.Compare: '1st May'(first), '2nd May '(second), '3rd May '(third).

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I hope you all have a enjoyable stay.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I hope you all have an enjoyable stay.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Always use an (NOT a) before a word beginning with a vowel sound: 'an egg', 'an envelope'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The child had been a deaf since birth.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The child had been deaf since birth.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use a/an before an adjective (e.g. 'deaf', 'British') unless the adjective is followed by a noun: 'Her husband is disabled.'Compare: 'The footbridge cannot be used by the disabled.' (= all people who are disabled)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One of the girls I share with is a British.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One of the girls I share with is British.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use a/an before an adjective (e.g. 'deaf', 'British') unless the adjective is followed by a noun: 'Her husband is disabled.'Compare: 'The footbridge cannot be used by the disabled.' (= all people who are disabled)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My husband is doing a MSc in civil engineering.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My husband is doing an MSc in civil engineering.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use an (NOT a) before an abbreviation that begins with a vowel sound: 'an MSc' 'an MP'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Sometimes it is difficult to live a honest life.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Sometimes it is difficult to live an honest life.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use an (NOT a) before words beginning with h when the h is not pronounced: 'an honour', 'an hour'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Since capital punishment was abandoned, the crime rate has increased.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Since capital punishment was abolished, the crime rate has increased.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Abandon = give up a plan, activity or attempt to do something, without being successful: 'Bad weather forced them to abandon the search.' 'Without government support, the project will have to be abandoned.'Abolish = remove a law, tradition or system, often by introducing a new law; do away with: 'In which year was slavery abolished in the United States?' 'I'd hate to see the monarchy abolished.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is difficult to reach abandoned places such as small country villages.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It is difficult to reach remote places such as small country villages.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Abandoned = left for ever by the owners or occupiers: 'The field was littered with abandoned cars.' 'Some of these old abandoned coal mines could be dangerous.'Remote = far away and difficult to reach: 'The tribe lives in a small remote mountain village.' 'We have now managed to bring famine relief to people in even the most remote areas.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: These machines are destroying our ability of thinking.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: These machines are destroying our ability to think.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Ability to do sth (NOT of doing): 'Nobody doubts his ability to get the job done quickly.' 'We need someone with the ability to work under intense pressure.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I want to improve my ability of reading.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I want to improve my reading ability.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Reading/writing/teaching/acting ability: 'Her acting ability was recognized at a very early age.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I want to improve my ability of English.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I want to improve my ability in English.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Ability in a language or subject: 'Sarah has demonstrated considerable ability in both maths and chemistry.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One man is able to destroy the whole world.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One man is capable of destroying the whole world.
common_error_corrections.explanation: If someone is able to do something, they can do it and it is not unusual or surprising if they do it: 'The doctor said that after a few days I'd be able to get out of bed.' 'Will you be able to play on Saturday?'If someone is capable of (doing) something, they do not usually do it, but it is possible for them to do it if they want to: 'I'm sure he's quite capable of getting here on time, but he can't be bothered.' 'The power station is capable of generating enough electricity for the whole region.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There are so many places to visit in London that I'm not able to decide where to go.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There are so many places to visit in London that I can't decide where to go.
common_error_corrections.explanation: With verbs of perception (e.g. see, hear, smell) and verbs of the mind (e.g. understand, decide, remember), we usually use can, can't, etc: 'I can't hear you. Could you speak a bit louder, please?' 'I think I can smell something burning.' 'Having met her new boss, I can see why she doesn't like him.' Note also the phrase can't/couldn't stop doing something: 'The book was so fascinating I couldn't stop reading it.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We weren't able to stop laughing.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We couldn't stop laughing.
common_error_corrections.explanation: With verbs of perception (e.g. see, hear, smell) and verbs of the mind (e.g. understand, decide, remember), we usually use can, can't, etc: 'I can't hear you. Could you speak a bit louder, please?' 'I think I can smell something burning.' 'Having met her new boss, I can see why she doesn't like him.' Note also the phrase can't/couldn't stop doing something: 'The book was so fascinating I couldn't stop reading it.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In some countries you are not able to drink until you are 21.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In some countries you can't drink until you are 21.
common_error_corrections.explanation: For actions that are controlled by laws or rules, use can, can't, etc, or be (not) allowed to: 'Now that they are both sixteen, they can get married.' 'The goalkeeper can touch the ball, but nobody else can.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Technology has made them able to grow their own food.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Technology has enabled them to grow their own food.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Enable = make someone able to do something: 'This scheme is designed to enable young people to find work.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was about leaving when the telephone rang.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was about to leave when the telephone rang.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be about to do sth (NOT doing).Compare: 'I was just leaving when the telephone rang.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I am always delighted when I receive a letter from you. About the party on December 26th, I shall be very pleased to attend.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I am always delighted when I receive a letter from you. With regard to the party on December 26th, I shall be very pleased to attend.
common_error_corrections.explanation: About may be used to introduce a topic (or change of topic), but only in informal styles: 'About that book you asked for - I'll get you a copy when I go to London.'In other styles, use with regard to, regarding, as for, as regards or as far as ... is concerned: 'With regard to the matter of unemployment, I would like to add a few remarks to those of the previous speaker.' 'I regret to inform you that Language and Culture is out of print. As regards your second question, I suggest that you write to the British Museum.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: People usually sleep with the doors and windows closed. About public transport, the bus and train services are excellent.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: People usually sleep with the doors and windows closed. As for public transport, the bus and train services are excellent.
common_error_corrections.explanation: About may be used to introduce a topic (or change of topic), but only in informal styles: 'About that book you asked for - I'll get you a copy when I go to London.'In other styles, use with regard to, regarding, as for, as regards or as far as ... is concerned: 'With regard to the matter of unemployment, I would like to add a few remarks to those of the previous speaker.' 'I regret to inform you that Language and Culture is out of print. As regards your second question, I suggest that you write to the British Museum.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It all depends on how different the new country is from your own. About myself, I haven't experienced any culture shock but then this is my second trip to the States.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It all depends on how different the new country is from your own. In my own case, I haven't experienced any culture shock but then this is my second trip to the States.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To show that you are going to start talking about your own personal experience or situation, use in my own case or (especially in informal styles) as for me/myself: 'Many people have benefited from the operation. In my own case, I began to feel better immediately.' 'Most of my friends like school. As for me, I can't wait to leave.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Taking all the above into account, one could say that tourism does more harm than good.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Taking all the above arguments into account, one could say that tourism does more harm than good.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Instead of using the above as a loose reference to something mentioned earlier, make the reference more precise by using the above + noun (or the + noun + above): 'the above reasons', 'the statement above '.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He likes reading, above all novels.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He likes reading, especially novels.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Above all means 'most importantly': 'Get plenty of sleep, eat lots of good food, and above all try to relax.' 'There were many qualities that made him a great leader. Above all, he had charisma.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There were above a hundred people in the crowd.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There were over a hundred people in the crowd.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use above with numbers (unless referring to points on a scale): 'He is over eighty years of age.' 'I receive over twenty letters a day.' Compare 'Don't let the temperature get above thirty degrees.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: This year English is above all my most important subject.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: This year English is by far my most important subject.
common_error_corrections.explanation: With a superlative form ('the most important'), use by far: 'The riot was by far the most horrific scene I'd ever witnessed.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I like to stay at home on a Sunday, as I've said above.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I like to stay at home on a Sunday, as I've already said.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Above is used in formal writing to refer to something that has been mentioned earlier: 'From the above arguments it can be seen that supporters of the dam project fall into two camps.' In informal styles, this use of above is inappropriate.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: What do you think of the above suggestion?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: What do you think of my/this suggestion?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Above is used in formal writing to refer to something that has been mentioned earlier: 'From the above arguments it can be seen that supporters of the dam project fall into two camps.' In informal styles, this use of above is inappropriate.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Where would you like to go above all?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Where would you like to go most of all?
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'more than anywhere/anything/anyone else', use most of all or the most: 'What worries me most of all is that the car is not roadworthy.' 'The one I liked the most was too expensive.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I would be grateful if you would send it to the address above-mentioned.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I would be grateful if you would send it to the above-mentioned address.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Above-mentioned comes before the noun: 'the above-mentioned person', 'the above-mentioned company'.Note that above may be used before or after the noun: 'the above address', 'the address above'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Since I was small, I've always wanted to go to abroad.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Since I was small, I've always wanted to go abroad.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go/live/be abroad (WITHOUT to, at, in etc).The only preposition that is used before abroad is from: 'She came back from abroad saying how much she had missed her home and family.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I would like to continue my studies in abroad.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I would like to continue my studies abroad.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go/live/be abroad (WITHOUT to, at, in etc)The only preposition that is used before abroad is from: 'She came back from abroad saying how much she had missed her home and family.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's a pity that you were absent from the training session.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
It's a pity that you missed the training session.
It's a pity that you weren't at the training session.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be absent = not be present at something that you are officially supposed to attend: 'Her teacher wanted to know why she'd been absent.'Miss = not be present at something: 'She's missed a lot of classes this term because of illness.' 'I wouldn't miss Sandro's party for the world!' (= I really want to go to it).Be at = be present at something: 'John won't be at the meeting. He's had to fly to Rome on business.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is absolutely important that you see a doctor immediately.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
It is very important that you see a doctor immediately.
It is absolutely essential that you see a doctor immediately.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The company will not accept to buy new machines.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The company will not agree to buy new machines.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You accept someone's advice, opinion, or suggestion BUT you agree (= say you are willing) to do something. Compare: 'I accepted her suggestion and agreed to see the doctor that evening.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The driver did not accept me to get on the bus.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The driver did not allow me to get on the bus.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You allow/permit someone to do something, or let them do it: 'Many parents do not allow/permit their children to watch violent films.' 'Many parents do not let their children watch violent films.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We can't accept a motorway to be built through our town.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We can't allow a motorway to be built through our town.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You allow/permit someone to do something, or let them do it: 'Many parents do not allow/permit their children to watch violent films.' 'Many parents do not let their children watch violent films.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Computers give us an easier access to information.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Computers give us easier access to information.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Access is an uncountable noun: 'The entrance has been widened to provide easier access for disabled people.' 'They have no right to refuse us access to the files.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Her car was involved in a big accident.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Her car was involved in a serious accident.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A bad/dreadful/nasty/serious/fatal accident. (NOT big).

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Could you help me look for an accommodation?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Could you help me look for accommodation?
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English accommodation (= a place to stay or live in) is always uncountable: 'For the first year we stayed in rented accommodation.'In American English both accommodation and accommodations (plural) are used.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Accommodations in London are very expensive.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Accommodation in London is very expensive.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English accommodation (= a place to stay or live in) is always uncountable: 'For the first year we stayed in rented accommodation.'In American English both accommodation and accommodations (plural) are used.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: To accomplish world unity, we need peace.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: To achieve world unity, we need peace.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you accomplish something, you manage to do it or complete it, especially something that gives you satisfaction: 'She felt that she could accomplish more through journalism.' 'During his five years as President, he accomplished very little.'When you achieve something, you manage to do or obtain what you have planned to do or obtain, especially after a lot of effort: 'The company intends to achieve all these goals within the next five years.' 'By the age of twenty, she had already achieved her ambition.'Note that achieve is also used to mean 'accomplish': 'By the end of the course, you will feel that you've really achieved something.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A balanced diet is accomplished by eating many different kinds of food.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A balanced diet is achieved by eating many different kinds of food.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you accomplish something, you manage to do it or complete it, especially something that gives you satisfaction: 'She felt that she could accomplish more through journalism.' 'During his five years as President, he accomplished very little.'When you achieve something, you manage to do or obtain what you have planned to do or obtain, especially after a lot of effort: 'The company intends to achieve all these goals within the next five years.' 'By the age of twenty, she had already achieved her ambition.'Note that achieve is also used to mean 'accomplish': 'By the end of the course, you will feel that you've really achieved something.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: According to me, we should spend more money on education.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In my opinion, we should spend more money on education.
common_error_corrections.explanation: According to + the writer/Dr Owen/her teachers/them etc (NOT me/us): 'According to Charles Anderson, the government should pay closer attention to public opinion.'To introduce your own opinion, use in my/our opinion: 'In my opinion, he didn't deserve a prison sentence.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We also have to take into account that the schools are overcrowded.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We also have to take into account the fact that the schools are overcrowded.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Take into account + the fact + that -clause: 'They should take into account the fact that these archaeological treasures are extremely valuable.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I cannot give you the accurate date of my arrival yet.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I cannot give you the exact date of my arrival yet.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Accurate is mainly used (1) to describe something said or written that contains no errors: 'Her novels are always historically accurate.' 'These figures can't be accurate, surely.' (2) to describe something that produces no errors: 'Are you sure the bathroom scales are accurate?'When you mean 'correct and as detailed as possible', use exact: 'The exact time is three minutes to seven.' 'Do you remember his exact words?' 'They'll be arriving next week - on Friday at three, to be exact.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I am beginning to accustom to the British way of life.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I am beginning to get accustomed to the British way of life.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be/become/get/grow accustomed to sth: 'Within a few minutes, my eyes had grown accustomed to the dark.'Note that, apart from in formal styles, most people prefer be/become/get/grow used to: 'I am beginning to get used to the British way of life.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Where I come from, we are not accustomed to see so many things in the shops.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Where I come from, we are not accustomed to seeing so many things in the shops.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be accustomed to doing sth (NOT to do): 'He was accustomed to leading a life of luxury.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After the run, I had an ache in my legs.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: After the run, my legs were aching.
choices: I had an ache in my legs
common_error_corrections.explanation: Ache is usually used either as a verb or in compounds with tooth, ear, head, back, stomach: 'I did some weight training on Monday and my shoulders have been aching ever since.' 'That radio of yours is giving me a headache.'Compare: 'After the run, I had pains in my legs.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I am interested in the way people act towards each other.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I am interested in the way people behave towards each other.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about what someone does on a particular occasion, act and behave are interchangeable: 'Passengers who left the flight in Rhodes said that they had seen two men acting/behaving very suspiciously.'When you are talking generally about what someone does or what people do, use behave: 'You can't expect all babies to behave the same.' 'From the way he behaves, anyone would think that he doesn't get paid.'The noun act is usually used when you want to comment on a particular thing that someone has done: 'It was an act of great courage.' 'These cowardly terrorist acts bring death and suffering to the innocent.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is time that human beings learned how to act properly, without killing each other.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It is time that human beings learned how to behave properly, without killing each other.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about what someone does on a particular occasion, act and behave are interchangeable: 'Passengers who left the flight in Rhodes said that they had seen two men acting/behaving very suspiciously.'When you are talking generally about what someone does or what people do, use behave: 'You can't expect all babies to behave the same.' 'From the way he behaves, anyone would think that he doesn't get paid.'The noun act is usually used when you want to comment on a particular thing that someone has done: 'It was an act of great courage.' 'These cowardly terrorist acts bring death and suffering to the innocent.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He refused to accept responsibility for his acts.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He refused to accept responsibility for his actions.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The noun act is usually used when you want to comment on a particular thing that someone has done: 'It was an act of great courage.' 'These cowardly terrorist acts bring death and suffering to the innocent.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The actions that we do everyday are made easier by computers.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The things that we do everyday are made easier by computers.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do and action cannot be used together. Use do + things/something/anything etc: 'She's always doing things for charity.' 'Don't do anything that might upset them.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If someone has done a wrong action, he should be punished.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If someone has done something wrong, he should be punished.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do and action cannot be used together. Use do + things / something / anything etc: 'She's always doing things for charity.' 'Don't do anything that might upset them.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is difficult to forgive those responsible for actions of terrorism.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It is difficult to forgive those responsible for acts of terrorism.
common_error_corrections.explanation: An/the act of (doing) sth (NOT action): 'Such acts of violence will not be tolerated.' 'For some people, the very act of talking to a doctor can help them to feel better.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Blackmail is the action of trying to obtain money from someone by threatening to expose them.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Blackmail is the act of trying to obtain money from someone by threatening to expose them.
common_error_corrections.explanation: An/the act of (doing) sth (NOT action): 'Such acts of violence will not be tolerated.' 'For some people, the very act of talking to a doctor can help them to feel better.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Few people are aware that an urgent action is needed.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Few people are aware that urgent action is needed.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about the idea or process of doing something, action is uncountable: 'There is too much talk and not enough action.'In the phrase take action, action is always uncountable: 'This illegal trade will continue unless action is taken to stop it.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The government should take an action to reduce the birth rate.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The government should take action to reduce the birth rate.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about the idea or process of doing something, action is uncountable: 'There is too much talk and not enough action.'In the phrase take action, action is always uncountable: 'This illegal trade will continue unless action is taken to stop it.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We'd like to know more about the actual crisis (Not the economic problems of the past).
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We'd like to know more about the present crisis (Not the economic problems of the past).
common_error_corrections.explanation: Actual = real (as opposed what is believed, planned or expected): 'People think he is over fifty but his actual age is forty-eight.' 'Although buses are supposed to run every fifteen minutes, the actual waiting time can be up to an hour.'Present/current = happening or existing now: 'No one can drive that car in its present condition.' 'Her current boyfriend works for Shell.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My actual job involves a lot of administration.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My present job involves a lot of administration.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Actual = real (as opposed what is believed, planned or expected): 'People think he is over fifty but his actual age is forty-eight.' 'Although buses are supposed to run every fifteen minutes, the actual waiting time can be up to an hour.'Present/current = happening or existing now: 'No one can drive that car in its present condition.' 'Her current boyfriend works for Shell.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I never get bored by this city. Actually, each time I return I find something new to interest me.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I never get bored by this city. In fact, each time I return I find something new to interest me.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When actually means 'in fact', it is usually used to correct a misunderstanding: 'People think we've got lots of money, but actually we're quite poor.' 'I'm sorry to have kept you waiting.' - 'Well actually I've only just arrived.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We need to produce and export more than we do actually.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We need to produce and export more than we do at present.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'at the present time', use at present, at the moment or currently (NOT actually): 'At present the company is very short of staff.' 'At the moment I'm working part-time in a travel agency.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The other ingredients are then added into the mixture.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The other ingredients are then added to the mixture.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Add sth to sth (NOT into): 'They are demanding that a new clause be added to the contract which will give them a share of the profits.' 'When a prefix is added to a word, you make a new word.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One hour is not long enough to admire all the exhibits.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One hour is not long enough to see all the exhibits.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use admire when you just mean 'see' or 'look at'. Admire means 'look at someone or something with a strong feeling of pleasure'. This meaning of admire is found mainly in novels and tourist brochures: 'Come and admire the magnificence of the Niagara Falls.' 'Rupert was sitting outside on the verandah, admiring the many jewels in the night sky.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I enjoyed admiring all the old buildings.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I enjoyed looking at all the old buildings.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use admire when you just mean 'see' or 'look at'. Admire means 'look at someone or something with a strong feeling of pleasure'. This meaning of admire is found mainly in novels and tourist brochures: 'Come and admire the magnificence of the Niagara Falls.' 'Rupert was sitting outside on the verandah, admiring the many jewels in the night sky.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Although it was a sad film, I admired it very much.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Although it was a sad film, I enjoyed it very much.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use admire when you mean 'enjoy'. Admire means 'have a very high opinion of someone': 'I've always admired people who think for themselves.' 'Lewis was probably best known and admired for his work on medieval literature.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Everybody admired your talk because it was lively and interesting.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Everybody enjoyed your talk because it was lively and interesting.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use admire when you mean 'enjoy'. Admire means 'have a very high opinion of someone': 'I've always admired people who think for themselves.' 'Lewis was probably best known and admired for his work on medieval literature.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I adore meeting new people.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I like/enjoy/love meeting new people.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Adore usually expresses a very strong feeling: 'She adores her grandchildren and is always buying them presents.' 'The one singer I absolutely adore is Whitney Houston.' If you use adore to mean 'like/enjoy/love', you may sound insincere.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I adore reading too.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I like/enjoy/love reading too.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Adore usually expresses a very strong feeling: 'She adores her grandchildren and is always buying them presents.' 'The one singer I absolutely adore is Whitney Houston.' If you use adore to mean 'like / enjoy / love', you may sound insincere.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Although the film has its advantages, it also has a serious flaw.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Although the film has its merits/good points, it also has a serious flaw.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Advantage = something that puts you in a better position than other people: 'A healthier lifestyle is just one of the advantages of living in the country.' 'The main advantage of using word processors is the amount of time you save.'Merit = a good quality; a strength: 'The merits of the new health programme are gradually being recognized.' 'We should judge each application on its own merits.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Television provides many advantages.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Television provides many benefits.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Benefit = a good result which improves your life or situation: 'Belonging to a union has a number of important benefits.' 'It's over a month since I got back from holiday, but I still feel the benefit.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: What are the advantages with studying in the United States?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: What are the advantages of/in/to studying in the United States?
common_error_corrections.explanation: The advantage/s of (doing/having) sth: 'He described the advantages of living in the countryside.' 'The advantages of independence soon became clear.'There are (several/many etc) advantages to (doing/having) sth: 'There are advantages to working in a supermarket.' 'There are clear advantages to such an approach.' 'Are there any advantages in appointing coordinators?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There are many advantages with having your own computer.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There are many advantages to/in/of having your own computer.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The advantage/s in (doing/having) sth: 'He described the advantages in living in the countryside.' 'The advantages in independence soon became clear.'There are (several/many etc) advantages to (doing/having) sth: 'There are advantages to working in a supermarket.' 'There are clear advantages to such an approach.' 'Are there any advantages in appointing coordinators?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have just seen your advertisement about a Chinese cook.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have just seen your advertisement for a Chinese cook.
common_error_corrections.explanation: An advertisement for sb/sth: 'an advertisement for Heinz tomato soup'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I am writing in reply to your advertisement of a part-time sales assistant.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I am writing in reply to your advertisement for a part-time sales assistant.
common_error_corrections.explanation: An advertisement for sb/sth: 'an advertisement for Heinz tomato soup'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I adviced him to tell the police.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I advised him to tell the police.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Advice is a noun. Advise is a verb.

common_error_corrections.explanation: FINALLY · IN THE END · EVENTUALLY · AT LAST · AFTER ALL · AT THE ENDFinally and lastly are used (1) at the beginning of a sentence) to introduce the past point in a speech, reply, essay etc: ‘finally, I’d like to consider the economic arguments.’ ‘Lastly, I’d like to thank you all for coming and wish you a safe journey home.’ (2) to introduce the last action in a sequence of actions or the last thing in a list: ‘Finally, as soon as you hear a beep, press the start button.’ ‘She showed us the new dress, then the blouse, and lastly the shoes.Finally and eventually are used to show that something happens after a long time or delay: ‘When the bus finally arrived it was full up.’ ‘Eventually the baby stopped crying and we managed to get some sleep.’Eventually and in the end are used to introduce the result or outcome of something: ‘In the end United won by three goals to two.’ ‘It seems more and more likely that the human race will eventually destroy itself.’At last means ‘after a long period of waiting or trying to do something’: ‘I’m pleased to hear that you are out of hospital at last.’ Unlike eventually, at last is often used in connection with the present situation, and expresses a sense of relief: ‘I can’t believe that we’re actually getting on the plane at last.’ ‘Do you mean that you’ve really stopped smoking at last?’After all means ‘despite what was planned, expected or believed’: ‘We stayed at home after all and watched the match on television.’ ‘I’m sorry to hear that you won’t be coming to London after all.’ After all is also used to remind someone of a fact which they should consider: ‘I’m not surprised you’re tired. After all, you didn’t get any sleep last night.’ ‘Why are you so upset about losing? After all, it’s only a game.’At the end refers to the point where something finishes: ‘Their house is at the end of the road.’ ‘Do you remember what happens at the end of the film?’ Unlike in the end, at the end is usually followed by of: ‘at the end of the lesson/course/road/year’.

common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'continue to be alive', use the verb live: 'Her grandmother lived to a great age.' 'The baby was four months premature and was not expected to live.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He spent all the journey talking about accidents.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He spent the whole journey talking about accidents.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Before the singular form of a countable noun we usually use whole or entire: 'We spent the whole lesson singing songs.' 'The entire document will have to be rewritten.' Note that sometimes both all and whole/entire are possible: 'It rained the whole/all the afternoon.' In these cases, whole/entire provides greater emphasis and often express a feeling of surprise, disappointment, satisfaction etc: 'I read the whole book in just two evenings.'

In these cases, whole/entire provides greater emphasis and often express a feeling of surprise, disappointment, satisfaction etc: 'I read the whole book in just two evenings.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: People envy her because she is good at all.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nobody understands all.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I like all the kinds of music.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: All of the young couples need a home of their own.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I didn't like the meal and couldn't eat all.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They also allow to the prisoners to keep birds.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They also allow the prisoners to keep birds.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Allow sb to do sth (NOT to sb): 'The principal doesn't allow them to wear jewelry to school.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's not allowed to talk in the library.

You aren't allowed to talk in the library.
Talking in the library isn't allowed.
choices: Talking in the library isn't allowed
You aren't allowed to talk in the library
It's not allowed to talk in the library

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I almost have forgotten what she looks like.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have almost forgotten what she looks like.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The suitcase almost was too heavy to lift.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My job takes me almost to every part of the world.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Outside Japan, almost nobody speaks Japanese.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Outside Japan, hardly anybody speaks Japanese.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Instead of saying almost no / nobody / never etc, it is more usual to say hardly any / anybody / ever etc: 'It was so early that there was hardly any traffic.' 'I hardly ever go to the cinema nowadays.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She almost couldn't breathe.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She could hardly breathe.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Almost is used with a negative verb when something does actually happen although, at the time, there is a strong possibility that it will not happen: 'I was feeling so tired that I almost didn't come.' 'The traffic was so heavy that she almost didn't get here in time.'When you mean 'only a little' or 'only with great difficulty', use hardly: 'We hardly know each other.' 'She was so tired that she could hardly keep her eyes open.' 'I can hardly hear myself think.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was very alone at first but then I made some friends.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was very lonely at first but then I made some friends.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Alone = without other people around you: 'I've thought about getting married, but I prefer living alone.'Lonely = sad because you are alone and feel that nobody loves you or cares about you: 'I didn't know anyone in Boston and felt very lonely.' 'Sarah hated the long lonely days in the empty house.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Children learn a lot by doing things alone.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Children learn a lot by doing things on their own.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On your own = without anyone's help or supervision; independently: 'He built the car all on his own.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Walking along the city after dark is not a good idea.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Walking through the city after dark is not a good idea.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Along = (moving) next to the side of something long such as a road or river: 'We walked along the Thames as far as Hampton Court.'Through = from one side of an area to another: 'The road goes through all the major towns.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Next July I'm going back to Hong Kong. I booked the tickets already.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Next July I'm going back to Hong Kong. I've booked the tickets already.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Already is usually used with the present perfect tense (NOT the past tense): 'If he's already seen the film, he won't want to see it again.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Most of the food is cold already when you get it.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Most of the food is already cold when you get it.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The war is not over already.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The war is not over yet.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Instead of using not + already, use not + yet: 'We haven't been paid yet.' 'The plane hasn't landed yet.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The new shop has not been opened already.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The new shop has not been opened yet.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Instead of using not + already, use not + yet: 'We haven't been paid yet.' 'The plane hasn't landed yet.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We also would like to be given more fresh food.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We would also like to be given more fresh food.

common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The school also has a gymnasium.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Besides the nature society, there also is a music society.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He doesn't also recommend winter holidays.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He doesn't recommend winter holidays either.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Women are often better at negotiating than men. Also, they don't give up so easily.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Women are often better at negotiating than men. What's more, they don't give up so easily.

Moreover, it can be addictive.' Also is not wrong but does not have the same persuasive force.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We decided to make alternate arrangements in case the hotel was fully booked.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We decided to make alternative arrangements in case the hotel was fully booked.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English alternate and alternative have different meanings.Alternate = (1) happening in turn, first one then the other: 'alternate periods of sun and rain' (2) every second (day, week, etc): 'Our local football team plays at home on alternate Saturdays.'Alternative = that may be used instead of the usual one or the one you had planned to use: 'In view of the roadworks, motorists are advised to use an alternative route.'In American English alternate is used with the same meaning as alternative.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Afterwards, we played altogether monopoly.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Afterwards, we all played monopoly.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'each person or thing (in a group)', use all after the subject (NOT altogether): 'The flowers had all died.' 'The children were all tired and hungry.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After dinner, we watch altogether television.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: After dinner, we all watch television.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'each person or thing (in a group)', use all after the subject (NOT altogether): 'The flowers had all died.' 'The children were all tired and hungry.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Come and spend the weekend with me. I live always at the same address in Croydon.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My immediate ambition is to find somewhere to live.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Not many people manage to satisfy their ambitions.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The main purpose of the visit is to develop a closer relationship among the two countries.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The main purpose of the visit is to develop a closer relationship between the two countries.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Try to avoid arousing anger and fear among the children.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Try to avoid arousing anger and fear in the children.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He is very popular among the people of Japan.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Among these problems, the most serious is the excessive growth of the world's population.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was lucky and won a big amount of money.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Cream cheese contains a high amount of fat.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Cream cheese contains a large amount of fat.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The kitchen is very ample and has a window overlooking the garden.

'He was given ample opportunity to express his opinion.'Spacious = large, with a lot of space: 'These ideal holiday homes are extremely spacious and within walking distance of the sea.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I made a lot of new friends during my stay in England and amused myself a lot.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The last three years have been the most amusing years of my life.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Most visitors find the museum extremely amusing.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Something that holds your attention (and makes you want to know more) is interesting (NOT amusing): 'The most interesting thing about the dinosaurs is their sudden disappearance.' common_error_corrections.explanation: Before a word beginning with h, use a if the h is pronounced: 'a house', 'a half', 'a horrible day'. However, the use of an here is considered old-fashioned and most people use a.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There is a beautiful and old church in the centre of the town.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was surprised and anger that he did not apologize.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He'll have to learn how to control his anger.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The following day their father suddenly announced them that he was leaving.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The prison is full of crooks, thieves and assassins.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The prison is full of crooks, thieves and murderers.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Choosing the right word: GENERAL WORDS and EXACT WORDS.Some words have a general meaning, e.g. big, beautiful, good, say, make, kill. These words are useful, especially when you begin to learn English, because you can make use of them in a wide range of situations:a big meal, a big kitchen, a big mistake etc.For each general word, however, there is usually another word or phrase which comes closer to what you want to say, and which may also sound more natural in the context:a substantial meal, a spacious kitchen, a serious mistake etc.A major step towards fluency in English is getting to know plenty of exact words which can replace the more general words you have learned. Here are some words which can be used instead of the general word kill.Murder. To murder someone is to kill them deliberately and unlawfully: ‘The key witness was murdered before he could testify.’ A person who does this is a murderer.Massacre. Massacre is used when you talk about the deliberate killing of a large number of people, especially people who cannot defend themselves: ‘Whole native populations were massacred when the European settles arrived.’Slaughter. Slaughter is used when you talk about the deliberate killing of a large number of people, especially in a particularly cruel way: ‘Men ran through the village burning houses and slaughtering anyone that got in their way.’To slaughter an animal is to kill it for its meat, skin etc, or as part of a religious ceremony: ‘The children couldn’t understand why the cattle had to be slaughtered.’Execute. To execute someone (or put someone to death) is to kill someone as a punishment, according to the law: ‘King Charles I was executed on 30th January 1639.’Assassinate. To assassinate someone is to deliberately kill a very famous or important person such as a political leader: ‘President Lincoln was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth.’ A person who does this is an assassin.Commit suicide. To commit suicide (or take your own life) is to deliberately kill yourself: ‘Rather than be taken prisoner, they preferred to commit suicide.’Destroy. To destroy an animal (or have it put down/to sleep) is to kill in a way that does not cause pain, especially because it is sick or injured: ‘The cat had developed cancer and had to be destroyed.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In the beginning of the century people travelled from Britain to Egypt by sea.

common_error_corrections.explanation: FIRST · FIRST OF ALL · AT FIRST · IN/AT THE BEGINNING'First, firstly and first of all introduce the first item in a list or sequence. The next item is normally introduced by then or second/secondly: ‘First, open all the windows. Then turn off the gas and, if necessary, call an ambulance.’ ‘These new computers have several advantages. First of all, they’re faster than the older machines. Secondly, they’re far easier to use. And thirdly, they’re more reliable.’ At first. At first introduces a situation which is in contrast with a later situation (after a change has taken place): ‘At first I didn’t like the climate, but after two years I got used to it.’In the beginning. Like at first, in the beginning introduces a situation which is in contrast with a later situation. However, in the beginning is less common and suggests that the speaker is looking a long way back into the past to the period of time immediately after something began: ’In the beginning, when the first settlers arrived, law and order didn’t exist.’At the beginning refers to (1) the point in time when something begins: ’At the beginning of each lesson there is usually a revision exercise.’(2) the place where something begins: ’At the beginning of the novel there is a long description of the farm where Daniel was born and grew up.’ Unlike in the beginning, at the beginning is usually followed by of: ’at the beginning of the week/holiday/film’.

common_error_corrections.explanation: CONTAIN · INCLUDE · ENCLOSE · CONSIST OF · COMPRISE · BE COMPOSED OF · BE MADE UP OFUse contain (1) when you say what a box, bottle, bag etc has inside it. ‘The bag contained some old clothes.’(2) when you mention one or more of the things that something is made of or has in it: ‘Water contains hydrogen and oxygen.’ ‘The film contained a number of violent scenes.’If something includes another thing, it has it as one of its parts: ‘The holiday package includes a two-day cruise along the Rhine.’ ‘The price includes a small charge for postage and packing.’Use enclose when you tell someone what you are putting in the envelope or parcel that you are sending them: ‘I’m enclosing a copy of the book review that you asked for.’Consist of, comprise, be composed of, be made up of. When you mention all the parts that something has in it, use consist of / comprise / be composed of / be made up of: ‘The book consists of six chapters and a brief introduction.’ ‘The Earth’s atmosphere is composed mainly of nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide.’ ‘The house comprises two bedrooms, a bathroom, a kitchen, and a living room.’ ‘The US government is made up of two legislative assemblies.’ Note that you will sometimes see comprised of two separate packages. AmE take): ‘She’s probably upstairs having a bath.’Have (your) breakfast: ‘We usually have breakfast in the kitchen.’Have (your) dinner: ‘We had dinner and then went for a walk.’Have a drink: ‘I’ll collapse if I don’t have a drink soon.’Have (an) experience: ‘He has no experience of running a large company.’Have fun: ‘You can’t stop people from having fun.’Have a holiday: ‘It’s almost a year since we had a real holiday.’Have an interview: ‘I’ve had six interviews but no one has offered me a job.’Have a lesson: ‘Every morning we have three fifty-minute lessons.’Have (your) lunch: ‘Isn’t it about time we had lunch?’Have an operation: ‘Before I had the operation I could hardly walk.’Have a party: ‘On Saturday we’re having a party.’Have a picnic: ‘If it’s sunny we could have a picnic.’Have a shower (or esp. Just do your best.’Do (or cause) damage: ‘The storm did a lot of damage to the crops.’Do an exercise: ‘Have you done your exercises today?’Do an experiment: ‘To do this experiment, you’ll need two eggs.’Do (sb) good: ‘The holiday has done him a lot of good.’Do harm: ‘A scandal would do his reputation a lot of harm.’Do your homework: ‘Have you done your homework yet?’Do a job: ‘I’ve got one or two jobs to do this evening.’Do the/some shopping: ‘Jake has gone into town to do some shopping.’Do research: ‘We need to do a lot more research.’Do things: ‘We’ve done lots of different things today.’Do your training: ‘Where did you do your training?’Note also: do something/anything etc: ‘I can’t come now – I’m doing something.’ ‘He hasn’t done anything wrong.'The phrase that follows the best (+ noun) usually begins with in (NOT of): 'one of the best restaurants in London', 'the best team in the league', 'some of the best students in the class'.

When you want to know about the type of work that someone does, the usual questions are What do you do? What does she do for a living? etc ‘What does your father do?’ - ‘He’s a police inspector.’Occupation and job have similar meanings. However, occupation is far less common than job and is used mainly in formal and official styles: ‘Please give brief details of your employment history and present occupation.’ ‘People in manual occupations seem to suffer less from stress.’Post/position. The particular job that you have in a company or organization is your post or position: ‘She’s been appointed to the post of deputy principal.’ ‘He’s applied for the position of sales manager.’ Post and position are used mainly in formal styles and often refer to jobs which have a lot of responsibility.Career. common_error_corrections.explanation: Choosing the right word: GENERAL WORDS and EXACT WORDS.Some words have a general meaning, e.g. big, beautiful, good, say, make, kill. These words are useful, especially when you begin to learn English, because you can make use of them in a wide range of situations:A big meal, a big kitchen, a big mistake etc.For each general word, however, there is usually another word or phrase which comes closer to what you want to say, and which may also sound more natural in the context:A substantial meal, a spacious kitchen, a serious mistake etc.A major step towards fluency in English is getting to know plenty of exact words which can replace the more general words you have learned. Here are some words which can be used instead of the general word kill.Murder. To murder someone is to kill them deliberately and unlawfully: ‘The key witness was murdered before he could testify.’ A person who does this is a murderer.Massacre. Massacre is used when you talk about the deliberate killing of a large number of people, especially people who cannot defend themselves: ‘Whole native populations were massacred when the European settles arrived.’Slaughter. Slaughter is used when you talk about the deliberate killing of a large number of people, especially in a particularly cruel way: ‘Men ran through the village burning houses and slaughtering anyone that got in their way.’To slaughter an animal is to kill it for its meat, skin etc, or as part of a religious ceremony: ‘The children couldn’t understand why the cattle had to be slaughtered.’Execute. To execute someone (or put someone to death) is to kill someone as a punishment, according to the law: ‘King Charles I was executed on 30th January 1639.’Assassinate. To assassinate someone is to deliberately kill a very famous or important person such as a political leader: ‘President Lincoln was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth.’ A person who does this is an assassin.Commit suicide. To commit suicide (or take your own life) is to deliberately kill yourself: ‘Rather than be taken prisoner, they preferred to commit suicide.’Destroy. To destroy an animal (or have it put down/to sleep) is to kill in a way that does not cause pain, especially because it is sick or injured: ‘The cat had developed cancer and had to be destroyed.'

PRICE · COST · COSTS · CHARGE · FEE · RATE · RENTAL · FARE · RENTPrice. The price of something is the amount of money that you must pay in order to buy it: ‘I’m interested in the car, but the price is too high.’ ‘Food prices are relatively low at present.’Cost. The cost of something is the amount of money you must pay to buy, do, make or use it: ‘the cost of having the car repaired was £340.’The cost of living (fixed phrase) = the general amount that the people living in a particular area or country have to pay for necessary goods and services: ‘In urban areas the cost of living tends to be higher.’Costs. Your costs are the total amount of money you spend over a period of time in order to make or produce something, or continue an activity: ‘Our costs have doubled over the last five years as a result of the increase in oil prices.’Charge. A charge is the amount of money that you must pay for a service or to be allowed to use something: ‘The waiter explained that the bill included a 10% service charge.’ ‘There is also a small charge for delivery and installation.’If you do not have to pay for something, it is provided free of charge: ‘The company has offered to install the software free of charge.’Fee. A fee is 
1 a charge that you must pay to be allowed to do something: ‘Most art galleries charge an entrance fee.’ ‘Every new student has to pay a registration fee.’ 
2 (usually fees) a charge that you must pay for professional services such as those provided by doctors, lawyers, consultants, tutors, schools etc: ‘My parents couldn’t afford the school fees.’ ‘Last year alone, the company paid over $12 million in legal fees.’Rate. A rate is the amount of money that you have to pay for a service or for hiring something, especially one that is calculated on an hourly, weekly or monthly basis: ‘His hourly rate is £60.’ ‘For a five-star hotel, the rates are very reasonable.’Fare. A fare is the cost of a journey on a buss, train etc: ‘How much is the train fare from Toronto to Montreal?’ ‘She spends $20 per week on bus fares.’Rent is the money you pay every week or month to live in or use a places that doesn’t belong to you: ‘The rent is £500 inclusive of bills.’

common_error_corrections.explanation: Shout = speak in a very loud voice, especially because you want someone to hear you or because you are angry: 'There's no need to shout. I'm not deaf, you know.' 'The demonstrators marched through the streets shouting: No more war! No more war!'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When he reached the point in his story when his friends were arrested and tortured, he began to cry.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When he reached the point in his story when his friends were arrested and tortured, he began to weep.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Cry = the opposite of laugh: 'As the child was running towards me, she fell over and began to cry.' 'Babies always cry when they're hungry.'Weep = cry quietly, usually because of great sadness. This word is mainly used in literary styles: 'He knelt down by his son's small grave and wept.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I didn't know whether to cry or laugh.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I didn't know whether to laugh or cry.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Laugh or cry is a fixed phrase: 'His jokes are so awful that you don't know whether to laugh or cry.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The year in Boston taught me a lot about the American culture.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The year in Boston taught me a lot about American culture.
common_error_corrections.explanation: American culture, British culture, etc (WITHOUT the): 'The lecture this afternoon is on the history of French culture and institutions.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: As yet, nobody has found a cure to AIDS or cancer.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: As yet, nobody has found a cure for AIDS or cancer.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A cure for a disease: 'Is there a cure for tuberculosis?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The best cure of a cold is a good night's sleep.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The best cure for a cold is a good night's sleep.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A cure for a disease: 'Is there a cure for tuberculosis?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The wound took several weeks to cure.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The wound took several weeks to heal.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Cuts, wounds, injuries, etc heal: 'Cuts generally take longer to heal in humid climates.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was the doctor who cured your head injury.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was the doctor who treated your head injury.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Doctors and nurses treat an injury, disease, sick person, etc: 'Serious burns must be treated as soon as possible.' 'The usual way of treating malaria is to give the patient large doses of quinine.' 'Some hospitals refuse to treat people who don't have medical insurance.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Those who are seriously ill take a long time to cure.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Those who are seriously ill take a long time to recover.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When people who have been ill or injured return to their normal state of health, they recover or get better: 'Some of the flood victims are still recovering in hospital.' 'It takes a long time to recover from glandular fever.' 'Within a month of the heart attack, he had fully recovered.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was this film that first aroused my curiosity on Korean culture.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It was this film that first aroused my curiosity about Korean culture.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Curiosity about sth: 'The article was inspired by her curiosity about plants and medicine.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Several passers-by stopped to look at the strange bicycle from curiosity.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Several passers-by stopped to look at the strange bicycle out of curiosity.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You do or ask something out of curiosity (NOT from): 'Just out of curiosity, what made you decide to marry him after all?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was curious what she would look like.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was curious to know what she would look like.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Curious about/as to: 'I'm curious as to how he knows our address.'Curious to see/know etc: 'We're all curious to see what his new girlfriend is like.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'm very curious of the country and its inhabitants.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm very curious about the country and its inhabitants.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Curious about/as to: 'I'm curious as to how he knows our address.'Curious to see/know etc: 'We're all curious to see what his new girlfriend is like.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The current world encourages creativity.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The modern world encourages creativity.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Current = happening or existing now, but not likely to last for a long time: 'How long has she been going out with her current boyfriend?' 'The current boom in long-haul travel has led to fierce competition among the major airlines.'Modern = used or existing in the period of history that we live in now, and not in an earlier period: 'What do you think of modern architecture?' 'Even by modern standards, the pyramids are a remarkable piece of engineering.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We need to know current English, not the language of Shakespeare.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We need to know modern English, not the language of Shakespeare.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Current = happening or existing now, but not likely to last for a long time: 'How long has she been going out with her current boyfriend?' 'Even by modern standards, the pyramids are a remarkable piece of engineering.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I went there hoping to learn something about Indian culture and custom.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I went there hoping to learn something about Indian culture and customs.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You talk about a country's customs (WITH s ): 'In Hong Kong I learned a lot about Chinese customs.'CULTURE · CUSTOM · HABIT · MANNER · MANNERS · TRADITIONCulture (1) the customs, ideas, art, etc, which are found in a particular society or group and which make it different from another society or group: ‘Obeying your parents is a hallmark of Asian culture.’(2) the art, music, literature, etc, that is produced by a particular society: ‘Professor Jackson is an expert on ancient Greek culture:’ ‘The Samba is an important part of Brazilian culture.’Custom (1) something that the people in a particular society have done (in the same way) for a very long time, and which they consider to be normal or polite: ‘One of their customs is to point with the thumb, not with the index finger.’ ‘According to local custom, his body was carried to the top of a hill and cremated.’ ‘His knowledge of Malay and Indonesian customs proved invaluable when we got to Bali.’(2) something that a person usually does in a particular situation: ‘His custom of making detailed preparatory drawings makes him unique amongst 18th century British painters.’ ‘On Wednesday evening, as was his custom, he went for a long walk.’Habit something that a person does repeatedly, often without realizing it: ‘She has a lot of little habits that I find really irritating.’ ‘In California I got into the habit of eating with just a fork.’Manner (singular) the way someone behaves towards people: ‘She impressed us all with her business-like manner.’ ‘His cheerful face and polite manner have won him a lot of friends.’Manners (plural) the way someone behaves towards people, especially when compared with what is accepted as polite behaviour: ‘The child has very good manners and always says thank you.’Tradition a belief, custom or way of doing something that has been passed on from one generation to the next: ‘The tradition was that when a man died, all his wealth and possessions would go to the eldest son.’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He has a custom of coughing before he speaks.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He has a habit of coughing before he speaks.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's very difficult for people to change their customs.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It's very difficult for people to change their habits.
common_error_corrections.explanation:
CULTURE · CUSTOM · HABIT · MANNER · MANNERS · TRADITION

Culture (1) the customs, ideas, art, etc, which are found in a particular society or group and which make it different from another society or group: ‘Obeying your parents is a hallmark of Asian culture.’

(2) the art, music, literature, etc, that is produced by a particular society: ‘Professor Jackson is an expert on ancient Greek culture:’ ‘The Samba is an important part of Brazilian culture.’

Custom (1) something that the people in a particular society have done (in the same way) for a very long time, and which they consider to be normal or polite: ‘One of their customs is to point with the thumb, not with the index finger.’ ‘According to local custom, his body was carried to the top of a hill and cremated.’ ‘His knowledge of Malay and Indonesian customs proved invaluable when we got to Bali.’

(2) something that a person usually does in a particular situation: ‘His custom of making detailed preparatory drawings makes him unique amongst 18th century British painters.’ ‘On Wednesday evening, as was his custom, he went for a long walk.’

Habit something that a person does repeatedly, often without realizing it: ‘She has a lot of little habits that I find really irritating.’ ‘In California I got into the habit of eating with just a fork.’

Manner (singular) the way someone behaves towards people: ‘She impressed us all with her business-like manner.’ ‘His cheerful face and polite manner have won him a lot of friends.’

Manners (plural) the way someone behaves towards people, especially when compared with what is accepted as polite behaviour: ‘The child has very good manners and always says thank you.’

Tradition a belief, custom or way of doing something that has been passed on from one generation to the next: ‘The tradition was that when a man died, all his wealth and possessions would go to the eldest son.’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Will I have to pay custom duty?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Will I have to pay customs duty?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Customs (WITH s) = the place where your bags are examined when you enter a country: 'We got held up at the customs while they went through our suitcases.'Customs duty (WITH s) = taxes that you have to pay to bring certain goods into a country: 'The customs duty on electrical goods is twenty percent of the retail price.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He cut the strip of photographs and gave one to me.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He cut up the strip of photographs and gave one to me.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Cut up = cut something into small pieces: 'Two-year-olds can't eat meat unless you cut it up for them.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Then you cut the carrots and put them into the saucepan.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Then you cut up the carrots and put them into the saucepan.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Cut up = cut something into small pieces: 'Two-year-olds can't eat meat unless you cut it up for them.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I cut the picture and stuck it on a sheet of paper.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I cut out the picture and stuck it on a sheet of paper.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Cut out = remove a part of something by cutting all around it: 'Each child had to draw a face and then cut it out.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: To build the motorway, they will have to cut a lot of trees.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: To build the motorway, they will have to cut down a lot of trees.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Cut down = make something tall (such as a tree) fall down by cutting through it close to the ground: 'All the elms were diseased and had to be cut down.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In the summer I cut my hair very short.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In the summer I have my hair cut very short.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Have/get your hair cut: 'When was the last time you had your hair cut?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: All the cutleries are in the top drawer.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: All the cutlery is in the top drawer.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Cutlery (= knives, forks, spoons etc) is an uncountable noun: 'You'll find some clean cutlery in the top drawer.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The fire caused a lot of damages.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The fire caused a lot of damage.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In its usual meaning, damage is an uncountable noun: 'The insurance company will pay for any damage.' 'The ceiling had suffered a great deal of damage.'Damages (plural noun) = a sum of money that someone is awarded in a court of law: 'She was awarded $3000 in damages.' 'She claimed damages of £2000 for wrongful dismissal.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The car crashed into a tree and suffered a severe damage.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The car crashed into a tree and suffered severe damage.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In its usual meaning, damage is an uncountable noun: 'The insurance company will pay for any damage.' 'The ceiling had suffered a great deal of damage.'Damages (plural noun) = a sum of money that someone is awarded in a court of law: 'She was awarded $3000 in damages.' 'She claimed damages of £2000 for wrongful dismissal.'

common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: During the protests, some students were killed and others were seriously injured/wounded.
