common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The summer in Japan is very hot and damp.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The summer in Japan is very hot and humid.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Damp = slightly wet, especially in a cold and unpleasant way: 'Our hotel room felt cold and damp.' 'On damp days, we have to dry the washing indoors.'Humid = warm and full of water vapour: 'The air in tropical forests is extremely humid.' 'I didn't expect Singapore to be so humid.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There were lots of young boys and girls dancing pop music.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There were lots of young boys and girls dancing to pop music.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Dance to a particular type/piece of music: 'What type of music do you prefer dancing to?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Then we danced with the music of 'Grease'.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Then we danced to the music of 'Grease'.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Dance to a particular type/piece of music: 'What type of music do you prefer dancing to?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I dare to say that the book is worth reading.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I daresay that the book is worth reading.
common_error_corrections.explanation: I daresay (also written I dare say) is a fixed phrase: 'I dare say that we'll be hearing from them again.' 'The team will put up a good performance, I daresay, but I don't think they'll win.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: 'How dare you to come in without knocking!' he shouted.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: 'How dare you come in without knocking!' he shouted.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When dare comes in front of the subject, use an infinitive WITHOUT to: 'How dare you say such a thing!' 'Dare I mention it to her? She'll be furious.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He dares to die rather than break his promise.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He is prepared to die rather than break his promise.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Dare (= have enough courage) is used mainly in negative sentences and questions: 'I wouldn't dare to take the car without permission.' 'She stood at the edge of the cliff, not daring to look down.'In affirmative sentences, use be ready/prepared/willing: 'Some people are prepared to do anything for money.' 'Despite the threat on his life, he's ready to testify.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I didn't enjoy the drink but I dared to try it again.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I didn't enjoy the drink but I was ready to try it again.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Dare (= have enough courage) is used mainly in negative sentences and questions: 'I wouldn't dare to take the car without permission.' 'She stood at the edge of the cliff, not daring to look down.'In affirmative sentences, use be ready/prepared/willing: 'Some people are prepared to do anything for money.' 'Despite the threat on his life, he's ready to testify.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: His mother thinks that somebody must have dared him steal the bicycle.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: His mother thinks that somebody must have dared him to steal the bicycle.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Dare sb to do sth: 'I dare you to drink it.' 'They dared me to do it again.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I daren't to ask her for any more money.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I daren't ask her for any more money.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Daren't do sth (WITHOUT to): 'I daren't tell George what happened or he'll be furious.'Compare: 'I don't dare tell/to tell George what happened ... .'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Soon it began to become dark and it was time to go home.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Soon it began to get dark and it was time to go home.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To refer to the time in the evening or at night when the daylight disappears, use get dark or (in formal styles) grow dark: 'In the winter it gets dark by five o'clock.' 'It began to grow dark and so we headed back to the shore.' To describe what happens when all the lights in a room, building, etc suddenly go out, use go dark or (especially in formal styles) be plunged into darkness: 'During the last storm the whole town was plunged into darkness.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The last candle went out and everything became dark.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The last candle went out and everything went dark.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To refer to the time in the evening or at night when the daylight disappears, use get dark or (in formal styles) grow dark: 'In the winter it gets dark by five o'clock.' 'It began to grow dark and so we headed back to the shore.' To describe what happens when all the lights in a room, building, etc suddenly go out, use go dark or (especially in formal styles) be plunged into darkness: 'During the last storm the whole town was plunged into darkness.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Doctors read these journals so as not to become out of date.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Doctors read these journals so as to keep up to date.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Out of date (before a noun out-of-date) is used in connection with information, ideas, knowledge, technology etc (NOT people): 'A significant proportion of what children are studying at school will be out of date within the space of a few years.'If you always have the latest information about something, you keep up to date (with developments) or keep abreast (of developments): 'Lecturers are expected to keep abreast of developments in their subject areas.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: On the date of your wedding, I shall be in England.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: On the day of your wedding, I shall be in England.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On the day of sth (NOT on the date of): 'On the day of my departure, I woke up very early.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have to pay the rent on the first date of the month.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have to pay the rent on the first day of the month.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On the day of sth (NOT on the date of): 'On the day of my departure, I woke up very early.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have an interview at the same date.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have an interview on the same date/on the same day.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On a specific date/day (NOT at/in): 'I'm afraid we have no rooms available on that date.'Note, however, the phrases at a later date and at some future date: 'The rest of the money can be paid at a later date.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Up to date, they still haven't answered our letter.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: To date, they still haven't answered our letter.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To date or up to/until now (NOT up to date): 'To date there are no signs that the situation is likely to improve.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My father is dead when I was still a baby.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My father died when I was still a baby.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Dead is an adjective and describes a state: 'I can't tell whether that plant is dead or alive.' A menu is a list of all the things that you can order in a restaurant: ‘I tried to read the menu but it was all in French.’ ‘Is there any fish on the menu?’Course. For machines and devices that are powered by electricity but do have transistors, microchips, valves, etc, use electric (NOT electronic): ‘an electric guitar’, ‘an electric train set’, ‘an electric razor’.Electrical means associated with electricity: ‘electrical systems’, ‘a course in electrical engineering’, ‘an electrical engineer’. 'To end the meal we had some coffee and an ice-cream.'FINALLY · IN THE END · EVENTUALLY · AT LAST · AFTER ALL · AT THE ENDFinally and lastly are used (1) at the beginning of a sentence) to introduce the past point in a speech, reply, essay etc: ‘finally, I’d like to consider the economic arguments.’ ‘Lastly, I’d like to thank you all for coming and wish you a safe journey home.’ (2) to introduce the last action in a sequence of actions or the last thing in a list: ‘Finally, as soon as you hear a beep, press the start button.’ ‘She showed us the new dress, then the blouse, and lastly the shoes.Finally and eventually are used to show that something happens after a long time or delay: ‘When the bus finally arrived it was full up.’ ‘Eventually the baby stopped crying and we managed to get some sleep.’Eventually and in the end are used to introduce the result or outcome of something: ‘In the end United won by three goals to two.’ ‘It seems more and more likely that the human race will eventually destroy itself.’At last means ‘after a long period of waiting or trying to do something’: ‘I’m pleased to hear that you are out of hospital at last.’ Unlike eventually, at last is often used in connection with the present situation, and expresses a sense of relief: ‘I can’t believe that we’re actually getting on the plane at last.’ ‘Do you mean that you’ve really stopped smoking at last?’After all means ‘despite what was planned, expected or believed’: ‘We stayed at home after all and watched the match on television.’ ‘I’m sorry to hear that you won’t be coming to London after all.’ After all is also used to remind someone of a fact which they should consider: ‘I’m not surprised you’re tired. common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Unfortunately, I didn't pass in the exam.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Pass/fail an examination (WITHOUT in): 'She passed all six examinations at the first attempt.'Compare: 'I passed the written paper but failed (on) the oral test.' 'She did well in chemistry but failed (in) maths.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Medicine is a good example for something that we pass from one generation to the next.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Medicine is a good example of something that we pass from one generation to the next.
common_error_corrections.explanation: An example of sth (NOT for): 'He is a classic example of a man who cannot control his ambition.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A manager is supposed to give a good example.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A manager is supposed to set a good example.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Set an example or set a good example = behave correctly so that the people who copy you will behave correctly: 'The school captain is expected to set a good example.'Compare: 'Instead of trying to explain the theory, he just gave us a few good examples.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Except smoke and traffic fumes, there are several other types of pollution.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Besides smoke and traffic fumes, there are several other types of pollution.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Except = not including; but not: 'She eats everything except fish.'Besides = in addition to: 'Besides football, he also plays tennis and badminton.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The old lady never spoke to anyone except someone came to visit her.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
The old lady never spoke to anyone unless someone came to visit her.
The old lady never spoke to anyone except when someone came to visit her.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Except (a preposition) cannot be followed by a clause that has a finite verb ('came'). Use unless (a conjunction) or except when, except while, except if, except that: 'Americans are just like any other people in the world, except that they are more tolerant.' 'He tends to ignore me except when he needs something.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I had never really spoken to him except saying hello.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I had never really spoken to him except to say hello.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about purpose, use except + to-v: 'I rarely go the market, except to buy vegetables.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They want nothing except seeing that the children are happy.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They want nothing except to see that the children are happy.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The choice of verb form after except is sometimes determined by a word that comes earlier in the sentence, e.g. want + to-v, good at + v-ing.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My brother is good at everything except to wash the dishes.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My brother is good at everything except washing the dishes.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The choice of verb form after except is sometimes determined by a word that comes earlier in the sentence, e.g. want + to-v, good at + v-ing.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In their free time they do nothing except going from one cafeteria to another.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In their free time they do nothing except go from one cafeteria to another.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do (anything/nothing/what you like etc) + except + bare infinitive: 'There was nothing I could do except sit and wait.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She was willing to do anything except to tell me her name.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She was willing to do anything except tell me her name.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do (anything/nothing/what you like etc) + except + bare infinitive: 'There was nothing I could do except sit and wait.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Every major city keeps changing and Lisbon is not an exception.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Every major city keeps changing and Lisbon is no exception.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be no exception is a fixed phrase: 'I never go out on Sundays, and this Sunday is no exception.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Is it possible to exchange the camera with a new one?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Is it possible to exchange the camera for a new one?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Exchange sth for sth (NOT with): 'The government is issuing coupons that can be exchanged for food.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is wonderful to be in London at last. I feel so exciting.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It is wonderful to be in London at last. I feel so excited.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Excuse me. I didn't know that you wanted to speak to me.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm sorry. I didn't know that you wanted to speak to me.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use excuse me (1) when you interrupt someone (2) when you are trying to get past someone (3) when you speak to someone you don't know: 'Excuse me but there's a long distance phone call for you.' 'Excuse me. Do you happen to know the way to the station?'To apologize to someone, use I'm sorry (or just sorry): 'I'm terribly sorry. I forgot we'd arranged a meeting.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Excuse me. I didn't mean to hurt you.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm sorry. I didn't mean to hurt you.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use excuse me (1) when you interrupt someone (2) when you are trying to get past someone (3) when you speak to someone you don't know: 'Excuse me but there's a long distance phone call for you.' 'Excuse me. Do you happen to know the way to the station?'To apologize to someone, use I'm sorry (or just sorry): 'I'm terribly sorry. I forgot we'd arranged a meeting.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When he got back home he excused himself and promised that he would never run away again.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When he got back home he apologized and promised that he would never run away again.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Excuse oneself = give a reason for one's actions: 'She excused herself from the meeting, saying that she was not feeling well.'Apologize = say you are sorry for (doing) something: 'The bank wrote to apologize for overcharging me.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He was sorry that he had lied to her and asked her to excuse him.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He was sorry that he had lied to her and asked her to forgive him.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Excuse is used only for minor faults and offences: 'I hope you'll excuse my untidy handwriting. I am trying to write this letter on a train.'Forgive is used for all faults and offences, both minor and major: 'I don't think he'll ever forgive me for calling off the wedding.' 'Don't forget her birthday or she'll never forgive you.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Before breakfast I do exercise and then have a shower.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Before breakfast I do some exercises and then have a shower.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Exercise (countable noun)= a movement or set of movements that you do regularly to keep or make (a part of) your body strong and healthy: 'These exercises will help to develop your calf muscles.' 'Sometimes he forgets to do his exercises.'Exercise (uncountable noun) = physical activity such as walking, swimming etc: 'The doctor says I don't get enough exercise.'Exercise (verb) = walk, jog, swim etc to stay healthy: 'Just because you're on a diet, it doesn't mean that you don't need to exercise.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I advise you to take as many exercises as you can.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
I advise you to take as much exercise as you can.
I advise you to exercise as much as you can.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Exercise (countable noun)= a movement or set of movements that you do regularly to keep or make (a part of) your body strong and healthy: 'These exercises will help to develop your calf muscles.' common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Make sure that you eat properly and don't forget to do your exercises.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You will never be able to speak fluently unless you do exercise.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You will never be able to speak fluently unless you practise.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Practise = do something regularly in order to develop a skill: 'Your driving will never improve if you don't practise.' 'If we're planning to go to Montreal next summer, I'll have to practise my French.' 'Whenever I start practising the violin, everyone leaves the room.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: An exhausting investigation finally revealed the cause of the accident.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: An exhaustive investigation finally revealed the cause of the accident.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Exhausting = causing tiredness: 'Pushing the car uphill was exhausting.'Exhaustive = so thorough or complete that not even the smallest detail or possibility is missed: 'Following exhaustive inquiries, the police are at last able to issue a description of the suspects.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The problem of hunger has been existing for centuries.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The problem of hunger has existed for centuries.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'm doing the course to expand my job opportunities.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm doing the course to increase my job opportunities.
common_error_corrections.explanation:
Expand = become (or make something become) larger in size, area or activity: 'Metals expand when they are heated.' 'Within three years this small business had expanded into a chain of department stores.' 
Increase = become (or make something become) larger in number, amount, cost, etc: 'Sales of new cars increased from 1.2 million in 1993 to 1.8 million in 1994.' 'By the year 2020 the government aims to increase the number of secondary schools by 50%.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The epidemic began to expand rapidly.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The epidemic began to spread rapidly.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about a disease, fire, war, social problem, feeling, etc, use spread: 'The army was called in to stop the riots from spreading.' 'Dissatisfaction with the present government seems to be spreading.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The newspapers are not allowed to expand political ideas.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The newspapers are not allowed to spread political ideas.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about news, information, ideas, etc, use spread: 'Within hours the news of the bank's collapse had spread all over the world.' 'I hope you haven't been spreading rumours.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After a few minutes he stopped speaking and expected their reaction.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: After a few minutes he stopped speaking and waited for their reaction.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use expect when you are talking about what someone thinks: 'We expected that the hotels in London would be very expensive, and we were right.' 'No one expected the President to resign.'Use wait for when you are talking about what someone does: 'How long do you usually have to wait for a bus?' 'I sat down and waited for my name to be called.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She was standing by the reception desk, expecting a taxi.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She was standing by the reception desk, waiting for a taxi.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use expect when you are talking about what someone thinks: 'We expected that the hotels in London would be very expensive, and we were right.' 'I sat down and waited for my name to be called.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I expect that you will be able to come to the party.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I hope that you will be able to come to the party.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use expect when you have a reason for thinking that something is going to happen: 'Her husband doesn't like travelling so I expect she'll come on her own.'Use hope to express a wish: 'I hope you have a safe journey.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I expect your visit and hope that you will be writing soon with the details.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm looking forward to your visit and hope that you will be writing soon with the details.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To say that you feel happy or excited about a future event, use look forward to: 'I'm really looking forward to this trip to Japan.' 'I look forward to meeting you at the Frankfurt Book Fair.'Note that look forward to (NOT expect) is often used at the end of a letter: 'I look forward to hearing from you.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You can expect that you won't be put in the same class as Helga.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You can't expect to be put in the same class as Helga.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Prices in Britain are not as expensive as in Japan.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Prices in Britain are not as high as in Japan.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The disadvantage is that the cost is very expensive.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The disadvantage is that the cost is very high.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Have no/little/some/considerable etc experience of (doing) sth:'Do you have any previous experience of looking after children?'

common_error_corrections.explanation: PRICE · COST · COSTS · CHARGE · FEE · RATE · RENTAL · FARE · RENTPrice. The price of something is the amount of money that you must pay in order to buy it: ‘I’m interested in the car, but the price is too high.’ ‘Food prices are relatively low at present.’Cost. The cost of something is the amount of money you must pay to buy, do, make or use it: ‘the cost of having the car repaired was £340.’The cost of living (fixed phrase) = the general amount that the people living in a particular area or country have to pay for necessary goods and services: ‘In urban areas the cost of living tends to be higher.’Costs. Your costs are the total amount of money you spend over a period of time in order to make or produce something, or continue an activity: ‘Our costs have doubled over the last five years as a result of the increase in oil prices.’Charge. A charge is the amount of money that you must pay for a service or to be allowed to use something: ‘The waiter explained that the bill included a 10% service charge.’ ‘There is also a small charge for delivery and installation.’If you do not have to pay for something, it is provided free of charge: ‘The company has offered to install the software free of charge.’Fee. A fee is 1 a charge that you must pay to be allowed to do something: ‘Most art galleries charge an entrance fee.’ ‘Every new student has to pay a registration fee.’ 2 (usually fees) a charge that you must pay for professional services such as those provided by doctors, lawyers, consultants, tutors, schools etc: ‘My parents couldn’t afford the school fees.’ ‘Last year alone, the company paid over $12 million in legal fees.’Rate. A rate is the amount of money that you have to pay for a service or for hiring something, especially one that is calculated on an hourly, weekly or monthly basis: ‘His hourly rate is £60.’ ‘For a five-star hotel, the rates are very reasonable.’Fare. A fare is the cost of a journey on a buss, train etc: ‘How much is the train fare from Toronto to Montreal?’ ‘She spends $20 per week on bus fares.’Rent is the money you pay every week or month to live in or use a places that doesn’t belong to you: ‘The rent is £500 inclusive of bills.’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She says that she feels herself trapped in the job.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She says that she feels trapped in the job.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The meeting provided a good opportunity for her to express her feeling.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The meeting provided a good opportunity for her to express her feelings.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Feelings (plural) = what you think or feel about something: 'My own feelings are that the marriage won't last more than a year.' 'Why does he always try to hide his feelings?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: As it got colder, my fingers lost feeling.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: As it got colder, my fingers went numb.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go numb = (of a part of your body) lose the ability to feel anything: 'While we were waiting for my jaw to go numb, the dentist told me about his holiday.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In front of them was a six-feet wall.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In front of them was a six-foot wall.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Using numbersDay, month, minute, mile, kilo etc are always SINGULAR when used (with a number) immediately before a noun: ‘a six-minute wait’, ‘a ten-second silence’, ‘a five-mile race’.My travel agent had arranged a 6-day coach tour.The company provides a three-month training course.Compare: ‘We waited for thirty minutes: ‘We had a thirty-minute wait.’When you say 100, 1000 etc, or write these numbers in words, use a hundred, a thousand (WITH a):The palace was build a thousand years ago.Compare: ‘The palace was built 1000 years ago.’For emphasis or to be exact, it is possible to use one instead of a:I am one hundred percent against the idea.After a/one/five/twelve etc, the words hundred, thousand, etc are always SINGULAR and are NOT followed by of:Five hundred children are born in the city every day.More than three thousand people were there.Similarly, of is NOT used after 100, 250, 3000 etc:If you kill 200 whales a year, they will soon disappear.Hundreds (of), thousands (of) etc are used only when you give a general idea of how many or how much: ‘There were hundreds of stars in the sky.’ ‘They’ve spent thousands (of pounds) on improvements to the house.’Use and between hundred and the next number. (In American English, and is often omitted, especially in formal styles.)BrE The club has about a hundred and thirty members.AmE The club has about a hundred (and) thirty members.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It shouldn't take more than ten minutes by feet to reach the underground.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It shouldn't take more than ten minutes on foot to reach the underground.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: That afternoon my fellows and I were at a swimming pool where there was a party going on.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: That afternoon my friends and I were at a swimming pool where there was a party going on.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Fellow = (informal) a man or person: 'The new manager seems a pleasant enough sort of fellow.'Your fellow students/workers = the people that you study or work with: 'I soon got to know my fellow students and made one or two good friends.'Friend = a person that you like and enjoy being with: 'I'm having lunch with a friend of mine.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My boss started to shout at me in front of all my fellows.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My boss started to shout at me in front of all my workmates.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To refer to someone you know because you work at the same place, use workmate or (especially of people in professional jobs) colleague: 'The police are questioning the missing woman's relatives and workmates.''I'd like you to meet a colleague of mine, Jean Armstrong.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Most females want to continue their careers after marriage.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Most women want to continue their careers after marriage.

'The female butterfly does not require additional salts.'Female is sometimes used to refer to a woman or girl, but many people find this use of the word offensive.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In 1992 she won the female marathon in Athens.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In 1992 she won the women's marathon in Athens.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Female is used mainly in scientific or technical styles: 'The male birds are usually more colourful than the females.' 'The female butterfly does not require additional salts.'Female is sometimes used to refer to a woman or girl, but many people find this use of the word offensive.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She has already packed all her belongings and I just have to fetch them to her new flat.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She has already packed all her belongings and I just have to take them to her new flat.
common_error_corrections.explanation: BRING · TAKE · LEAD · SEND · FETCH · CARRY · COLLECT · PICK UPBring means ‘come with sb/sth’ (NOT ‘go’): ‘Could you bring me a glass of water, please?’ ‘I’ll see you tomorrow at the club, and remember to bring your tennis racket!’Take means ‘go with sb/sth’ (NOT ‘come’): ‘You take the shopping indoors and I’ll put the car away.’ ‘When I go on holiday, I like to take a good book with me.’You usually take someone home, to school or to a cinema/restaurant/airport etc (NOT bring / lead / send / carry): ‘Lucy took us to Stratford to see a play.’ ‘If you need a lift to the station, as Peter to take you.’Lead. If you lead someone to a place, you guide them there by walking in front of them, holding them by the arm, etc: ‘Some blind people like to be led across the road.’ ‘The children led me through the wood to their secret hiding place.’Send. If you send a person somewhere, you tell them to go there. You do not go with them: ‘My company sends one of us to Singapore every six months.’Fetch. If you fetch something, you go the place where it is and come back with it: ‘We waited at reception while the porter fetched our luggage.’Carry. If you go somewhere with something in your hands, in your arms, on your back etc, you carry it: ‘She carried her chair into the garden and sat in the sun.’ ‘In some countries women carry their babies on their backs.’Collect / fetch. If you collect or fetch someone (from somewhere), you go there and bring them back with you: ‘I have to collect the children from school at 4 o’clock.’Pick up. If you pick up someone (at a place), you go to the place where they are waiting, usually in a car or other vehicle, and then take them somewhere: ‘I’ll pick you up at your house just after seven. That gives us half an hour go get to the stadium.’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'll come and fetch you at the airport.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
I'll come and fetch you from the airport.
I'll come and collect you from the airport.
I'll come and pick you up at the airport.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'd caught a cold and had a high fever.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'd caught a cold and had a high temperature.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When someone feels rather ill and their body is hotter than usual, they have a (high) temperature: 'I feel as if I've got a temperature.' 'She's in bed with a high temperature.'A fever usually refers to a (dangerously) high body temperature, or the disease that produces this: 'In the steaming jungle he had contracted a fever.' 'It seemed as if the fever would shake him to pieces.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: With the few money he had been given, he bought an apple and some cheese.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: With the little money he had been given, he bought an apple and some cheese.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Few is used with plural countable nouns: 'very few cars'.Little is used with uncountable nouns: 'very little traffic'.Compare: 'He had very little money, just a few coins.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Few minutes later the sales manager arrived.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A few minutes later the sales manager arrived.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A few = not many: 'I saw her just a few days ago.'Few = hardly any: 'Few people die of smallpox nowadays.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They spent the whole night fighting against the fire.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They spent the whole night fighting the fire.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about an event or something that lasts only a short time, use fight sb/sth (WITHOUT against): 'He said he would fight anyone who tried to stop him.' 'The best way to fight a cold is to get plenty of sleep.'You can use either fight sb/sth or fight against sb/sth when you are talking about a long struggle to overcome things such as poverty, disease, injustice or oppression: 'The ANC has spent half a century fighting (against) racism.' 'The group was founded in 1983 to fight (against) the military regime.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Why were the boys fighting against each other?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Why were the boys fighting each other?
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about an event or something that lasts only a short time, use fight sb/sth (WITHOUT against): 'He said he would fight anyone who tried to stop him.' common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My shoes were filled with water so I took them off.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My shoes were full of water so I took them off.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be filled with = containing so many or so much that there is no empty space left: 'The first drawer was filled with neat piles of shirts.' 'The front page is filled with the most important news items.'Be full of = (1) containing a large number or amount: 'The kitchen was full of flies.' 'The essay was full of mistakes.' (2) be filled with: 'The kettle was full of boiling water.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The eight o'clock train is usually filled with office workers.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The eight o'clock train is usually full of office workers.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be filled with = containing so many or so much that there is no empty space left: 'The first drawer was filled with neat piles of shirts.' 'The front page is filled with the most important news items.'Be full of = (1) containing a large number or amount: 'The kitchen was full of flies.' 'The essay was full of mistakes.' (2) be filled with: 'The kettle was full of boiling water.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You'll have to fill an application form.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You'll have to fill in an application form.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Fill in/out a form, coupon etc: 'To open a new account, you have to fill in an application form.' 'Remember to fill out the counterfoil.'Fill in an empty space on a form, coupon etc: 'Just fill in Section A.'Fill in details on a form: 'Fill in your name and address and then sign the form at the bottom.'Note that fill out is more common in American English.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was difficult to understand people for a long time but finally I got used to their accent.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It was difficult to understand people for a long time but eventually I got used to their accent.
common_error_corrections.explanation: FINALLY · IN THE END · EVENTUALLY · AT LAST · AFTER ALL · AT THE ENDFinally and lastly are used (1) at the beginning of a sentence) to introduce the past point in a speech, reply, essay etc: ‘finally, I’d like to consider the economic arguments.’ ‘Lastly, I’d like to thank you all for coming and wish you a safe journey home.’ (2) to introduce the last action in a sequence of actions or the last thing in a list: ‘Finally, as soon as you hear a beep, press the start button.’ ‘She showed us the new dress, then the blouse, and lastly the shoes.Finally and eventually are used to show that something happens after a long time or delay: ‘When the bus finally arrived it was full up.’ ‘Eventually the baby stopped crying and we managed to get some sleep.’Eventually and in the end are used to introduce the result or outcome of something: ‘In the end United won by three goals to two.’ ‘It seems more and more likely that the human race will eventually destroy itself.’At last means ‘after a long period of waiting or trying to do something’: ‘I’m pleased to hear that you are out of hospital at last.’ Unlike eventually, at last is often used in connection with the present situation, and expresses a sense of relief: ‘I can’t believe that we’re actually getting on the plane at last.’ ‘Do you mean that you’ve really stopped smoking at last?’After all means ‘despite what was planned, expected or believed’: ‘We stayed at home after all and watched the match on television.’ ‘I’m sorry to hear that you won’t be coming to London after all.’ After all is also used to remind someone of a fact which they should consider: ‘I’m not surprised you’re tired. After all, you didn’t get any sleep last night.’ ‘Why are you so upset about losing? After all, it’s only a game.’At the end refers to the point where something finishes: ‘Their house is at the end of the road.’ ‘Do you remember what happens at the end of the film?’ Unlike in the end, at the end is usually followed by of: ‘at the end of the lesson/course/road/year’.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'd like to find why nobody likes me.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'd like to find out why nobody likes me.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Find = discover something by chance or by looking for it: 'Did you ever find the sunglasses you lost?' 'I can't find my comb. Have you seen it anywhere?'Find out = get information about something that you want to know: 'He's gone to find out which gate the plane leaves from.' 'I think we should find out exactly what's missing before we start accusing people.'

common_error_corrections.explanation: Catch fire: 'One of the engines had overheated and caught fire.'

common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Eventually, the fire went out and the room got colder.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go out = (of a coal fire, cigarette, candle etc) stop burning: 'The problem with cigars is that they keep going out.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: At first, I would like to introduce myself.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: First of all, I would like to introduce myself.
common_error_corrections.explanation: FIRST · FIRST OF ALL · AT FIRST · IN/AT THE BEGINNING'First, firstly and first of all introduce the first item in a list or sequence. The next item is normally introduced by then or second/secondly: ‘First, open all the windows. Then turn off the gas and, if necessary, call an ambulance.’ ‘These new computers have several advantages. First of all, they’re faster than the older machines. Secondly, they’re far easier to use. And thirdly, they’re more reliable.’ At first. At first introduces a situation which is in contrast with a later situation (after a change has taken place): ‘At first I didn’t like the climate, but after two years I got used to it.’In the beginning. Like at first, in the beginning introduces a situation which is in contrast with a later situation. However, in the beginning is less common and suggests that the speaker is looking a long way back into the past to the period of time immediately after something began: ’In the beginning, when the first settlers arrived, law and order didn’t exist.’At the beginning refers to (1) the point in time when something begins: ’At the beginning of each lesson there is usually a revision exercise.’(2) the place where something begins: ’At the beginning of the novel there is a long description of the farm where Daniel was born and grew up.’ Unlike in the beginning, at the beginning is usually followed by of: ’at the beginning of the week/holiday/film’.

common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I had never seen such brightly coloured fish before.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The plural form of fish is usually fish: 'Did you catch any fish?' 'The fish in the market are always fresh.'The plural form fishes is used mainly in stories for small children and in scientific or technical styles (to refer to different species of fish).

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You should see a doctor or specialist to find out which type of diet will fit you.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Match (or go with) = (of clothes, soft furnishings, etc) look good when seen together: 'We chose a dark green carpet to go with our yellow curtains.' 'I can't wear blue shoes with a black skirt - they don't match.'Keep fit (WITHOUT in): 'She keeps fit by jogging five miles every day.'Compare: 'Cycling to work helps me to keep in shape.'

common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A little exercise will help you to keep fit.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Keep fit (WITHOUT in): 'She keeps fit by jogging five miles every day.'Compare: 'Cycling to work helps me to keep in shape.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was just about to enter the station when someone grabbed me by the shoulders and threw me to the floor.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was just about to enter the station when someone grabbed me by the shoulders and threw me to the ground.
common_error_corrections.explanation: FLOOR · GROUND · GROUNDS · LAND · TERRITORY · SOILThe floor is the surface that you walk on when you are indoors: ‘Our cat likes to sit on the floor under my desk.’ ‘It’s about time someone cleaned the kitchen floor.’The ground is the surface that you walk on when you are outdoors: ‘The ground was covered with snow.’ ‘In the middle of the forest was a bare patch of marshy ground.’Grounds refers to the area surrounding and belonging to a school, hospital, hotel, stately home, etc, usually enclosed by a wall or fence: ‘Parking within the hospital grounds is strictly prohibited.’Land refers to (1) an area of ground that is owned or used by someone, or that is controlled by a particular country: ‘All the land from here to the stream belongs to the Pattersons. Disagreements about land have led to many wars.’(2) (also the land) the part of the Earth’s surface that is not covered by water: ‘After three days at sea, I was looking forward to being on land again.’Territory is the area that is controlled by a particular country, army or power: ‘One of the results of losing the war was that the country had to give up almost half its territory.’ ‘They had wandered by mistake into enemy territory.’Soil is the material in which plants and trees grow: ‘This plant needs rich soil to grow well.’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The fire started at the seventh floor.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The fire started on the seventh floor.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On the ground/first/second etc floor (NOT in/at): 'The canteen is downstairs, on the ground floor.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Room 229 was in the second floor.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Room 229 was on the second floor.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On the ground/first/second etc floor (NOT in/at): 'The canteen is downstairs, on the ground floor.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I think I have caught a flu.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I think I have caught (the) flu.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Flu or the flu (NOT a flu): 'They are both off work with flu.' 'Even our doctor is down with the flu.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You can go in your own car or follow me.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You can go in your own car or come with me.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Follow means 'move in the same direction as someone or something that is moving in front of you': 'I have a feeling that the car behind is following us.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The child was caught stealing foods.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The child was caught stealing food.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Food is nearly always uncountable: 'We need to go out and buy some food.' It is countable only when it refers to a particular kind of food: 'baby foods', 'health foods'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is a disgrace to serve such a poor food.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It is a disgrace to serve such poor food.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Food is nearly always uncountable: 'We need to go out and buy some food.' It is countable only when it refers to a particular kind of food: 'baby foods', 'health foods'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was fool to believe him.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
I was a fool to believe him.
I was foolish to believe him.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Fool is a countable noun and refers to a person: 'She thinks I'm a fool for lending him the money.'The adjective is foolish: 'You were right. It was foolish of me to lend him the money.' 'This foolish idea could ruin everything.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Whenever there is a strike, we have to go to work by foot.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Whenever there is a strike, we have to go to work on foot.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go/travel (somewhere) by car/bus/train/air BUT on foot: 'We left the car at the bridge and travelled the rest of the way on foot.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I do badly in tests for I am lazy.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I do badly in tests because I am lazy.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use for to mean 'because'. This usage has almost disappeared and is found only in very formal styles.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have come to London for learning English.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have come to London to learn English.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To explain 'why' someone does something, use a to -infinitive (NOT for): 'She opened the door to let the cat out.' In formal styles, in order to is also possible: 'UN troops have been sent to the trouble spot in order to restore peace.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I studied in Freiburg for to be a kindergarden teacher.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I studied in Freiburg to be a kindergarden teacher.
common_error_corrections.explanation: For never comes immediately in front of a to -infinitive. Compare: 'It will be difficult for John to say no.' 'The suitcase is too heavy for anyone to carry all that way.' (for + sb/sth + to -infinitive).

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Being married makes it easier for to answer this question.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Unemployment has become a serious problem for the last few years.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Unemployment has become a serious problem over the last few years.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use for to say 'how long': 'He was with the company for forty years.' 'He hasn't eaten anything for the last two days.'Use over/during/in to say 'when', especially when this is a long period of time: 'She's been a great help to me in recent months.' 'During the next ten years he worked his way up from office boy to general manager.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'm waiting here for almost an hour.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I've been waiting here for almost an hour.
common_error_corrections.explanation: For actions and situations which began in the past and continue up to 'now' (the moment of speaking), use the present perfect tense: 'I've been working part-time for the last six months.' 'We haven't seen each other for the past eight months.'Note that in informal American English the past tense is also used for this purpose.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I didn't do any travelling for the last two years.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I haven't done any travelling for the last two years.
common_error_corrections.explanation: For actions and situations which began in the past and continue up to 'now' (the moment of speaking), use the present perfect tense: 'I've been working part-time for the last six months.' 'We haven't seen each other for the past eight months.'Note that in informal American English the past tense is also used for this purpose.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The government should forbid cigarette advertising.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The government should ban cigarette advertising.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Ban (or prohibit) = forbid someone from doing something by making it illegal: 'The proposed treaty banning all nuclear testing has received widespread approval.' 'International Law prohibits the use of chemical weapons.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There should be a law which forbids to have more than two children.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There should be a law which forbids couples to have/from having more than two children.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Forbid + sb + to do/from doing sth: 'My parents have forbidden me to stay out after ten o'clock.' 'Her father ought to forbid her from seeing the boy again.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We must not forget Japan's economic force.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We must not forget Japan's economic power.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Frce = the use of power or strength: 'The demonstrators were made to leave the building by force.'Power = the ability to control people and events: 'I think the police have too much power.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The sovereign has very little force nowadays.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The sovereign has very little power nowadays.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Force = the use of power or strength: 'The demonstrators were made to leave the building by force.'Power = the ability to control people and events: 'I think the police have too much power.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Some foreigner students feel homesick.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Some foreign students feel homesick.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Foreigner is a noun and refers to a person: 'As a foreigner who had only just arrived in England, I found the phrase 'car boot sale' very confusing.'The adjective is foreign: 'I enjoy visiting foreign countries.' 'His wife teaches English as a foreign language.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In my job I have to speak foreigner languages.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In my job I have to speak foreign languages.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Foreigner is a noun and refers to a person: 'As a foreigner who had only just arrived in England, I found the phrase 'car boot sale' very confusing.'The adjective is foreign: 'I enjoy visiting foreign countries.' 'His wife teaches English as a foreign language.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nobody lives forever.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nobody lives for ever.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Forever = continually; all the time: 'He is forever asking me for more pocket money.'For ever = for always: 'He promised that he would love me for ever and a day.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Would you please check whether I have forgotten a black handbag in Room 21.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Would you please check whether I have left a black handbag in Room 21.
common_error_corrections.explanation: If you forget to take something with you, you leave it somewhere. Do not use forget if you mention a place: 'If the keys aren't in your jacket, you must have left them in the restaurant.' 'I've left all my money at home.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was a good fortune that the driver was able to stop in time.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It was fortunate/lucky that the driver was able to stop in time.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Good fortune is quite rare. It occurs mainly in the phrase have the good fortune to do sth: 'He had the good fortune to marry a woman who was both kind and understanding.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I look forward to hearing from you. Friendly, Leine.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I look forward to hearing from you. Yours, Leine.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Although I was a stranger, they treated me very friendly.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
Although I was a stranger, the treatment I received was very friendly.
Although I was a stranger, they treated me in a very friendly way.
choices: the treatment I received was very friendly
they treated me in a very friendly way
common_error_corrections.explanation: Friendly is an adjective (NOT an adverb): 'Our new neighbours are very friendly.' 'She gave me a friendly smile.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When I heard the thunder I frightened for a moment.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When I heard the thunder I was frightened for a moment.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Frighten (transitive) = make someone afraid: 'Take that silly mask off - you're frightening the baby.'Be frightened = be afraid: 'Don't be frightened. It's only thunder.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have been living in England from last September.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have been living in England since last September.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use from ... to ... when you mean 'from one time in the past to another': 'I lived in England from 1986 to 1989.'Use since when you mean 'from a time in the past until now': 'I've been standing here since 9 o'clock and not one bus has come along.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She asked if I'd seen any plays from Shakespeare.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She asked if I'd seen any plays by Shakespeare.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A play, novel, painting, etc by a writer or artist (NOT from): 'The reading passage was from a novel by Anita Brookner.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's a short, knee-length coat from white wool.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It's a short, knee-length coat made of white wool.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The bus stop is outside the post office, in front of the library.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The bus stop is outside the post office, opposite the library.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In front of = in a position directly before: 'There was a bus in front of the car and a truck behind it.' 'All I could see was the enormous hat of the woman sitting in front of me.'Opposite = on the other side of the street, room, etc facing: 'The police station is directly opposite the town hall.' 'He looked out of his bedroom window at the house opposite.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The shop sells fruits and vegetables.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The shop sells fruit and vegetables.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Fruit (= fruit in general) is an uncountable noun: 'We eat lots of fruit in our family.' 'Would anyone care for a piece of fruit?' (= an orange, apple, pear etc)Fruits (= particular types of fruit) is rarely used in British English.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I never buy tinned fruits.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I never buy tinned fruit.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Fruit (= fruit in general) is an uncountable noun: 'We eat lots of fruit in our family.' 'Would anyone care for a piece of fruit?' (= an orange, apple, pear etc)Fruits (= particular types of fruit) is rarely used in British English.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The editor said that my letter was too long to be fully published.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The editor said that my letter was too long to be published in full.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Fully = completely: 'a fully equipped kitchen', 'a fully furnished apartment', 'The next three flights to Chicago are fully booked.'In full = without any part missing or removed: 'Your $100 deposit will be refunded in full.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A good novel can give you a lot of fun.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A good novel can give you a lot of pleasure.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about something that provides intellectual or spiritual satisfaction, such as a piano concert or a visit to an art gallery, use enjoyment/enjoyable or pleasure/pleasurable: 'Reading is her one source of pleasure.' 'We spent an enjoyable afternoon at the art gallery.'Fun is usually used in connection with light-hearted events and activities such as games, picnics, or children's parties: 'John's parties are always great fun.' 'Let's go to the beach and have some fun.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The game we played was very fun.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The game we played was a lot of fun.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Fun is a noun (NOT an adjective): 'a lot of fun', 'not much fun', 'great fun'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: College life is not very fun.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: College life is not much fun.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Fun is a noun (NOT an adjective): 'a lot of fun', 'not much fun', 'great fun'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In future, when my youngest child has started school, I'd like to get a job.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In the future, when my youngest child has started school, I'd like to get a job.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In future = from now on (commonly used in announcements and warnings): 'In future anyone arriving late for class will not be admitted.'In the future = at some time in the future: 'In the future it is quite possible that a new source of energy will be discovered.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: For two weeks' work, I gain about 700,000 yen.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: For two weeks' work, I earn about 700,000 yen.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Earn or (especially in informal styles) get /make (a sum of) money by going to work, from investments, etc (NOT gain): 'She earns $4,000 a month.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Without a job it's impossible to gain any money.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Without a job it's impossible to earn any money.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Earn or (especially in informal styles) get /make (a sum of) money by going to work, from investments, etc (NOT gain): 'She earns $4,000 a month.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My father was a very gentle man, always helping people.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My father was a very kind man, always helping people.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Gentle = (1) used to describe someone who never shows anger or impatience in what they say or do: 'His brother was always ready for a fight, but Tim was quiet and gentle.'(2) not loud, forceful or rough: 'He spoke to the child in a quiet, gentle voice so as not to frighten her.' 'She found the doctor's gentle manner very reassuring.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The shop assistant asked me gently what I wanted.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The shop assistant asked me politely what I wanted.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Gently = in a way that will not hurt or damage anything: 'She held the little bird very gently.'Politely = in a way that shows good manners: 'He politely refused her offer, saying that he didn't want to trouble her.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I wonder if you would gently lend us a room for one of the monthly meetings.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I wonder if you would kindly lend us a room for one of the monthly meetings.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In polite formal requests, use if you would/could kindly (or if you would be so kind as to): 'I would be very grateful if you would kindly allow Julian to leave school early on Tuesday.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She gave to him some cheese sandwiches.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She gave him some cheese sandwiches.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Give something to somebody BUT give somebody something (WITHOUT to).Compare: 'They gave a medal to each member of the team.' 'They gave each member of the team a medal.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They always give to the new students a warm welcome.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They always give the new students a warm welcome.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Give sth to sb BUT give sb sth (WITHOUT to).Compare: 'They gave a medal to each member of the team.' 'They gave each member of the team a medal.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I would be glad if you could send me an application form.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I would be grateful if you could send me an application form.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To make a formal request, use would be grateful if (NOT glad): 'We would be grateful if you could consider this matter at your earliest convenience.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She was a very glad person, and very intelligent.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She was a very happy person, and very intelligent.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Glad (not used in front of a noun) = pleased and happy about something in particular: 'I'm so glad your wife is feeling better.' 'I'm glad it wasn't my turn to pay.'Happy = enjoying life: 'She's a lot happier now that the examinations are over.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We hope that you will like this school and be glad here.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We hope that you will like this school and be happy here.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Glad (not used in front of a noun) = pleased and happy about something in particular: 'I'm so glad your wife is feeling better.' 'I'm glad it wasn't my turn to pay.'Happy = enjoying life: 'She's a lot happier now that the examinations are over.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He wears an old-fashioned glasses which make him look intelligent.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He wears old-fashioned glasses which make him look intelligent.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Glasses (= spectacles) is a plural noun: 'I wear glasses just for reading.' 'Have you seen my glasses?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have to vacuum the floors and clean the glasses of the windows.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have to vacuum the floors and clean the windows.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pane (or window-pane) = a sheet of glass used in a window: 'The two cracked panes will have to be replaced.'Note that pane and window-pane are rarely used. Their meaning is usually expressed by window.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The sunlight poured in through the glasses of the bedroom window.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The sunlight poured in through (the panes of) the bedroom window.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pane (or window-pane) = a sheet of glass used in a window: 'The two cracked panes will have to be replaced.'Note that pane and window-pane are rarely used. Their meaning is usually expressed by window.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: 'Have you ever gone to France?' she asked.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: 'Have you ever been to France?' she asked.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English, been is used when someone has visited a place and returned. Gone is used when the person is still in the place they are visiting. Compare: 'Peter has gone to Paris.' (= he has not yet returned) 'Peter has been to Paris.' (= he has visited Paris and returned)In American English gone can be used instead of been.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The next morning she went to see us at the hotel.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The next morning she came to see us at the hotel.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Come is used for movement towards the speaker/listener: 'Come in and sit down for a few minutes.' 'When can I come and see you?'Go is used for movement in other directions: 'Could you go upstairs and turn the lights off?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: How do I go to the Holiday Inn?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: How do I get to the Holiday Inn?
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'arrive', use get (to): 'I got to the classroom five minutes late.' 'When does the train get there?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He was lost and didn't know how to go back home.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He was lost and didn't know how to get back home.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'arrive', use get (to): 'I got to the classroom five minutes late.' 'When does the train get there?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We go to swim every day on holiday.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We go swimming every day on holiday.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go swimming/sightseeing/shopping etc: 'They've probably gone fishing.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They've gone for camping on Lantau Island.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They've gone camping on Lantau Island.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go swimming / sightseeing / shopping etc: 'They've probably gone fishing.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: That evening my boyfriend and I went out to walk.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: That evening my boyfriend and I went for a walk.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go for a walk/swim/jog etc: 'Would anyone like to go for a drive?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We reached our goal just after three o'clock.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Goal = something that you hope to achieve: 'The company's goal is to double its share of the personal computer market.'Destination = the place that you are travelling to: 'The immigration officer wanted to know my destination and how long I was planning to stay.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's a navy blue coat with golden buttons.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Golden is used in idiomatic expressions such as 'a golden opportunity', 'a golden handshake', 'a golden wedding anniversary', and in the phrase 'golden hair' (used mainly in literary styles).To describe something that is made of gold or is the colour of gold, use gold: 'a gold bracelet', 'a black dress with red and gold stripes down the front'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The purse contained six golden coins.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The purse contained six gold coins.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Do you know when the plane is gonna land?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Do you know when the plane is going to land?

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The principal is gonna give a talk in the morning.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The principal is going to give a talk in the morning.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use gonna (= going to) or wanna (= want to) unless you are trying to represent informal conversation.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I don't speak English very good.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I don't speak English very well.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Good is an adjective: 'She is a very good singer.'Well is an adverb: 'She sings very well.'Be good at (doing) sth: 'He's good at all science subjects.' 'Are you any good at chess?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I hope I'll do good in tomorrow's test.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I hope I'll do well in tomorrow's test.
common_error_corrections.explanation: If you are successful (in a test, interview etc), you do well (in it): 'I did quite well in maths and chemistry but my physics result was very disappointing.'It is no good/use (doing sth) = it is pointless: 'It's no good having a car if you can't drive.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My sister is very good in squash.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My sister is very good at squash.

common_error_corrections.explanation: FLOOR · GROUND · GROUNDS · LAND · TERRITORY · SOILThe floor is the surface that you walk on when you are indoors: ‘Our cat likes to sit on the floor under my desk.’ ‘It’s about time someone cleaned the kitchen floor.’The ground is the surface that you walk on when you are outdoors: ‘The ground was covered with snow.’ ‘In the middle of the forest was a bare patch of marshy ground.’Grounds refers to the area surrounding and belonging to a school, hospital, hotel, stately home, etc, usually enclosed by a wall or fence: ‘Parking within the hospital grounds is strictly prohibited.’Land refers to (1) an area of ground that is owned or used by someone, or that is controlled by a particular country: ‘All the land from here to the stream belongs to the Pattersons.’‘ Disagreements about land have led to many wars.’(2) (also the land) the part of the Earth’s surface that is not covered by water: ‘After three days at sea, I was looking forward to being on land again.’Territory is the area that is controlled by a particular country, army or power: ‘One of the results of losing the war was that the country had to give up almost half its territory.’ ‘They had wandered by mistake into enemy territory.’Soil is the material in which plants and trees grow: ‘This plant needs rich soil to grow well.’

common_error_corrections.explanation: Avoiding sexism in your writingIn the past, when people referred to a member of a group containing both men and women (or boys and girls), they used the pronouns he/him/his:A good doctor listens carefully to his patients.Anyone who wants to join should give his name to the secretary.Nowadays, many people feel that this usage is unfair to women. If you want to avoid the danger of seeming sexist, you can use one of the following alternatives.Use They/Them/Their to refer back to an indefinite pronoun (anyone, somebody etc):Anyone who wants to join should give their name to the secretary.Some people object to this usage in formal styles, insisting that they (plural) does not agree in number with anyone (singular). This usage is nevertheless very common.Make all the forms plural:Good doctors listen carefully to their patients.Those who want to join should give their name to the secretary.Design the sentence in such a way that a personal pronoun is not needed. For example, instead of saying ‘If anyone wants to go now, he may do so’, just say ‘Anyone who wants to go now may do so.’Use he or she, his or her, etc:A good doctor listens carefully to his or her patients.This alternative is found in formal writing, and so is the use of he/she, his/her, s/he, etc.However, they are generally felt to produce awkward and unnatural sentences, especially when they are repeated, as in:If a doctor listens to his or her patients, he or she will be in a better position to help them.

If you want to avoid the danger of seeming sexist, you can use one of the following alternatives.Use They/Them/Their to refer back to an indefinite pronoun (anyone, somebody etc):Anyone who wants to join should give their name to the secretary.Some people object to this usage in formal styles, insisting that they (plural) does not agree in number with anyone (singular). This usage is nevertheless very common.Make all the forms plural:Good doctors listen carefully to their patients.Those who want to join should give their name to the secretary.Design the sentence in such a way that a personal pronoun is not needed. For example, instead of saying ‘If anyone wants to go now, he may do so’, just say ‘Anyone who wants to go now may do so.’Use he or she, his or her, etc:A good doctor listens carefully to his or her patients.This alternative is found in formal writing, and so is the use of he/she, his/her, s/he, etc.However, they are generally felt to produce awkward and unnatural sentences, especially when they are repeated, as in:If a doctor listens to his or her patients, he or she will be in a better position to help them.

common_error_corrections.explanation: JOB · DO · OCCUPATION · POST/POSITION · CAREER · TRADE · PROFESSIONJob. Your job is what you do to earn your living: ‘You’ll never get a job if you don’t have any qualifications.’ ‘She’d like to change her job but can’t find anything better.’ Your job is also the particular type of work that you do: ‘John’s new job sounds really interesting.’ ‘I know she works for the BBC but I’m not sure what job she does.’A job may be full-time or part-time (NOT half-time or half-day): ‘All she could get was a part-time job at a petrol station.’Do (for a living). When you want to know about the type of work that someone does, the usual questions are What do you do? What does she do for a living? etc ‘What does your father do?’ - ‘He’s a police inspector.’Occupation and job have similar meanings. However, occupation is far less common than job and is used mainly in formal and official styles: ‘Please give brief details of your employment history and present occupation.’ ‘People in manual occupations seem to suffer less from stress.’Post/position. The particular job that you have in a company or organization is your post or position: ‘She’s been appointed to the post of deputy principal.’ ‘He’s applied for the position of sales manager.’ Post and position are used mainly in formal styles and often refer to jobs which have a lot of responsibility.Career. Your career is your working life, or the series of jobs that you have during your working life: ‘The scandal brought his career in politics to a sudden end.’ ‘Later on in his career, he became first secretary at the British Embassy in Washington.’Your career is also the particular kind of work for which you are trained and that you intend to do for a long time: ‘I wanted to find out more about careers in publishing.’Trade. A trade is a type of work in which you do or make things with your hands: ‘Most of the men had worked in skilled trades such as carpentry or printing.’ ‘My grandfather was a bricklayer by trade.’Profession. A profession is a type of work such as medicine, teaching, or law which requires a high level of training or education: ‘Until recently, medicine has been a male-dominated profession.’ ‘She entered the teaching profession in 1987.’

common_error_corrections.explanation: CONTAIN · INCLUDE · ENCLOSE · CONSIST OF · COMPRISE · BE COMPOSED OF · BE MADE UP OFUse contain (1) when you say what a box, bottle, bag etc has inside it. ‘The bag contained some old clothes.’(2) when you mention one or more of the things that something is made of or has in it: ‘Water contains hydrogen and oxygen.’ ‘The film contained a number of violent scenes.’If something includes another thing, it has it as one of its parts: ‘The holiday package includes a two-day cruise along the Rhine.’ ‘The price includes a small charge for postage and packing.’Use enclose when you tell someone what you are putting in the envelope or parcel that you are sending them: ‘I’m enclosing a copy of the book review that you asked for.’Consist of, comprise, be composed of, be made up of. When you mention all the parts that something has in it, use consist of / comprise / be composed of / be made up of: ‘The book consists of six chapters and a brief introduction.’ ‘The Earth’s atmosphere is composed mainly of nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide.’ ‘The house comprises two bedrooms, a bathroom, a kitchen, and a living room.’ ‘The US government is made up of two legislative assemblies.’ Note that you will sometimes see comprised of two separate packages. Most careful users consider this to be incorrect, preferring: ‘This investment scheme comprises two separate packages.’
