When you want to know about the type of work that someone does, the usual questions are What do you do? What does she do for a living? etc ‘What does your father do?’ - ‘He’s a police inspector.’Occupation and job have similar meanings. However, occupation is far less common than job and is used mainly in formal and official styles: ‘Please give brief details of your employment history and present occupation.’ ‘People in manual occupations seem to suffer less from stress.’Post/position. The particular job that you have in a company or organization is your post or position: ‘She’s been appointed to the post of deputy principal.’ ‘He’s applied for the position of sales manager.’ Post and position are used mainly in formal styles and often refer to jobs which have a lot of responsibility.Career. Your career is your working life, or the series of jobs that you have during your working life: ‘The scandal brought his career in politics to a sudden end.’ ‘Later on in his career, he became first secretary at the British Embassy in Washington.’Your career is also the particular kind of work for which you are trained and that you intend to do for a long time: ‘I wanted to find out more about careers in publishing.’Trade. A trade is a type of work in which you do or make things with your hands: ‘Most of the men had worked in skilled trades such as carpentry or printing.’ ‘My grandfather was a bricklayer by trade.’Profession. A profession is a type of work such as medicine, teaching, or law which requires a high level of training or education: ‘Until recently, medicine has been a male-dominated profession.’ ‘She entered the teaching profession in 1987.’

When you travel to a place that is far away or to a place that you visit regularly, you go on/make a journey (NOT do/have): ‘You can’t go on a journey to Alaska without making careful preparations.’ ‘The journey to work takes about half an hour by train.’ ‘If the roads are flooded, we’ll have to make the journey by boat.’Trip. When you go to a place and come back again, especially for a short visit, you go on/make/take a trip: ‘How was your trip to San Francisco?’ ‘She’s away on a business trip and won’t be back until Monday.’Travel (uncountable) is the general activity of moving about the world or from place to place. ‘She enjoys foreign travel immensely.’ ‘New computer technology has made air travel considerably safer.’ A word with a similar meaning is travelling. (NOT ‘of travel’)In compounds nouns, travel is used: ‘foreign travel’, ‘air travel’ (NOT ‘air travelling’).Travels. Someone’s travels (plural) are the journeys they make (and the experiences they have) during a long visit to one or more foreign countries: ‘I accompanied the South African team throughout their travels in Australia and New Zealand.’ ‘We filmed a lot of wild animals on our travels.’A voyage is a long journey in a boat or ship: ‘Heavy seas and strong winds made the voyage from Europe very unpleasant.’A tour is a journey that you make for pleasure during which you visit a number of different places within a country, region etc: ‘For our next holiday we’re going on a ten-day tour of the Lake District.’ Politicians and entertainers sometimes go on a tour as part of their work, making a planned series of visits in order to meet people or perform: ‘The Prime Minister will be returning on Monday from a three-week tour of Southeast Asia.’A tour is also a short trip around a city, factory, museum etc: ‘After lunch we were taken on a guided tour of York Minster.’

common_error_corrections.explanation: Slightly + adjective + noun: 'a slightly solemn expression'Choosing the right word: GENERAL WORDS and EXACT WORDS.Some words have a general meaning, e.g. big, beautiful, good, say, make, kill. These words are useful, especially when you begin to learn English, because you can make use of them in a wide range of situations:A big meal, a big kitchen, a big mistake etc.For each general word, however, there is usually another word or phrase which comes closer to what you want to say, and which may also sound more natural in the context:A substantial meal, a spacious kitchen, a serious mistake etc.A major step towards fluency in English is getting to know plenty of exact words which can replace the more general words you have learned. Here are some words which can be used instead of the general word kill.Murder. To murder someone is to kill them deliberately and unlawfully: ‘The key witness was murdered before he could testify.’ A person who does this is a murderer.Massacre. Massacre is used when you talk about the deliberate killing of a large number of people, especially people who cannot defend themselves: ‘Whole native populations were massacred when the European settles arrived.’Slaughter. Slaughter is used when you talk about the deliberate killing of a large number of people, especially in a particularly cruel way: ‘Men ran through the village burning houses and slaughtering anyone that got in their way.’To slaughter an animal is to kill it for its meat, skin etc, or as part of a religious ceremony: ‘The children couldn’t understand why the cattle had to be slaughtered.’Execute. To execute someone (or put someone to death) is to kill someone as a punishment, according to the law: ‘King Charles I was executed on 30th January 1639.’Assassinate. To assassinate someone is to deliberately kill a very famous or important person such as a political leader: ‘President Lincoln was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth.’ A person who does this is an assassin.Commit suicide. To commit suicide (or take your own life) is to deliberately kill yourself: ‘Rather than be taken prisoner, they preferred to commit suicide.’Destroy. To destroy an animal (or have it put down/to sleep) is to kill in a way that does not cause pain, especially because it is sick or injured: ‘The cat had developed cancer and had to be destroyed.'

common_error_corrections.explanation: CULTURE · CUSTOM · HABIT · MANNER · MANNERS · TRADITIONCulture: (1) the customs, ideas, art, etc, which are found in a particular society or group and which make it different from another society or group: ‘Obeying your parents is a hallmark of Asian culture.’(2) the art, music, literature, etc, that is produced by a particular society: ‘Professor Jackson is an expert on ancient Greek culture:’ ‘The Samba is an important part of Brazilian culture.’Custom: (1) something that the people in a particular society have done (in the same way) for a very long time, and which they consider to be normal or polite: ‘One of their customs is to point with the thumb, not with the index finger.’ ‘According to local custom, his body was carried to the top of a hill and cremated.’ ‘His knowledge of Malay and Indonesian customs proved invaluable when we got to Bali.’(2) something that a person usually does in a particular situation: ‘His custom of making detailed preparatory drawings makes him unique amongst 18th century British painters.’ ‘On Wednesday evening, as was his custom, he went for a long walk.’Habit: something that a person does repeatedly, often without realizing it: ‘She has a lot of little habits that I find really irritating.’ ‘In California I got into the habit of eating with just a fork.’Manner: (singular) the way someone behaves towards people: ‘She impressed us all with her business-like manner.’ ‘His cheerful face and polite manner have won him a lot of friends.’Manners: (plural) the way someone behaves towards people, especially when compared with what is accepted as polite behaviour: ‘The child has very good manners and always says thank you.’Tradition: a belief, custom or way of doing something that has been passed on from one generation to the next: ‘The tradition was that when a man died, all his wealth and possessions would go to the eldest son.’

common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: American culture is all about freedom and equality.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Every society has its own laws and manners.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Every society has its own laws and traditions/customs.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One of the biggest differences I noticed was the American manner of being polite to strangers.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One of the biggest differences I noticed was the American custom of being polite to strangers.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We were taught how to speak in a good manner.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We were taught how to speak properly.
common_error_corrections.explanation: If you do something in the right way, you do it properly: 'Failure to use the equipment properly may result in serious injury.' 'Since George passed away, Mavis has stopped eating properly.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One of the policemen started asking me many questions.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One of the policemen started asking me a lot of questions.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Many and much are used mainly in questions and negative sentences: 'Does he have many friends?' 'It appears that he doesn't have many friends.' In affirmative sentences, phrases such as a lot of and plenty of are used.Note however that many and much are used in affirmative sentences after too, so, and as ('You ask too many questions.') and sometimes in formal styles ('Many accidents arise as a result of negligence').

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We are given many tests.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We are given a lot of tests.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's important to understand why there is so many violence in our world.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It's important to understand why there is so much violence in our world.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I had never seen so many and bright stars in the sky.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I had never seen so many bright stars in the sky.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There are not many and interesting Sunday newspapers.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There are not many interesting Sunday newspapers.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Many + adjective + noun (WITHOUT and): 'He is convinced that many serious accidents could be prevented.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Her only distinguishing mark is her long blond hair.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Her only distinguishing feature is her long blond hair.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A mark on someone's face or body is a small area of skin that is a different colour from the rest: 'You've got two dark red marks on your nose where your glasses have been.'Things such as the colour of someone's eyes and hair, and the shape of their nose, chin and mouth are their features: 'As soon as he began to describe her features, I realized that he was talking about Mandy.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Before buying a cassette recorder, I asked my friend if he could recommend a good mark.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Before buying a cassette recorder, I asked my friend if he could recommend a good make.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Mark (also Mk) = a model, type or version (used mainly in trade names): 'a Mk II Jaguar'.Make = a particular type of car, washing machine, camera, etc: 'If you want a really good make, go for a Nikon or a Pentax.' 'Which make of television do you prefer, Sony or Panasonic?'Brand = a particular type of soap, toothpaste, butter, cigarette, etc: 'I'm tired of being told which brand of washing powder I should use.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: As for cigarettes, there are many different marks.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: As for cigarettes, there are many different brands.

'Which make of television do you prefer, Sony or Panasonic?'Brand = a particular type of soap, toothpaste, butter, cigarette, etc: 'I'm tired of being told which brand of washing powder I should use.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The magazine gives a list of all the computers in the market.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The magazine gives a list of all the computers on the market.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On the market (NOT in) = available in shops for people to buy; for sale: 'It's not the cheapest machine on the market, but it's certainly the best.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Why didn't you invite me to your marriage?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Why didn't you invite me to your wedding?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Marriage = the ceremony of becoming husband and wife considered from a purely religious or legal point of view: 'Her parents are against the marriage.'Wedding = the occasion when this ceremony takes place and the celebrations that follow it: 'I never see most of my relatives apart from at weddings.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have just received your marriage invitation.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have just received your wedding invitation.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She is married with a post office worker.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She is married to a post office worker.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be/get married to sb (NOT with): 'How long has she been married to him?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He's going to ask her to marry with him.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He's going to ask her to marry him.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Marry sb (WITHOUT with/to): 'Isn't he the man who married Elizabeth Taylor?'Get married (to sb): 'I can still remember the day I got married. United were playing at Wembley.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: His daughter is expected to marry to a viscount.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: His daughter is expected to marry a viscount.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Marry sb (WITHOUT with/to): 'Isn't he the man who married Elizabeth Taylor?'Get married (to sb): 'I can still remember the day I got married. United were playing at Wembley.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After they get marry, they're going abroad.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: After they get married, they're going abroad.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Marry sb (WITHOUT with/to): 'Isn't he the man who married Elizabeth Taylor?'Get married (to sb): 'I can still remember the day I got married. United were playing at Wembley.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have a master in Hotel Management.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have a master's in Hotel Management.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The green jacket doesn't match to the trousers.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The green jacket doesn't match the trousers.
common_error_corrections.explanation: One thing matches / doesn't match another thing (WITHOUT to/with): 'You can't wear that blue tie. It doesn't match your shirt.'Compare: 'The green jacket doesn't go with the trousers.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We chose the sunflowers to match with the wallpaper.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We chose the sunflowers to match the wallpaper.
common_error_corrections.explanation: One thing matches/doesn't match another thing (WITHOUT to/with): 'You can't wear that blue tie. It doesn't match your shirt.'Compare: 'The green jacket doesn't go with the trousers.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In today's material society, most people think only about money.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In today's materialistic society, most people think only about money.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Material = connected with the physical needs that people have (as opposed to spiritual or intellectual needs): 'In material terms they are very well off, but spiritually they are deprived.'Materialistic = believing that money and the things that money can buy are more important than anything else: 'Modern society is becoming increasingly materialistic.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Mathematics are my favourite subject.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Mathematics is my favourite subject.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Mathematics (the subject) is an uncountable noun: 'Mathematics is compulsory. Even if you don't like it, you still have to take it.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It doesn't matter the nationality of the archaeologists.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The nationality of the archaeologists doesn't matter.
choices: The nationality of the archaeologists doesn't matter
It doesn't matter the nationality of the archaeologists
common_error_corrections.explanation: It doesn't matter + clause: 'It doesn't matter if you can't answer all the questions. Just do your best.' subject + doesn't matter: 'The results don't matter. Just do your best.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Doesn't matter the time.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The time doesn't matter.
common_error_corrections.explanation: It doesn't matter + clause: 'It doesn't matter if you can't answer all the questions. Just do your best.' Subject + doesn't matter: 'The results don't matter. Just do your best.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: No matter he tries hard, he never succeeds in passing.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: No matter how hard he tries, he never succeeds in passing.
common_error_corrections.explanation: No matter how/who/whether etc + subject + verb: 'No matter how much you help him, he never seems grateful.' 'No matter how late you set off, the roads are always busy.' 'No matter who you ask, they all say the same thing.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The matter is that we won't have enough room in the car to take your mother with us.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The problem is that we won't have enough room in the car to take your mother with us.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Matter is used to mean 'problem' or 'trouble' only in questions and negative sentences: 'What's the matter?' 'Is anything the matter?' 'There's nothing the matter.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After the sauna they run and jump in the river, no matter if it's freezing or not.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: After the sauna they run and jump in the river, no matter whether it's freezing or not.
common_error_corrections.explanation: No matter + wh- word (NOT if /nothing): 'I'm not interested in the job, no matter how much they offer me.' 'No matter what you do for her, she's never grateful.'Note that no matter whether tends to sound awkward and there are usually simpler alternatives: 'After the sauna they run and jump in the river, whether it's freezing or not.' 'Rich or poor, they all come to us for advice.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: No matter they are rich or poor, they all come to us for advice.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: No matter whether they are rich or poor, they all come to us for advice.
common_error_corrections.explanation: No matter + wh- word (NOT if /nothing): 'I'm not interested in the job, no matter how much they offer me.' 'No matter what you do for her, she's never grateful.'Note that no matter whether tends to sound awkward and there are usually simpler alternatives: 'After the sauna they run and jump in the river, whether it's freezing or not.' 'Rich or poor, they all come to us for advice.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: No matter the recession, sales remained high.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In spite of the recession, sales remained high.
common_error_corrections.explanation: No matter is always followed by a wh- clause: 'No matter what they did, they couldn't put the fire out.' 'No matter how cold it gets, we'll keep warm somehow.'In front of a noun phrase, use in spite of/despite: 'In spite of the temperature outside, we managed to keep warm.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The flight attendant told us that there wasn't any matter; it was just a storm.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The flight attendant told us that nothing was the matter; it was just a storm.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Nothing/something is the matter or there is nothing/something the matter: 'I think there's something the matter with the central heating. It's cold in here.' 'Don't worry. Nothing's the matter. It's just a tiny cut.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He isn't matured enough to get married.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He isn't mature enough to get married.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use matured/mature when you are talking about wine, cheese etc: 'The whisky is kept here until it has matured/is mature.'When you are talking about people, the usual word is mature: 'He's very mature for a boy of sixteen.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Replacing such a politically matured leader will not be easy.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Replacing such a politically mature leader will not be easy.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use matured/mature when you are talking about wine, cheese etc: 'The whisky is kept here until it has matured/is mature.'When you are talking about people, the usual word is mature: 'He's very mature for a boy of sixteen.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If I hadn't seen the car coming, I may have been killed.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If I hadn't seen the car coming, I might have been killed.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To refer to something in the past that was possible but did not actually happen, use might have or could have (NOT may have): 'If you had worked harder, you might have passed the exam.'Compare: 'I may have left it at home - I'm not sure.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Maybe you'll find the film very boring.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You may find the film very boring.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Instead of using maybe ... will, use may + infinitive: 'They may decide that our offer is too low, of course.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Maybe you will have problems breathing.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You may have problems breathing.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Instead of using maybe ... will, use may + infinitive: 'They may decide that our offer is too low, of course.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Maybe this helps to explain why there are so many divorces.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Perhaps this helps to explain why there are so many divorces.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Maybe is used mainly in informal styles: 'Maybe you should see a doctor.'Perhaps is used in all styles: 'Perhaps he's gone home already.' 'Perhaps there are other factors that need to be considered.'

common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I got myself a drink and sat down on the sofa.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: What can I tell you about me?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: What can I tell you about myself?

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I still remember the day me and my sister went to Buenos Aires by bus.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I still remember the day my sister and I went to Buenos Aires by bus.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The pattern me and ... is sometimes heard in informal styles but is widely regarded as non-standard. The usual pattern is ... and I: 'George and I have opened a joint account.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You will be able to try some of the traditional meals.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You will be able to try some of the traditional dishes.
common_error_corrections.explanation: MEAL · MENU · COURSE · DISH · THE DISHES · PLATEMeal. A meal is the food that you eat at about the same time each day: ‘After the meal we went to a discotheque.’ ‘We usually have our main meal in the evening.’Menu. A menu is a list of all the things that you can order in a restaurant: ‘I tried to read the menu but it was all in French.’ ‘Is there any fish on the menu?’Course. A meal may be served in separate stages. Each stage is called a course: ‘The main course was disappointing, but the dessert was excellent.’ ‘I’m not hungry enough to eat a three-course meal.’Dish. A dish is (1) the food prepared in a particular way and served as a meal or part of a meal: ‘My favourite Italian dish is lasagne.’ ‘For the main course there were six different meal dishes to choose from.’(2) a (usually shallow) container that food is placed in and then cooked or served: ‘I hope this dish is ovenproof!’The dishes. The dishes is a collective term for all the plates, bowls, cups, etc, that are used during a meal: ‘Whose turn is it to wash the dishes tonight?’Plate. A plate is (1) a (usually round) flat object that food is placed on, especially just before it is eaten: ‘All the clean plates are still in the dishwasher.’ ‘I’d never seen anyone put so much food on their plate.’(2) (also plateful) the amount of food on a plate: ‘How can you eat two large plates of spaghetti and still feel hungry?’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We always take our meals in the canteen.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We always have our meals in the canteen.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English the phrase is have a meal (NOT take): 'In the evening we had a three-course meal.'In American English both take a meal and have a meal are used, although take a meal (more formal) is not very common.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Being a good flight attendant means to make your passengers feel relaxed.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Being a good flight attendant means making your passengers feel relaxed.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Mean to do sth = intend to do something: 'I've been meaning to write to you for ages.'Mean doing sth (or mean + that clause) = involve doing something: 'The new job will mean getting up an hour earlier in the morning.' 'The new job will mean that I have to get up ....'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He was determined to get the money by all means.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He was determined to get the money by whatever means.
common_error_corrections.explanation: By all means (= certainly) is used in formal spoken English to show that you are happy to accept someone's request or suggestion: 'Would you mind if I stayed a bit longer?' 'By all means.'When you mean 'by using any method, even if it is unkind or illegal', use by any means or by whatever means (are available/necessary): 'They are determined to get their hands on the property by whatever means are necessary.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They intend to become famous by all means, even if they have to risk their lives.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They intend to become famous by whatever means, even if they have to risk their lives.
common_error_corrections.explanation: By all means (= certainly) is used in formal spoken English to show that you are happy to accept someone's request or suggestion: 'Would you mind if I stayed a bit longer?' 'By all means.'When you mean 'by using any method, even if it is unkind or illegal', use by any means or by whatever means (are available/necessary): 'They are determined to get their hands on the property by whatever means are necessary.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Learning English is a means to improve one's career prospects.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Learning English is a means of improving one's career prospects.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Means of (doing) sth = a way or method: 'It's time we stopped using force as a means of settling disputes.' 'There must be an easier means of gaining their confidence.'Means to do sth (or means of doing sth) = the thing that is required or necessary (to make something possible): 'These people have lost the means to support their families.' 'They would like to stop the war but lack the means to do so.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: By no means I want to suggest that people like being unemployed.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: By no means do I want to suggest that people like being unemployed.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In my opinion, the authorities have to take even stricter measurements to save our archaeological treasures.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In my opinion, the authorities have to take even stricter measures to save our archaeological treasures.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Measurement = the length, width etc of something: 'You can't buy new curtains without knowing the window measurements.'Measure = an action intended to have a particular effect; a law or ruling: 'New measures are to be introduced in the fight against crime.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Television is a very powerful media.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Television is a very powerful medium.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about television, radio and newspapers, use medium for singular reference: 'Children learn as much through the medium of television as they do by going to school.'Use media (WITHOUT -s) for plural and group reference: 'the mass media', 'the news media'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The medias, such as radio and television, tell us what is happening in the world.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The media, such as radio and television, tell us what is happening in the world.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about television, radio and newspapers, use medium for singular reference: 'Children learn as much through the medium of television as they do by going to school.'Use media (WITHOUT -s) for plural and group reference: 'the mass media', 'the news media'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In January 1990, the international news media was excited because it appeared that Mandela might be released.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In January 1990, the international news media were excited because it appeared that Mandela might be released.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The media usually takes a plural verb, especially in formal styles: 'The media have shown considerable interest in the trial.' A singular verb is sometimes heard in everyday conversation, but some careful users consider this to be incorrect.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After drinking the medicine, I felt sleepy.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: After taking the medicine, I felt sleepy.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Take/have your medicine (NOT drink): 'Have you taken/had your medicine today?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The medium score was about 6 out of 10.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The average score was about 6 out of 10.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Medium = neither large nor small, neither tall nor short, etc: 'The waiter was of medium height and walked with a slight limp.'Average = calculated by adding a set of quantities together and then dividing this total by the number of quantities in the set: 'The average age of students entering the college this year is 19.' 'Since 1991 house prices have been falling at an average annual rate of 8%.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My ability in English is about medium.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My ability in English is about average.
common_error_corrections.explanation: If someone's level of skill or ability is neither high nor low, it is average: 'Elizabeth shows above average intelligence for a child of three.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Could you meet with me outside the station?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Could you meet me outside the station?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Meet with sb (mainly American English) = have a (previously arranged) meeting with someone: 'We met with their representatives to discuss the problem.'Meet sb (British and American English) = be in the same place as someone by chance or arrangement: 'Guess who I met on the way to the bank this morning?' 'I suggest we meet back here in an hour's time.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The next time I met with her was in the supermarket.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The next time I met her was in the supermarket.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Meet with sb (mainly American English) = have a (previously arranged) meeting with someone: 'We met with their representatives to discuss the problem.'Meet sb (British and American English) = be in the same place as someone by chance or arrangement: 'Guess who I met on the way to the bank this morning?' 'I suggest we meet back here in an hour's time.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Hello John. It's good to meet you.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Hello John. It's good to see you.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you greet someone you know well, or talk about meeting them, use see (NOT meet): 'I hope you'll come and see us again soon.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I can't wait to meet you again at Christmas.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I can't wait to see you again at Christmas.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you greet someone you know well, or talk about meeting them, use see (NOT meet): 'I hope you'll come and see us again soon.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Following his death, a statue was erected to memorize him.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Following his death, a statue was erected in his memory.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Memorize = learn something so that you are able to repeat it exactly: 'Fortunately, I had memorized her telephone number and was able to ring her from the station.'In memory of sb, to the memory of sb or as a memorial (to sb) = a permanent reminder of someone after they have died: 'The charity was set up in memory of the late Lord Hinton.' 'It was built as a memorial to all those who died in the war.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Each visitor received a small gift as a memory.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Each visitor received a small gift as a souvenir.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Memory = something that you remember and see as a picture in your mind, especially an experience that you had a long time ago: 'The old teddy bear brought back vivid memories of my childhood.'Souvenir = something that you buy or obtain in a particular place (especially while on holiday) and keep to remind you of it: 'The vase is a souvenir of my week in Venice.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I bought six postcards and a few small memories.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I bought six postcards and a few small souvenirs.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Memory = something that you remember and see as a picture in your mind, especially an experience that you had a long time ago: 'The old teddy bear brought back vivid memories of my childhood.'Souvenir = something that you buy or obtain in a particular place (especially while on holiday) and keep to remind you of it: 'The vase is a souvenir of my week in Venice.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Casanova recorded his adventures in his memories.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Casanova recorded his adventures in his memoirs.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To refer to someone's written account of (a period in) their life, use memoirs (pronounced /'memwA:z/): 'The former President's long awaited memoirs are to be published next month.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You will remain in our memory and we all hope that you'll visit Greece again next summer.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We won't forget you and we all hope that you'll visit Greece again next summer.
choices: You will remain in our memory
common_error_corrections.explanation: You promise that you will not/never forget someone or the time you spent with them: 'I'll never forget the magic week we spent together in Rome.' The phrase remain in one's memory is grammatical but sounds unnatural.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have many happy memories about my childhood.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have many happy memories of my childhood.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Memory of sth: 'He smiled to himself at the memory of his son's first day at school.' 'The order and discipline of the job brought back memories of his army days.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nowadays world peace is menaced.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nowadays world peace is threatened.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Menace is usually used as a noun or adjective: 'These street gangs are a social menace.' 'He was convicted of menacing behaviour.' Menace is not often used as a verb. It appears mainly in formal styles and means 'make or try to make someone feel their life or safety is in great danger': 'His mighty war machine continues to menace neighbouring countries.'When you are talking about something which is a danger to peace, survival, safety, health, happiness, etc, use threaten: 'These poisonous liquids threaten the drinking water supply of two million people.' 'AIDS could threaten the economic well-being of Asian countries.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Old cars are easier to mend.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Old cars are easier to repair.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Mend (or repair) a roof, fence, watch, radio, camera, puncture etc: 'Once you've mended the kettle, we can have a cup of tea.'Repair a vehicle or something that is wrong with a vehicle: 'How will you get to work while your car is being repaired?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Modern society provides us with material comforts but very few mental rewards.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Modern society provides us with material comforts but very few spiritual rewards.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Mental = affecting or taking place in the mind: 'People who have had mental illnesses are often unwilling to talk about them.'Spiritual = connected with the part of a person which has very deep thoughts and feelings: 'African music has a spiritual quality which is often lacking in Western music.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The first place that foreigners think of when I mention about Indonesia is Bali.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The first place that foreigners think of when I mention Indonesia is Bali.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Mention sth (WITHOUT about): 'I don't suppose she mentioned her new address?' 'They mentioned how helpful you had been.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: For the main menu we had fish, rice and vegetables.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: For the main course we had fish, rice and vegetables.
common_error_corrections.explanation: MEAL · MENU · COURSE · DISH · THE DISHES · PLATEMeal. A meal is the food that you eat at about the same time each day: ‘After the meal we went to a discotheque.’ ‘We usually have our main meal in the evening.’Menu. A menu is a list of all the things that you can order in a restaurant: ‘I tried to read the menu but it was all in French.’ ‘Is there any fish on the menu?’Course. A meal may be served in separate stages. Each stage is called a course: ‘The main course was disappointing, but the dessert was excellent.’ ‘I’m not hungry enough to eat a three-course meal.’Dish. A dish is (1) the food prepared in a particular way and served as a meal or part of a meal: ‘My favourite Italian dish is lasagne.’ ‘For the main course there were six different meal dishes to choose from.’(2) a (usually shallow) container that food is placed in and then cooked or served: ‘I hope this dish is ovenproof!’The dishes. The dishes is a collective term for all the plates, bowls, cups, etc, that are used during a meal: ‘Whose turn is it to wash the dishes tonight?’Plate. A plate is (1) a (usually round) flat object that food is placed on, especially just before it is eaten: ‘All the clean plates are still in the dishwasher.’ ‘I’d never seen anyone put so much food on their plate.’(2) (also plateful) the amount of food on a plate: ‘How can you eat two large plates of spaghetti and still feel hungry?’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My favourite menu is cheese and mushroom omelette.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My favourite dish is cheese and mushroom omelette.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We'll have to find new methods of amusing ourselves.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We'll have to find new ways of amusing ourselves.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Method (of/for doing sth) is used mainly in technical styles: 'Farming methods have undergone many changes in recent years.' 'The research project aims to develop new methods for trapping solar energy.'In non-technical styles, use way (of doing/to do sth): 'There are several ways of answering the question.' 'The best way to contact him is by fax.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Some companies are taking new methods for coping with environmental problems.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Some companies are adopting new methods for coping with environmental problems.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Adopt a method: 'This new method of treating the disease has been widely adopted.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We usually eat during the midday and again in the evening.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We usually eat at midday and again in the evening.
common_error_corrections.explanation: At midday (NOT during): 'At midday the sun is directly overhead.' Compare: 'During the middle of the day the sun is very hot.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The girl was of middle height and was wearing a blue suit.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The girl was of medium height and was wearing a blue suit.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about someone's height, weight, etc, use medium (NOT middle): 'The man that police wish to question is of medium height and has a small black moustache.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The wallet was middle brown and contained sixty dollars.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The wallet was medium brown and contained sixty dollars.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you describe the colour of something, use medium (NOT middle): 'a medium grey suit' (= neither light grey nor dark grey but somewhere in between).In the middle of (NOT on): 'The cat dropped the mouse right in the middle of the kitchen floor.' 'What do we do if the fire alarm starts ringing in the middle of an examination?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: On the middle of September she is going on maternity leave.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In the middle of September she is going on maternity leave.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In the middle of (NOT on): 'The cat dropped the mouse right in the middle of the kitchen floor.' 'What do we do if the fire alarm starts ringing in the middle of an examination?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Sitting next to me was a middle age man, probably about forty.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Sitting next to me was a middle-aged man, probably about forty.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The adjective is middle-aged (WITH -d): 'They would prefer a middle-aged woman to a young girl.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The Rolling Stones are all middle-age now.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The Rolling Stones are all middle-aged now.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The adjective is middle-aged (WITH -d): 'They would prefer a middle-aged woman to a young girl.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The history of the town dates back to the Middle Age.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The history of the town dates back to the Middle Ages.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Middle age = the period in a person's life between youth and old age: 'People who live this type of life are lucky if they reach middle age.'Middle Ages = the period in European history from about 1100 to 1500 AD: 'Life in the Middle Ages was very simple.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Arabic is spoken all over Middle East.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Arabic is spoken all over the Middle East.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The Middle East, the Far East (WITH the): 'Bahrain is in the Middle East.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Her plane is due to land in about midnight.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Her plane is due to land at about midnight.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A lot of new doctors migrate to America where they can earn more money.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A lot of new doctors emigrate to America where they can earn more money.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Migrate = (of birds, animals and people) travel from one place to spend a length of time in another, especially to find food, water, warmer weather, etc: 'How do birds know when to migrate and how do they find their way back home?'Emigrate = (of people) leave your own country and make your home in another one: 'There were no jobs back home so we decided to emigrate.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Belgium has ten millions inhabitants.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Belgium has ten million inhabitants.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Using numbers.Day, month, minute, mile, kilo etc are always SINGULAR when used (with a number) immediately before a noun: ‘a six-minute wait’, ‘a ten-second silence’, ‘a five-mile race’.My travel agent had arranged a 6-day coach tour.The company provides a three-month training course.Compare: ‘We waited for thirty minutes: ‘We had a thirty-minute wait.’When you say 100, 1000 etc, or write these numbers in words, use a hundred, a thousand (WITH a):The palace was build a thousand years ago.Compare: ‘The palace was built 1000 years ago.’For emphasis or to be exact, it is possible to use one instead of a:I am one hundred percent against the idea.After a/one/five/twelve etc, the words hundred, thousand, etc are always SINGULAR and are NOT followed by of:Five hundred children are born in the city every day.More than three thousand people were there.Similarly, of is NOT used after 100, 250, 3000 etc:If you kill 200 whales a year, they will soon disappear.Hundreds (of), thousands (of) etc are used only when you give a general idea of how many or how much: ‘There were hundreds of stars in the sky.’ ‘They’ve spent thousands (of pounds) on improvements to the house.’Use and between hundred and the next number. (In American English, and is often omitted, especially in formal styles.)BrE The club has about a hundred and thirty members.AmE The club has about a hundred (and) thirty members.

(In American English, and is often omitted, especially in formal styles.)BrE The club has about a hundred and thirty members.AmE The club has about a hundred (and) thirty members.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We hung just over a million of little electric bulbs on the trees.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We hung just over a million little electric bulbs on the trees.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In the last ten years, more than two million of people have come to Milan to find work.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In the last ten years, more than two million people have come to Milan to find work.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nearly half million people entered the country.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nearly half a million people entered the country.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I don't mind to wait a bit longer.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I don't mind waiting a bit longer.
common_error_corrections.explanation: (Not) mind doing sth: 'Would you mind posting this letter for me when you go into town?'Come/spring to mind (WITHOUT my, his, their, etc): 'When I'm planning a camping holiday, the first thing that comes to mind is the weather.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was raining but we didn't mind it.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It was raining but we didn't mind.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When the object of mind can be understood from the context, mind is not followed by a pronoun: 'Do you mind waiting a few minutes?' 'No, I don't mind.'Bear in mind (NOT have): 'Something else you need to bear in mind is the fact that not all countries have public transport.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The first thing that comes to my mind when I think about France is wine.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The first thing that comes to mind when I think about France is wine.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Come/spring to mind (WITHOUT my, his, their, etc): 'When I'm planning a camping holiday, the first thing that comes to mind is the weather.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Having in mind that the roads will be busy, I think that we should make an early start.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Bearing in mind that the roads will be busy, I think that we should make an early start.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Bear in mind (NOT have): 'Something else you need to bear in mind is the fact that not all countries have public transport.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The train arrived at exactly twelve past three.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The train arrived at exactly twelve minutes past three.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When telling the time, minutes must be used after all numbers exceptfive, ten, twenty, and twenty-five.Compare: 'It's twenty (minutes) past ten.' (minutes can be used) 'It's twenty-three minutes past ten.' (minutes must be used)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The college is a twenty minutes bus ride from my flat.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The college is a twenty-minute bus ride from my flat.

(In American English, and is often omitted, especially in formal styles.)BrE The club has about a hundred and thirty members.AmE The club has about a hundred (and) thirty members.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Her flight was held up on account of the mist.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Her flight was held up on account of the fog.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Mist = tiny drops of water in the air that make it difficult to see things that are far away: 'As the day wore on, the early morning mist quickly disappeared.'Fog = very thick mist: 'Traffic on several stretches of the M1 was slowed to a walking pace this morning as the result of thick fog.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It doesn't matter if you do a slight mistake.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It doesn't matter if you make a slight mistake.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Make a mistake (NOT do): 'It's easy to make mistakes when you're tired.'DO · HAVE · MAKE · TAKEMany phrases begin with a very common very such as do, make, have, or take: ‘I felt very nervous about taking the test but, after having a long talk with Mrs Fisher, I decided I would just do my best and try not to make too many silly mistakes.’ These verbs can be combined with some nouns but not with others and since they do not have a clear meaning of their own, choosing the right combination can be a problem. Phrases which tend to cause difficulty are shown below.HAVE:Have a bath (or esp. AmE take): ‘She’s probably upstairs having a bath.’Have (your) breakfast: ‘We usually have breakfast in the kitchen.’Have (your) dinner: ‘We had dinner and then went for a walk.’Have a drink: ‘I’ll collapse if I don’t have a drink soon.’Have (an) experience: ‘He has no experience of running a large company.’Have fun: ‘You can’t stop people from having fun.’Have a holiday: ‘It’s almost a year since we had a real holiday.’Have an interview: ‘I’ve had six interviews but no one has offered me a job.’Have a lesson: ‘Every morning we have three fifty-minute lessons.’Have (your) lunch: ‘Isn’t it about time we had lunch?’Have an operation: ‘Before I had the operation I could hardly walk.’Have a party: ‘On Saturday we’re having a party.’Have a picnic: ‘If it’s sunny we could have a picnic.’Have a shower (or esp. AmE take): ‘It only takes me a minute to have a shower.’TAKE:Take/do an examination: ‘Why do we have to take so many tests?’Take (your) medicine: ‘Don’t forget to take your medicine.’Take a pill: ‘He refuses to take sleeping pills.’Take/do a test: ‘The last test I took was a disaster.’MAKE:Make an effort: ‘I had to make a big effort not to laugh.’Make a journey: ‘It was the first journey he’d made all on his own.’Make a mistake: ‘He has made a serious mistake.’Make a noise: ‘How can one small child make so much noise?’Make progress: ‘I made very little progress at the start of the course.’DO:Do your best: ‘Don’t worry, Tim. Just do your best.’Do (or cause) damage: ‘The storm did a lot of damage to the crops.’Do an exercise: ‘Have you done your exercises today?’Do an experiment: ‘To do this experiment, you’ll need two eggs.’Do (sb) good: ‘The holiday has done him a lot of good.’Do harm: ‘A scandal would do his reputation a lot of harm.’Do your homework: ‘Have you done your homework yet?’Do a job: ‘I’ve got one or two jobs to do this evening.’Do the/some shopping: ‘Jake has gone into town to do some shopping.’Do research: ‘We need to do a lot more research.’Do things: ‘We’ve done lots of different things today.’Do your training: ‘Where did you do your training?’Note also: do something/anything etc: ‘I can’t come now – I’m doing something.’ ‘He hasn’t done anything wrong.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Dear Mister Southcroft ...
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Dear Mr Southcroft ...

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Basement flats are often dark and moist.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Basement flats are often dark and damp.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Moist = slightly wet, especially in a pleasant way: 'The bread was still nice and moist.' 'These plants prefer a warm, moist atmosphere.'Damp = slightly wet, especially in a cold and unpleasant way: 'Our hotel room felt cold and damp.' 'On damp days, we have to dry the washing indoors.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In that moment the door opened.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: At that moment the door opened.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In a moment = very soon: 'I'll have to go in a moment.'At that moment = at that particular time: 'Just at that moment the telephone rang.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: At the moment the girl opened her eyes.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: At that moment the girl opened her eyes.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are telling a story or reporting what happened, use at that moment: 'At that moment the car skidded on the ice and went off the road.'Compare: 'At the moment I'm working in a restaurant.' (= now, at the present time)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: At the moment I saw him, I knew something was wrong.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The moment I saw him, I knew something was wrong.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The moment (WITHOUT at) = as soon as: 'He fell in love with Samantha the moment he set eyes on her.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'd like to see him in my office the moment he will arrive.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'd like to see him in my office the moment he arrives.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is impossible to visit all the monuments of London in one day.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It is impossible to see all the sights of London in one day.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Monument = (1) a structure, usually made of stone, that is built to remind people of an important event or famous person; memorial: 'The inscription at the foot of the monument read: To all those who gave their lives so that others could live in freedom.(2) a building or structure that is preserved because of its historical importance: 'If you are interested in ancient monuments you will find the Pyramids fascinating.'See the sights = visit the interesting places in a city or country: 'I wanted to look round Moscow and see the sights.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The mood of the castle depends on the weather.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The atmosphere of the castle depends on the weather.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Mood = the way someone feels at a particular time, such as happy, angry, etc: 'I'd keep clear of George this morning - he's in one of his bad moods.'Atmosphere = the general impression that a place gives you: 'Their house always has a warm, friendly atmosphere.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The streets were very crowded and had a holiday mood.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
The streets were very crowded and had a holiday atmosphere.
The streets were full of people in a holiday mood.
choices: very crowded and had a holiday mood
very crowded and had a holiday atmosphere
full of people in a holiday mood

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In Taiwan the food is more cheaper than in England.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In Taiwan the food is cheaper than in England.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use more with the -er form of an adjective or adverb: 'Leather bags are more expensive but they tend to last longer.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: These machines make farming much more easier.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: These machines make farming much easier.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use more with the -er form of an adjective or adverb: 'Leather bags are more expensive but they tend to last longer.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My wife had left the hotel and I no more needed a double room.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My wife had left the hotel and I no longer needed a double room.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When talking about time, use no longer (NOT no more): 'The offices are no longer occupied.'Note the alternative: 'My wife had left the hotel and I didn't need a double room any more.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Some women more or less are forced to work nowadays.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Some women are more or less forced to work nowadays.
common_error_corrections.explanation: More or less is usually placed immediately in front of the word or phrase that it modifies: 'The two words have more or less the same meaning.' 'My wife and I met each other more or less by accident.' 'That's more or less everything you need to know.'In everyday conversation more or less also comes at the end of a sentence: 'I guess that's everything you need to know, more or less.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: At morning I wake up at 6.30.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In the morning I wake up at 6.30.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The trains are very crowded in morning.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The trains are very crowded in the morning.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Where I come from, the most teachers have to teach at two schools in order to earn enough.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Where I come from, most teachers have to teach at two schools in order to earn enough.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'nearly all', use most (NOT the most): 'Most universities provide a wide range of courses.'Use the most in comparisons: 'Which city has the most tourists?' 'Rome and Florence are indeed beautiful, but Venice is by far the most romantic.'Use (the) most when comparing one person or thing with all others: 'This is the most ridiculous excuse I've ever heard.'When comparing just two people or things, use (the) more: 'Which is (the) more expensive - an ALR or an IBM?'Note that in everyday conversation some people use (the) most instead of (the) more, but careful users consider this to be incorrect.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Both girls are clever but Edna is the most intelligent.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Both girls are clever but Edna is (the) more intelligent.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use (the) most when comparing one person or thing with all others: 'This is the most ridiculous excuse I've ever heard.'When comparing just two people or things, use (the) more: 'Which is (the) more expensive - an ALR or an IBM?'Note that in everyday conversation some people use (the) most instead of (the) more, but careful users consider this to be incorrect.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We see each other mostly every day.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We see each other almost every day.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use almost/nearly with all/every/everyone etc (NOT mostly): 'Almost everyone in the office has had a cold recently.'Compare: 'The students here are mostly Swiss or German.' (= most of the students here...)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Mostly every family has a television.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nearly every family has a television.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use almost/nearly with all/every/everyone etc (NOT mostly): 'Almost everyone in the office has had a cold recently.'Compare: 'The students here are mostly Swiss or German.' (= most of the students here...)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's an old car and the motor is very noisy.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It's an old car and the engine is very noisy.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Motor = the part of a machine which turns electrical power into movement: 'My video camera isn't working. Either the battery is flat or there's something wrong with the motor.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When they saw that I couldn't move myself, they called an ambulance.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When they saw that I couldn't move, they called an ambulance.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Our English teacher is called Mr John.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Our English teacher is called Mr (John) Smith.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Mr/Mrs/Miss/Ms (+ first name) + surname: 'Mrs Waters', 'Mr Clive Upton'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Dear Mr,
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Dear Sir,
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are writing a formal letter and you know the surname of the addressee, begin Dear Mr Smith, Dear Mrs Jones, Dear Ms Simpson etc. When you do not know the person's surname, begin Dear Sir, Dear Madam or Dear Sir/Madam.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Dear Mr/Mrs,
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Dear Sir/Madam,
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are writing a formal letter and you know the surname of the addressee, begin Dear Mr Smith, Dear Mrs Jones, Dear Ms Simpson etc. When you do not know the person's surname, begin Dear Sir, Dear Madam or Dear Sir/Madam.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Dear Mr Alan Jones,
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Dear Mr Jones,
common_error_corrections.explanation: Dear is followed by Mr/Mrs/Ms + surname only (NOT first name + surname): 'Dear Mrs Jackson'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We don't need to hire that much employees.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We don't need to hire that many employees.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Much + uncountable noun: 'There isn't much traffic today.' 'There was too much furniture in the room.'Many + plural (countable) noun: 'There aren't many cars today.' 'There were too many chairs in the room.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There are as much disadvantages as advantages.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There are as many disadvantages as advantages.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Much + uncountable noun: 'There isn't much traffic today.' 'There was too much furniture in the room.'Many + plural (countable) noun: 'There aren't many cars today.' 'There were too many chairs in the room.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There are too much people in Mexico.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There are too many people in Mexico.
