common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nowadays, there are much more criminals than policemen.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nowadays, there are far more criminals than policemen.
common_error_corrections.explanation: At the beginning of a phrase that ends with a plural (countable) noun, use far (NOT much). Compare 'much more traffic', 'far more cars'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I make much too many mistakes.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I make far too many mistakes.
common_error_corrections.explanation: At the beginning of a phrase that ends with a plural (countable) noun, use far (NOT much). Compare 'much more traffic', 'far more cars'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: As a doctor he earns much money.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: As a doctor he earns a lot of money.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: British culture is much different from ours.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: British culture is very different from ours.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Much is used before an adjective (1) in questions and negative sentences: 'Is British culture much different from ours?' 'No, it isn't much different.' (2) before comparative forms: 'His last novel was much longer and much more interesting.' (3) before certain past participles acting as adjectives: 'Her drawings are much admired.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We were much afraid that we would miss the flight.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We were very afraid that we would miss the flight.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Much is used before an adjective (1) in questions and negative sentences: 'Is British culture much different from ours?' 'No, it isn't much different.' (2) before comparative forms: 'His last novel was much longer and much more interesting.' (3) before certain past participles acting as adjectives: 'Her drawings are much admired.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nowadays I prefer classical musics.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nowadays I prefer classical music.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Music is an uncountable noun: 'Her hobbies are gardening and music.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Are we allowed to play a pop music?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Are we allowed to play pop music?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Music is an uncountable noun: 'Her hobbies are gardening and music.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After leaving school, he joined a music band.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: After leaving school, he joined a band.
common_error_corrections.explanation: (Jazz/rock) band or (pop/rock) group (NOT music band): 'The band's new album has just been released.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: People are not as careful as they must be and drop their litter in the streets.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: People are not as careful as they should be and drop their litter in the streets.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use must (or have to) when, for example, there is a law or rule and you are not free to choose or decide for yourself: 'Candidates must answer all the questions in Part A and two questions in Part B.'Use should (or ought to) when, for example, someone advises you to do something but you are free to choose or decide for yourself: 'At the end of the examination, you should check your answers.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The pupils mustn't go to the meeting if they don't want to.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The pupils needn't go to the meeting if they don't want to.
choices: mustn't go to the meeting if
needn't go to the meeting if
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use must not/never when you mean that it is essential that someone does not do something: 'The door to the X-ray room must never be opened when the red light is on.'When you mean that it is not necessary for someone to do something, use needn't or don't need/have to: 'You needn't pay now. You can wait until the furniture has been delivered.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You must be pleased to hear that I've already got the tickets.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You'll be pleased to hear that I've already got the tickets.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you inform someone of something, use will be + pleased/interested + to hear/know/learn (NOT must): 'You will be pleased to know that your old friend Peter has been promoted to Associate Professor.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If you can't find her, she must hide somewhere.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If you can't find her, she must be hiding somewhere.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you do not actually know where someone is or what they are doing, but certain facts allow you to guess, use must be or must be doing: 'If she isn't in her office, she must be in the canteen.' 'If she's in the canteen, she must be having her lunch.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: This beautiful village is named 'Cadaques'.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: This beautiful village is called 'Cadaques'.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mention the name by which someone or something is known, use call/be called (NOT name/be named): 'Most people call him Bob but he prefers to be called Robert.'Compare: 'They've named/called the baby Louise.' (= the name they have chosen for the baby is Louise)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I stayed in and watched a film named 'The Clockwork Orange'.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I stayed in and watched a film called 'The Clockwork Orange'.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mention the name by which someone or something is known, use call/be called (NOT name/be named): 'Most people call him Bob but he prefers to be called Robert.'Compare: 'They've named/called the baby Louise.' (= the name they have chosen for the baby is Louise)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: What we used to name 'the Cold War' is now over.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: What we used to call 'the Cold War' is now over.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mention the name by which someone or something is known, use call/be called (NOT name/be named): 'Most people call him Bob but he prefers to be called Robert.'Compare: 'They've named/called the baby Louise.' (= the name they have chosen for the baby is Louise)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They named their children from their grandparents.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They named their children after their grandparents.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Name a child after sb: 'We've decided to name her Sarah, after her grandmother.'In American English name a child for sb is also possible, although not very common.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When immersed in water, the cloth narrows.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When immersed in water, the cloth shrinks.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Narrow (of roads, rivers, etc) = become less wide: 'Just beyond the bend, the river begins to narrow.'Shrink (especially of cloth) = become smaller as a result of being wet or placed in water: 'I suggest you buy the larger size just in case it shrinks.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's hard to tell which nation he comes from.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It's hard to tell which country he comes from.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A person comes from, lives in, feels part of, etc a particular country (NOT nation): 'Some people in this country think that the leadership is too weak.' 'People living in former Soviet bloc countries are undergoing a difficult period of transition.'Nation is less common than country and is mainly used when a country is considered as a political or economic structure: 'Japan has become the richest nation in the world.' 'Representatives from the world's leading industrial nations will meet next month in Geneva.'Note the alternative: 'I couldn't tell his nationality.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My name is Iman Jalil and my nationality is Iraqi.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My name is Iman Jalil and I come from Iraq.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The usual way of referring to someone's nationality is to use come from: 'Most of the students in my class come from Oman or Bahrain.'Nationality is used mainly in formal styles: 'Visitors of Swedish nationality do not require a visa.' 'Despite being born in Germany, these children do not have an automatic right to German nationality.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The airport extension is strongly opposed by the natives.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The airport extension is strongly opposed by the local residents.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Nowadays the noun native is usually used in formal styles to refer to the place where someone was born: 'His real name was Harvey Pepper, a native of Montreal.' or to the country/region where a particular animal or plant has always grown: 'This useful herb is a native of southern Europe, but has adjusted well to colder climates.'To refer to the people who live in and around a village, town or city, and have shared interests and activities, use local residents, local population or (in informal styles) locals: 'Local residents are against the motorway proposal.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have always found the nature fascinating.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have always found nature fascinating.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Nature (= the natural world of birds, trees, rivers, etc) is never used with the: 'We must stop destroying nature before it is too late.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He decided to visit a friend who lived very near from where he was at that moment.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He decided to visit a friend who lived very near (to) where he was at that moment.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Near or near to (NOT near from): 'The post office is near (to) the bank.' 'If we moved to Dallas, we would be nearer to my parents.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I went near to the girl and told her my name.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I went up to the girl and told her my name.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I sometimes meet friends in a near restaurant.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I sometimes meet friends in a nearby restaurant.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To say that something is only a short distance from a place, use nearby: 'I stopped at one of the nearby cottages and asked the way.' 'It's very convenient having a supermarket nearby.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I ran to the telephone box which was near to call an ambulance.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I ran to the telephone box nearby to call an ambulance.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To say that something is only a short distance from a place, use nearby: 'I stopped at one of the nearby cottages and asked the way.' 'It's very convenient having a supermarket nearby.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Their house is nearby the new airport.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Their house is near the new airport.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Nearby is used as an adjective or adverb: 'We flew from a nearby airport.' 'There is an airport nearby.'When you need a preposition, use near: 'The hotel is near the sea.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In the countryside there is nearly no pollution.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In the countryside there is hardly any pollution.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Instead of saying nearly no/nobody/never etc, use hardly any/anybody/ever etc: 'Hardly any of my friends are married.' 'Hardly anybody objected to the idea.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was then that I felt the necessity to improve my English.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It was then that I felt the need to improve my English.
common_error_corrections.explanation: If something is a necessity, you must have it or do it, or it must happen:'If you saw the terrible conditions in which these people are living, you would appreciate the necessity to step up foreign aid.' 'For anyone who runs a large business, a computer is an absolute necessity.'Need has a similar meaning to necessity but it is also used in connection with something that you want to do/have/happen (although it is not essential): 'I began to feel the need for a change of life style.' 'Don't you ever feel the need to do something more creative?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is no need to tell the police about the accident.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There is no need to tell the police about the accident.
common_error_corrections.explanation: There is no need to do sth (NOT it is ...): 'There's no need to start getting upset.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There is a great need of international understanding.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There is a great need for international understanding.
common_error_corrections.explanation: 'To be in need of something', but 'to have/there's a need for something'. Also, when used as a subject it is usually "need for".

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We have an urgent need of a new secretary.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We are in urgent need of a new secretary.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be in need of sth (= require): 'The car is in need of a good clean.' 'Are you in need of any assistance?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'm in urgent need for a loan.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm in urgent need of a loan.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be in need of sth (= require): 'The car is in need of a good clean.' 'Are you in need of any assistance?'Remember: To be in need of something, but to have a need for something.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: For a long time I have felt the need of improving my French.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: For a long time I have felt the need to improve my French.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A need to do sth (NOT of/for doing): 'I don't understand their need to sell the house.'In affirmative sentences, use need to do sth (WITH to): 'I need to get to the airport by seven at the latest.'Compare (1) the negative forms: 'She doesn't need to stay if she doesn't want to.' 'She needn't stay if she doesn't want.'(2) the question forms: 'Does she need to stay any longer?' 'Need she stay any longer?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Tina needs leave her house at seven o'clock every morning.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Tina needs to leave her house at seven o'clock every morning.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In affirmative sentences, use need to do sth (WITH to): 'I need to get to the airport by seven at the latest.'Compare (1) the negative forms: 'She doesn't need to stay if she doesn't want to.' 'She needn't stay if she doesn't want.'(2) the question forms: 'Does she need to stay any longer?' 'Need she stay any longer?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Needless to say that his films are very popular with children.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Needless to say, his films are very popular with children.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Needless to say (an adverb meaning 'of course') is NOT followed by a that clause.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Some teachers neglect how much a student can take in during one lesson.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Some teachers forget how much a student can take in during one lesson.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Neglect = (1) fail to look after someone or something properly: 'The garden has been badly neglected and will require a lot of attention.'(2) (formal) fail to do something, especially something that you ought to do: 'The public are demanding to know why the government neglected to warn them of the oil shortage.'Forget = fail to realize something (and be guided by it): 'Children tend to forget that their parents like to have fun too.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There was a negligent amount of liquid in the test tube.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There was a negligible amount of liquid in the test tube.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Negligent = failing to take proper care, especially in your job; careless: 'The court decided that the pilot of the crashed aircraft had been negligent.'Negligible = (of an amount) so small that it has no effect and can be ignored: 'The cost of maintaining the machine is negligible.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Inside the examination room we could neither smoke or talk.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Inside the examination room we could neither smoke nor talk.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Neither ... nor ... (NOT neither ... or ...): 'The sales assistant was neither friendly nor helpful.'Compare: 'You can either come with me or wait here.'After neither and neither ... nor ... the verb is affirmative (NOT negative): 'Neither applicant had the right qualifications.' 'Neither the teachers nor the students had been informed.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: His parents neither shouted at him or smacked him.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: His parents neither shouted at him nor smacked him.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Neither ... nor ... (NOT neither ... or ...): 'The sales assistant was neither friendly nor helpful.'Compare: 'You can either come with me or wait here.'After neither and neither ... nor ... the verb is affirmative (NOT negative): 'Neither applicant had the right qualifications.' 'Neither the teachers nor the students had been informed.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have neither studied the language nor the culture.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have studied neither the language nor the culture.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Neither should be placed immediately before the first of the connected items and nor immediately before the second. Compare: 'I have neither studied nor experienced the culture.'After neither + singular noun, the verb is singular: 'Neither player wants a transfer.'After neither of + plural noun, careful users prefer a singular verb: 'Neither of the players wants a transfer.' Some people use a plural verb, especially in informal styles: 'Neither of the players want a transfer.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Neither John's father nor mine couldn't understand the problem.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Neither John's father nor mine could understand the problem.
common_error_corrections.explanation: After neither and neither ... nor ... the verb is affirmative (NOT negative): 'Neither applicant had the right qualifications.' 'Neither the teachers nor the students had been informed.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Neither teachers are coming.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
Neither teacher is coming.
Neither of the teachers is coming.
common_error_corrections.explanation: After neither + singular noun, the verb is singular: 'Neither player wants a transfer.'After neither of + plural noun, careful users prefer a singular verb: 'Neither of the players wants a transfer.' Some people use a plural verb, especially in informal styles: 'Neither of the players want a transfer.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Thinking she might be hurt, I felt very nervous.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Thinking she might be hurt, I felt very anxious.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Nervous = worried and unable to relax, especially because you lack confidence: 'There's no need to be so nervous. It's only an interview.'Anxious = very worried about something which may happen or may have happened: 'I knew that there were no sharks around but all the same I couldn't help feeling anxious.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: What really made me nervous was the way he kept pulling my sleeve.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: What really irritated me was the way he kept pulling my sleeve.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Nervous = worried and unable to relax: 'I hate the way the teacher watches me when I'm working - it makes me feel nervous.'Irritate = (of something unpleasant that happens repeatedly or continuously) make someone feel slightly angry; annoy: 'His attempts to sound important irritate people.'Note the alternative: 'What I found really irritating was the way ... '

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I asked him to never arrive late.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I asked him never to arrive late.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Never and not usually go immediately in front of a to infinitive: 'He's promised never to do it again.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You never can get really good beef in our local supermarket.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You can never get really good beef in our local supermarket.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My father did never have the opportunity to go to university.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My father never had the opportunity to go to university.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do is often used with not to make negative statements: 'I didn't answer the letter.' 'She doesn't invite strangers.' However, do is NOT used in this way with never: 'I never answered the letter.' 'She never invites strangers.'The exception to this rule is when do is used for emphasis: 'You never did tell me why you decided to leave your last job.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She said some of the rudest things I have never heard in all my life.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She said some of the rudest things I have ever heard in all my life.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Never = at no time: 'I've never met his wife.' 'I had never met his wife before yesterday.'Ever = at any time: 'Have you ever met his wife?'Note that ever is often used after a superlative: 'His wife is the kindest person I've ever met.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: 'Nobody will never find me,' he thought.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: 'Nobody will ever find me,' he thought.
common_error_corrections.explanation: After nobody/nothing/rarely and other words with a negative meaning, use ever (NOT never): 'After she won the national lottery, nothing was ever the same again.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Never I had seen such an ugly face.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Never had I seen such an ugly face.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was born and grew up in Switzerland, nevertheless Italy is the country that I have grown to love and where I now live.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
I was born and grew up in Switzerland. Nevertheless, Italy is the country that I have grown to love and where I now live.
I was born and grew up in Switzerland but (nevertheless) Italy is the country that I have grown to love and where I now live.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The news are never very good nowadays.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The news is never very good nowadays.
common_error_corrections.explanation: News is an uncountable noun: 'Why do Clive's letters never contain any news?' 'There's one piece of news that I'm sure will interest you.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'm looking forward to hearing a good news from you.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm looking forward to hearing some good news from you.
common_error_corrections.explanation: News is an uncountable noun: 'Why do Clive's letters never contain any news?' 'There's one piece of news that I'm sure will interest you.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'm looking forward to seeing you on next Sunday.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm looking forward to seeing you next Sunday.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have some spare time this week but the next week I'll have to start work.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have some spare time this week but next week I'll have to start work.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There is a nice and quiet room where I do my work.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
There is a nice quiet room where I do my work.
The room where I do my work is nice and quiet.
choices: There is a nice and quiet room where I do my work
The room where I do my work is nice and quiet
There is a nice quiet room where I do my work
common_error_corrections.explanation: Two-part adjectival phrases with nice such as 'nice and quiet, and 'nice and clean' are always placed after the noun they modify: 'The house is always nice and tidy.' Do not use and after nice when it comes in front of a noun: 'Right now I could do with a nice cold drink.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I don't like driving in the night.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I don't like driving at night.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was about nine o'clock in the night when we heard a noise outside.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It was about nine o'clock at night when we heard a noise outside.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: 'Where were you in the night of June 3rd?' he asked.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: 'Where were you on the night of June 3rd?' he asked.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: No one of us regrets volunteering.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
None of us regrets volunteering.
Not one of us regrets volunteering.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'not one', use none or (for emphasis) not one: 'None of the children could tell the time.' 'Not one of the trainees has a medical background.'No one and nobody cannot be followed by of unless the phrase introduced by of is descriptive: 'No one of any importance was at the meeting.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nobody have complained about the noise.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nobody has complained about the noise.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Nobody/no one + singular verb: 'Is nobody going to help you?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When I arrived, there were nobody at home.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When I arrived, there was nobody at home.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Nobody/no one + singular verb: 'Is nobody going to help you?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He closed the door quietly so that nobody wouldn't hear him.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He closed the door quietly so that nobody would hear him.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nobody has done something yet.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nobody has done anything yet.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I turned on the radio but there was no noise.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I turned on the radio but there was no sound.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Noise = (1) loud unpleasant sounds heard as a single mass: 'The noise of the traffic gave me a headache.' 'People were making such a lot of noise that I couldn't hear what she was saying.' (2) a sound that is unpleasant and/or without meaning: 'The radio suddenly started making a funny noise.' 'What was that noise?'Sound = something that is heard or received by the ear, especially something that you recognize or can give a meaning to: 'I've always loved the sound of a classical guitar.' 'I could hear the sound of someone crying in the next room.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He was woken up by the noise of broken glass.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He was woken up by the sound of broken glass.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Noise = (1) loud unpleasant sounds heard as a single mass: 'The noise of the traffic gave me a headache.' 'People were making such a lot of noise that I couldn't hear what she was saying.' (2) a sound that is unpleasant and/or without meaning: 'The radio suddenly started making a funny noise.' 'What was that noise?'Sound = something that is heard or received by the ear, especially something that you recognize or can give a meaning to: 'I've always loved the sound of a classical guitar.' 'I could hear the sound of someone crying in the next room.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was woken up by a big noise outside the room.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was woken up by a loud noise outside the room.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Loud noise (NOT big): 'Habitual exposure to loud noises can damage the ear.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The restaurant was full and there was a loud noise.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The restaurant was full and there was a lot of noise.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A loud noise (countable) describes what you hear when, for example, somebody slams a door or drops a plate. To refer to continuous noise made during an activity, use noise as an uncountable noun: 'They don't know the difference between music and noise.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You can talk as long as you don't make a loud noise.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You can talk as long as you don't make a lot of noise.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A loud noise (countable) describes what you hear when, for example, somebody slams a door or drops a plate. To refer to continuous noise made during an activity, use noise as an uncountable noun: 'They don't know the difference between music and noise.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Mr Tong was nominated manager of the company in 1984.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Mr Tong was appointed manager of the company in 1984.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Nominate = suggest someone for election or selection (for a job or position): 'We need to nominate someone to take over from Harry as our new public relations officer.'Appoint = give someone a job or position: 'Mr H. Wilks has been officially appointed as the society's new public relations officer.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I checked the essay for mistakes but I couldn't find none.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I checked the essay for mistakes but I couldn't find any.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I told the police officer that in my opinion none of the two drivers was responsible.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I told the police officer that in my opinion neither of the two drivers was responsible.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When talking about two people or things, use neither. For three or more, use none.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The cafeteria is always crowded in the noon.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The cafeteria is always crowded at noon.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He told me to not spend too long in the sun.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He told me not to spend too long in the sun.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Not and never usually go immediatley in front of a to infinitive:'Try not to worry about anything.' 'It's hard not to feel sorry for him.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He has hurt his back and can't do nothing.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He has hurt his back and can't do anything.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I wrote him a notice saying that the package had arrived.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I wrote him a note saying that the package had arrived.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Notice = a short written statement giving information or directions, usually found in a public place: 'There was a notice on the wall saying"Private property. No parking."Note = a short informal letter or written message from one person to another: 'Just a quick note to say that Helen had a baby boy yesterday.'

Your job is what you do to earn your living: ‘You’ll never get a job if you don’t have any qualifications.’ ‘She’d like to change her job but can’t find anything better.’ Your job is also the particular type of work that you do: ‘John’s new job sounds really interesting.’ ‘I know she works for the BBC but I’m not sure what job she does.’A job may be full-time or part-time (NOT half-time or half-day): ‘All she could get was a part-time job at a petrol station.’Do (for a living). When you want to know about the type of work that someone does, the usual questions are What do you do? What does she do for a living? etc ‘What does your father do?’ - ‘He’s a police inspector.’Occupation and job have similar meanings. However, occupation is far less common than job and is used mainly in formal and official styles: ‘Please give brief details of your employment history and present occupation.’ ‘People in manual occupations seem to suffer less from stress.’Post/position. The particular job that you have in a company or organization is your post or position: ‘She’s been appointed to the post of deputy principal.’ ‘He’s applied for the position of sales manager.’ Post and position are used mainly in formal styles and often refer to jobs which have a lot of responsibility.Career. Your career is your working life, or the series of jobs that you have during your working life: ‘The scandal brought his career in politics to a sudden end.’ ‘Later on in his career, he became first secretary at the British Embassy in Washington.’Your career is also the particular kind of work for which you are trained and that you intend to do for a long time: ‘I wanted to find out more about careers in publishing.’Trade. A trade is a type of work in which you do or make things with your hands: ‘Most of the men had worked in skilled trades such as carpentry or printing.’ ‘My grandfather was a bricklayer by trade.’Profession. A profession is a type of work such as medicine, teaching, or law which requires a high level of training or education: ‘Until recently, medicine has been a male-dominated profession.’ ‘She entered the teaching profession in 1987.’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One of the eggs were bad.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One of the eggs was bad.
common_error_corrections.explanation: After a phrase beginning with one of, the verb is singular: 'One of the main disadvantages is the cost of the battery.'However when one of is followed by a relative clause, the verb in the relative clause can be singular or plural, depending on the meaning: 'I had a long talk to one of his daughters, who is married to an architect.' 'We were introduced to one of the consultants, who were gathered together in the foyer.' In cases where a singular verb and a plural verb seem equally possible, careful users generally prefer a plural verb: 'Peter is one of those people who are always prepared to help.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She is one of those children who refuses to share things.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She is one of those children who refuse to share things.
common_error_corrections.explanation: After a phrase beginning with one of, the verb is singular: 'One of the main disadvantages is the cost of the battery.'However when one of is followed by a relative clause, the verb in the relative clause can be singular or plural, depending on the meaning: 'I had a long talk to one of his daughters, who is married to an architect.' 'We were introduced to one of the consultants, who were gathered together in the foyer.' In cases where a singular verb and a plural verb seem equally possible, careful users generally prefer a plural verb: 'Peter is one of those people who are always prepared to help.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After we had been to Helen's house, we went to Paul's one.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: After we had been to Helen's house, we went to Paul's.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Avoid one/ones immediately after an -'s/-s' form, especially in formal styles: 'No, it's not mine - it's my wife's.' Compare: 'John's new one is the same as yours.' (= -'s/-s' form + adjective + noun)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If you can carry those books, I'll bring these ones.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If you can carry those books, I'll bring these.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Avoid ones immediately after these/those, especially in formal styles: 'Within this group, there are those who are willing to take risks and those who are more cautious.'Compare: 'These plastic ones are cheaper.' (= these/those + adjective + noun)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: This book will be of interest to all those ones involved in the tourist industry.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: This book will be of interest to all those involved in the tourist industry.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Avoid ones immediately after these/those, especially in formal styles: 'Within this group, there are those who are willing to take risks and those who are more cautious.'Compare: 'These plastic ones are cheaper.' (= these/those + adjective + noun)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: All the shoes and handbags they sell are handmade ones.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: All the shoes and handbags they sell are handmade.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Avoid one/ones after an adjective which can be used on its own, especially in formal styles: 'The new proposals are impractical.'Compare: 'We could do with a new one/some new ones.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: British children have more opportunities than Tunisian ones.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: British children have more opportunities than Tunisian children.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Ones is usually used to refer to things: 'Rechargeable batteries are more expensive than ordinary ones.' 'The red ones are fine, but I prefer the white ones.' Ones may also be used to refer to particular people: 'The older children laughed but the younger ones were scared.'In general statements about groups of people, ones is usually avoided: 'French students have to work harder than British students.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Young people learn more quickly than older ones.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Young people learn more quickly than older people.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Ones is usually used to refer to things: 'Rechargeable batteries are more expensive than ordinary ones.' 'The red ones are fine, but I prefer the white ones.' Ones may also be used to refer to particular people: 'The older children laughed but the younger ones were scared.'In general statements about groups of people, ones is usually avoided: 'French students have to work harder than British students.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One mustn't waste ones time when there is so much to do.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One mustn't waste one's time when there is so much to do.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Getting married for economic reasons is not a good start to ones married life.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Getting married for economic reasons is not a good start to one's married life.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One cannot succeed unless he works hard.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One cannot succeed unless one works hard.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English (unlike American English) it is not possible to change from one to he/his/her/ etc.Note, however, that most speakers find the repetition of one awkward and try to avoid it: 'One cannot succeed without working hard.' 'Success calls for a lot of hard work.'Avoiding sexism in your writingIn the past, when people referred to a member of a group containing both men and women (or boys and girls), they used the pronouns he/him/his:A good doctor listens carefully to his patients.Anyone who wants to join should give his name to the secretary.Nowadays, many people feel that this usage is unfair to women. If you want to avoid the danger of seeming sexist, you can use one of the following alternatives.Use They/Them/Their to refer back to an indefinite pronoun (anyone, somebody etc):Anyone who wants to join should give their name to the secretary.Some people object to this usage in formal styles, insisting that they (plural) does not agree in number with anyone (singular). This usage is nevertheless very common.Make all the forms plural:Good doctors listen carefully to their patients.Those who want to join should give their name to the secretary.Design the sentence in such a way that a personal pronoun is not needed. For example, instead of saying ‘If anyone wants to go now, he may do so’, just say ‘Anyone who wants to go now may do so.’Use he or she, his or her, etc:A good doctor listens carefully to his or her patients.This alternative is found in formal writing, and so is the use of he/she, his/her, s/he, etc.However, they are generally felt to produce awkward and unnatural sentences, especially when they are repeated, as in:If a doctor listens to his or her patients, he or she will be in a better position to help them.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The children get on well one another.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The children get on well with one another.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They had good opinions one another.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They had good opinions of one another.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Only when it started to rain he noticed that he had left his raincoat somewhere.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Only when it started to rain did he notice that he had left his raincoat somewhere.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He not only was a talented pianist but also a great composer.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He was not only a talented pianist but also a great composer.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The position of not only should be the same as the position of but also (i.e. immediately before an object, immediately before a main verb, etc).Compare: 'He injured not only his shoulder but also his elbow.' ('his shoulder' and 'his elbow' are both objects) 'He not only injured his back but also hurt his head.' ('injured' and 'hurt' are both verbs)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The level of pollution can only be reduced by the introduction of new laws.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The level of pollution can be reduced only by the introduction of new laws.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To avoid confusion in written English, only is usually placed as near as possible to the word or phrase that it modifies. Compare: 'Alison only posted the letter to Mr Jones.' (= she didn't write it) 'Alison posted only the letter to Mr Jones.' (= she didn't post the other letters)In spoken English the position of only is less important because the speaker uses stress to make the meaning clear.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If you only would stay longer, your English would improve.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
If only you would stay longer, your English would improve.
If you would only stay longer, your English would improve.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When if only is used to express a wish, the two words usually stay together: 'If only I could stop smoking.' Sometimes, only is placed in front of the main verb 'If I could only stop smoking.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Not only I passed, but I got a distinction.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Not only did I pass, but I got a distinction.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I got out of bed and opened the radio to listen to the news.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I got out of bed and turned/switched on the radio to listen to the news.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Turn on/off (or switch on/off) a light/radio/television (NOT open/close): 'The children are not allowed to turn on the television without permission.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If anyone tried to open a new topic, she would immediately interrupt.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If anyone tried to introduce a new topic, she would immediately interrupt.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Introduce a (new) topic/subject/argument (NOT open): 'You can't introduce new material in the last section of a report.'Use opened to describe an action and open to describe a state. Compare: 'The shop was opened at 8 a.m. and stayed open until 6 p.m.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I couldn't buy a newspaper because the shop wasn't opened.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I couldn't buy a newspaper because the shop wasn't open.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use opened to describe an action and open to describe a state. Compare: 'The shop was opened at 8 a.m. and stayed open until 6 p.m.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Have you heard what happened to the last patient he operated?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Have you heard what happened to the last patient he operated on?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Operate on sb: 'He is too weak at the moment to be operated on.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My niece was recently operated for appendicitis.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My niece was recently operated on for appendicitis.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Operate on sb: 'He is too weak at the moment to be operated on.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My mother is taking an operation tomorrow.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My mother is having an operation tomorrow.
common_error_corrections.explanation:
DO · HAVE · MAKE · TAKE
Many phrases begin with a very common very such as do, make, have, or take: ‘I felt very nervous about taking the test but, after having a long talk with Mrs Fisher, I decided I would just do my best and try not to make too many silly mistakes.’ These verbs can be combined with some nouns but not with others and since they do not have a clear meaning of their own, choosing the right combination can be a problem. Phrases which tend to cause difficulty are shown below.HAVEHave a bath (or esp. AmE take): ‘She’s probably upstairs having a bath.’Have (your) breakfast: ‘We usually have breakfast in the kitchen.’Have (your) dinner: ‘We had dinner and then went for a walk.’Have a drink: ‘I’ll collapse if I don’t have a drink soon.’Have (an) experience: ‘He has no experience of running a large company.’Have fun: ‘You can’t stop people from having fun.’Have a holiday: ‘It’s almost a year since we had a real holiday.’Have an interview: ‘I’ve had six interviews but no one has offered me a job.’Have a lesson: ‘Every morning we have three fifty-minute lessons.’Have (your) lunch: ‘Isn’t it about time we had lunch?’Have an operation: ‘Before I had the operation I could hardly walk.’Have a party: ‘On Saturday we’re having a party.’Have a picnic: ‘If it’s sunny we could have a picnic.’Have a shower (or esp. AmE take): ‘It only takes me a minute to have a shower.’TAKETake/do an examination: ‘Why do we have to take so many tests?’Take (your) medicine: ‘Don’t forget to take your medicine.’Take a pill: ‘He refuses to take sleeping pills.’Take/do a test: ‘The last test I took was a disaster.’MAKEMake an effort: ‘I had to make a big effort not to laugh.’Make a journey: ‘It was the first journey he’d made all on his own.’Make a mistake: ‘He has made a serious mistake.’Make a noise: ‘How can one small child make so much noise?’Make progress: ‘I made very little progress at the start of the course.’DODo your best: ‘Don’t worry, Tim. Just do your best.’Do (or cause) damage: ‘The storm did a lot of damage to the crops.’Do an exercise: ‘Have you done your exercises today?’Do an experiment: ‘To do this experiment, you’ll need two eggs.’Do (sb) good: ‘The holiday has done him a lot of good.’Do harm: ‘A scandal would do his reputation a lot of harm.’Do your homework: ‘Have you done your homework yet?’Do a job: ‘I’ve got one or two jobs to do this evening.’Do the/some shopping: ‘Jake has gone into town to do some shopping.’Do research: ‘We need to do a lot more research.’Do things: ‘We’ve done lots of different things today.’Do your training: ‘Where did you do your training?’Note also: do something/anything etc: ‘I can’t come now – I’m doing something.’ ‘He hasn’t done anything wrong.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Mr Barrett is going to get an operation on his back.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Mr Barrett is going to have an operation on his back.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: According to Henry's opinion, less money should be spent on weapons.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
In Henry's opinion, less money should be spent on weapons.
According to Henry, less money should be spent on weapons.
common_error_corrections.explanation: According to sb: 'According to Peter, deforestation is a serious problem.'In sb's opinion (NOT according to ... opinion): 'In Peter's opinion, deforestation is a very serious problem.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They are not afraid of saying their opinions.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They are not afraid of expressing their opinions.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Express/give your opinion (NOT say): 'The newspapers express a wide range of political opinions.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There is an opportunity that David's father will come tonight.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There is a chance that David's father will come tonight.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you talk about the likelihood of something happening, use chance (NOT opportunity): 'I think she has a good chance of passing.' 'There's very little chance that anyone has survived the crash.'Compare: 'Tomorrow's test will be an opportunity/a chance for you to find out how much you know.' (= a particular time when something is possible)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I oppose to violence.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I am opposed to violence.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Oppose sth (WITHOUT to) = think that something is wrong and try to stop it from happening or being accepted: 'Many leading scientists vigorously opposed Darwin's ideas.'Be opposed to sth = feel strongly that something is wrong: 'Many people are opposed to the use of fur by the clothing industry.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: People have opposite opinions about this matter.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: People have different opinions about this matter.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use opposite and the opposite of only when you mean that two things are as different as it is possible to be: 'I thought that the medicine would make him sleepy, but it had the opposite effect.' 'The opposite of long is short.' 'The two men went off in opposite directions.' (= one went to the left and one to the right)To describe people's opinions, life styles, ways of thinking etc, the usual word is different: 'These two schools of thought are completely different.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The Americans I met were opposite to what I had imagined.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The Americans I met were very different from what I had imagined.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use opposite and the opposite of only when you mean that two things are as different as it is possible to be: 'I thought that the medicine would make him sleepy, but it had the opposite effect.' 'The opposite of long is short.' 'The two men went off in opposite directions.' (= one went to the left and one to the right).To describe people's opinions, life styles, ways of thinking etc, the usual word is different: 'These two schools of thought are completely different.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My own country and the USA are totally opposite of each other.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My own country and the USA are totally different (from each other).
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use opposite and the opposite of only when you mean that two things are as different as it is possible to be: 'I thought that the medicine would make him sleepy, but it had the opposite effect.' 'The opposite of long is short.' 'The two men went off in opposite directions.' (= one went to the left and one to the right)To describe people's opinions, life styles, ways of thinking etc, the usual word is different: 'These two schools of thought are completely different.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The opposite woman was knitting a cardigan.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The woman opposite was knitting a cardigan.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When opposite means 'facing the speaker or the person/place being talked about', it comes immediately after the noun: 'The house opposite is also for sale.'One thing is opposite another thing (WITHOUT to/of): 'The nearest bus stop is opposite the bank.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: On the wall opposite to the door, there was a large painting.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: On the wall opposite the door, there was a large painting.
common_error_corrections.explanation: One thing is opposite another thing (WITHOUT to/of): 'The nearest bus stop is opposite the bank.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The phone booths are opposite of the tube station.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The phone booths are opposite the tube station.
common_error_corrections.explanation: One thing is opposite another thing (WITHOUT to/of): 'The nearest bus stop is opposite the bank.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: At night we used to go out with our friends or stayed at home listening to music.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: At night we used to go out with our friends or stay at home listening to music.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you use or to join two verbs, both verbs should have the same form. Compare: 'We used to go to the cinema or watch the television.' 'We went to the cinema or watched the television.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I think the microphone or the recording mechanism are broken.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I think the microphone or the recording mechanism is broken.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When each of the nouns joined by or is singular, the verb is usually singular: 'It is important to understand what one's son or daughter expects out of life.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Her oral English is very fluent and clear.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Her spoken English is very fluent and clear.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The use of oral to mean 'spoken' is restricted to certain technical phrases used in education: 'oral skills', 'an oral examination'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was so excited that I forgot to order them to check that the camera was working properly.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was so excited that I forgot to ask them to check that the camera was working properly.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You cannot order someone to do something unless you have the power to do so. Compare: 'The teacher ordered the child to sit down.' 'She asked her teacher if he could check her homework.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I've ordered two seats for tomorrow night's performance.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I've booked two seats for tomorrow night's performance.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Turning on the radio, I noticed immediately that it was out of order.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Turning on the radio, I noticed immediately that it was not working properly.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The phrase out of order is used mainly on notices stating that things such as public telephones, ticket machines, photocopiers etc are not working.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Archaeological treasures should be kept in the original country.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Archaeological treasures should be kept in the country of origin.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Country of origin = the country where something was made or discovered: 'They refuse to release these antiquities until the country of origin is properly established.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Many craftsmen have given up their original skills to work in factories.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Many craftsmen have given up their traditional skills to work in factories.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Original = (1) completely new: 'Nobody expected that the bikini, with its daringly original design, would catch on as it did.'(2) the one that exists first (usually followed later by other ones): 'The original edition contained only 170 pages.' 'The tennis court to the side of the house was the idea of the original owner.'Traditional = done or used by a group or society for a very long time: 'The dancers were wearing traditional African dress.' 'Kumar gave the traditional Hindu greeting.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She was wearing an original Japanese 'yukata'.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She was wearing a traditional Japanese 'yukata'.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Original = (1) completely new: 'Nobody expected that the bikini, with its daringly original design, would catch on as it did.'(2) the one that exists first (usually followed later by other ones): 'The original edition contained only 170 pages.' 'The tennis court to the side of the house was the idea of the original owner.'Traditional = done or used by a group or society for a very long time: 'The dancers were wearing traditional African dress.' 'Kumar gave the traditional Hindu greeting.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One of our teachers originates from Scotland.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One of our teachers comes from Scotland.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Originate is used in connection with things, ideas, customs etc (NOT people): 'No one really knows how the solar system originated.'If you are born in and/or grow up in a particular place, town, country etc, you come from that place: 'Where does Agneta come from - Sweden or Norway?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: 'Alcohol', 'alcove' and 'sofa' originate in Arabic.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: 'Alcohol', 'alcove' and 'sofa' come from Arabic.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Words that enter a language from other languages come from (or are derived from) those languages: 'The name 'terrier' comes from the Latin word 'terra' meaning 'the earth'.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: 'Go and play with some others children,' she said.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: 'Go and play with some other children,' she said.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When used before a noun, other never has an s: 'Do you have any other shoes besides the brown ones?'Compare: 'Besides the brown shoes, do you have any others?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It tells us all about nouns, verbs, adjectives and others.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It tells us all about such things as nouns, verbs and adjectives.
choices: such things as nouns, verbs and adjectives
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use and others at the end of a list of examples. In some styles it is possible to use etc for this purpose, but in formal styles it is safer to use such as (or such ... as): 'Candidates' performance in the test was influenced by factors such as age, sex, attitude and first language.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Remember to get there early otherwise you may not get a seat.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
Remember to get there early. Otherwise you may not get a seat.
Remember to get there early or you may not get a seat.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Unlike or, otherwise is an adverb (NOT a conjunction): 'I'm glad that you told me about the show being cancelled. Otherwise I'd have travelled all the way to Glasgow for nothing.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When we came out the restaurant, it was half past eleven.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When we came out of the restaurant, it was half past eleven.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Verb of movement + out: 'I'm afraid Mr Baker has just gone out.'Verb of movement + out of + somewhere (NOT out or out from): 'I've just seen Mr Baker going out of the building.'In informal conversation, out is sometimes used instead of out of: 'I saw someone jump out the window.' However, careful users consider this to be incorrect.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She suddenly stood up and ran out from the room.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She suddenly stood up and ran out of the room.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Verb of movement + out: 'I'm afraid Mr Baker has just gone out.'Verb of movement + out of + somewhere (NOT out or out from): 'I've just seen Mr Baker going out of the building.'In informal conversation, out is sometimes used instead of out of: 'I saw someone jump out the window.' However, careful users consider this to be incorrect.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She makes the dog stay outdoor during the summer.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She makes the dog stay outdoors during the summer.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Outdoor (WITHOUT -s) is an adjective: 'He enjoys the outdoor life.'Outdoors (WITH -s) is an adverb: 'He likes to work outdoors.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There are lots of outdoors activities in and around Coimbra.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There are lots of outdoor activities in and around Coimbra.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The new airport makes it easy to go outside the country.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The new airport makes it easy to get out of the country.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'away from', use (get/go) out of (NOT outside): 'It does you good to get out of the city now and again.' 'Without a false passport, he would never have been able to get out of the country.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'll be going outside London for a few days.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'll be going out of London for a few days.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you mean 'away from', use (get/go) out of (NOT outside): 'It does you good to get out of the city now and again.' 'Without a false passport, he would never have been able to get out of the country.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She was listening outside of the door.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She was listening outside the door.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English, outside is not used with of: 'You aren't allowed to park outside the bank.'In American English, both outside and outside of are used.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In spite of the film's many faults, in the overall it's worth seeing.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In spite of the film's many faults, on the whole it's worth seeing.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On the whole = in general: 'On the whole, the people I've been dealing with have been very cooperative.'Compare: 'Her overall command of English is excellent.' 'On the whole her command of English is excellent.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: England is okay on the overall, although some places are very dirty.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: England is okay on the whole, although some places are very dirty.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On the whole = in general: 'On the whole, the people I've been dealing with have been very cooperative.'Compare: 'Her overall command of English is excellent.' 'On the whole her command of English is excellent.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The important thing is your score in overall.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The important thing is your overall score.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Overall may be used as an adjective or adverb (NOT as a noun after in/on): 'The examination counts for 60 per cent of your overall grade.' 'You would have done better overall if you hadn't spent so long on the essay question.'Overall = (adv) (1) including everything: 'How much will the holiday cost, overall?' (2) generally: 'Overall, the weather in this area is good.'Overall = (adj) including everything: 'We're concerned about the overall effect of these films on younger viewers.'Above all = most importantly: 'Get plenty of sleep, eats lots of good food, and above all try to relax.' 'The sort of person we are looking for must be well qualified, suitably experienced, easy to get on with, and above all able to work independently.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: His idea of a good time included the sun, the sea, jokes, laughter, and overall friendship.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: His idea of a good time included the sun, the sea, jokes, laughter, and above all friendship.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Overall = (adv) (1) including everything: 'How much will the holiday cost, overall?' (2) generally: 'Overall, the weather in this area is good.'Overall = (adj) including everything: 'We're concerned about the overall effect of these films on younger viewers.'Above all = most importantly: 'Get plenty of sleep, eats lots of good food, and above all try to relax.' 'The sort of person we are looking for must be well qualified, suitably experienced, easy to get on with, and above all able to work independently.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I suddenly realized that my driving licence was overdue.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I suddenly realized that my driving licence had expired.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be/become overdue is used of payments, library books, video films that you have rented, etc: 'Even if the books are only one day overdue, you still have to pay a fine.'Expire is used of a licence, contract, membership card, etc: 'I wanted to pay by Visa but my card had expired.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I recently stayed an overnight at your hotel.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I recently stayed overnight at your hotel.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Overnight is used as an adverb and adjective (NOT as a noun):'I missed the connecting flight and had to stay at the airport overnight.' 'If we travel overnight, we'll be there in time for breakfast.' 'The overnight coach arrives in London at six in the morning.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I am writing to complain about my overnight at your hotel.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I am writing to complain about the night I spent at your hotel.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Overnight is used as an adverb and adjective (NOT as a noun):'I missed the connecting flight and had to stay at the airport overnight.' 'If we travel overnight, we'll be there in time for breakfast.' 'The overnight coach arrives in London at six in the morning.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They come here looking for work owing to the wages are higher.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They come here looking for work because the wages are higher.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Owing to is a preposition (NOT a conjunction): 'Owing to various political and economic factors, the land reclamation project has been discontinued.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I had the whole beach for my own.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I had the whole beach to myself.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Own (= belonging to you, or only to be used by you) is used either in front of a noun, or in the phrase of your own: 'I wish I had my own car.' 'I wish I had a car of my own.'Have sb/sth (all) to yourself = be the only person or people in a place, using something, talking to someone, etc: 'After the children had gone, we had the house all to ourselves.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He's decided to resign and work for his own.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He's decided to resign and work for himself.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do/want sth for yourself (NOT for your own): 'He's kept all the money for himself.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They want everything for their own.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They want everything for themselves.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do/want sth for yourself (NOT for your own): 'He's kept all the money for himself.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I didn't have a room for my own but had to share one.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I didn't have a room of my own but had to share one.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Of your own (NOT for): 'Timothy has now decided that he wants a bicycle of his own.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I now have enough money to buy an own car.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I now have enough money to buy my own car.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Own always follows my/her/their/Jill's etc (NOT an) 'their own children', 'her own flat', 'Tina's own radio'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I want to learn English in my own pace.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I want to learn English at my own pace.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You do something at your own pace (NOT in/by etc): 'With computer assisted language learning, students can work at their own pace.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I bought six eggs and a package of tea.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I bought six eggs and a packet of tea.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He smokes about one package a day.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He smokes about one packet a day.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There are so many unnecessary packages nowadays.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There is so much unnecessary packaging nowadays.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I enclose a stamped addressed envelope and a cheque for £5 for postage and package.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I enclose a stamped addressed envelope and a cheque for £5 for postage and packing.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The operation was successful but I still feel very painful.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The operation was successful but I still feel a lot of pain.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Painful = causing pain: 'The finger I trapped in the door is still very painful.' 'The child wriggled free and gave me a painful kick on the ankle.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The old pair next door have been married for 65 years.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The old couple next door have been married for 65 years.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pair usually refers to things (e.g. 'a pair of scissors/socks') or to two people who are seen (doing something) together: 'It's about time the pair of you did some work.' 'The German pair need just two more points for the match.' Pair also refers to two animals that stay together and produce young: 'a pair of swifts with a family to feed'.The usual word for a husband and wife (or two people in a similar relationship) is couple: 'Married couples should benefit from the new tax legislation.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Have you always worn a pair of glasses?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Have you always worn glasses?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pair of is usually used for individual reference (NOT general reference): 'I've bought two pairs of shoes for the children.'Compare: 'They sell shoes and handbags.' (NOT 'pairs of shoes').

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Each of us was given a clean paper to write on.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Each of us was given a clean sheet of paper to write on.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When it refers to the material that you write on, paper is an uncountable noun: 'The printer has run out of paper.' 'On the back of the piece of paper she had written her address.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I beg your pardon, but I was very busy and couldn't spare the time.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm sorry, but I was very busy and couldn't spare the time.
common_error_corrections.explanation: I beg your pardon is used (1) to apologize to a stranger because you have bumped into them by accident, sat in their seat by mistake, etc: 'I beg your pardon. I didn't know the tabel was reserved.'(2) to politely ask someone to repeat what they have said: 'Does this bus go to Marble Arch?' 'I beg your pardon?' 'This bus, does it go to Marble Arch?'(3) when someone has said something that makes you feel surprised, shocked, angry etc: 'Who's that man with the long nose?' 'I beg your pardon! That happens to be my husband.'Note that in formal situations you can use excuse/forgive me instead of I'm sorry: 'Please excuse me for taking so long to answer your letter.'Pardon (formal) = forgive: 'I'm sure they will pardon the occasional mistake.'Excuse = give someone permission to stay away from school, work etc, or leave a classroom, meeting etc: 'Can I be excused from swimming today please? I've got a cold.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'd like to beg your pardon because I was late.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
I'm sorry I was late.
Please forgive me for being late.
choices: I'd like to beg your pardon because I was

I've got a cold.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I asked the teacher if I could be pardoned for a few minutes.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I asked the teacher if I could be excused for a few minutes.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pardon (formal) = forgive: 'I'm sure they will pardon the occasional mistake.'Excuse = give someone permission to stay away from school, work etc, or leave a classroom, meeting etc: 'Can I be excused from swimming today please? I've got a cold.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The car was parking outside the flat all night.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The car was parked outside the flat all night.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use park when you are talking about what a driver does: 'You're not allowed to park (your car) in the city centre.' 'Where've you parked (your car)?'To talk about a vehicle that has been left somewhere and is not moving, use parked: 'That Ford van has been parked there for over a week.' 'The street is always full of parked cars.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It took me an hour to find a parking.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It took me an hour to find a parking space.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A parking space/place = a place in a street, car park etc where a vehicle can be left: 'My first attempt to back into the parking space was a disaster.'A car park (AmE parking lot) = a large open area or building where cars can be left: 'The supermarket has its own car park.'Parking (uncountable noun) = space(s) where vehicles can be left: 'Parking is available at Whitefriars Street.' 'There's ample parking in front of the hotel.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: What the town needs is an underground parking.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
What the town needs is underground parking.
What the town needs is an underground car park.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A parking space/place = a place in a street, car park etc where a vehicle can be left: 'My first attempt to back into the parking space was a disaster.'A car park (AmE parking lot) = a large open area or building where cars can be left: 'The supermarket has its own car park.'Parking (uncountable noun) = space(s) where vehicles can be left: 'Parking is available at Whitefriars Street.' 'There's ample parking in front of the hotel.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He refuses to part from his old camera.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He refuses to part with his old camera.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Part from a person: 'The two sisters were parted from each other when they were sent to different schools.'Part with a thing: 'Getting them to part with the money won't be easy.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A part of the difficulty was caused by her poor English.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Part of the difficulty was caused by her poor English.
common_error_corrections.explanation: It is unusual to use a before part of unless part of has an adjective in front of it. Compare: 'Lack of money was part of the problem.' 'Lack of money was a large part of the problem.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The country is vast and occupies the most part of the continent.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The country is vast and occupies most of the continent.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Most of (NOT most part of): 'She spent most of the morning in bed.'Note however the fixed phrase for the most part (= almost completely; mainly): 'The machines have for the most part been replaced.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: For the most part of his life he was devoted to his work.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: For most of his life he was devoted to his work.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Most of (NOT most part of): 'She spent most of the morning in bed.'Note however the fixed phrase for the most part (= almost completely; mainly): 'The machines have for the most part been replaced.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The annual celebration takes part in Valencia on 19th March.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The annual celebration takes place in Valencia on 19th March.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you take part in an activity, you do it together with other people: 'Altogether there are seventy-three competitors taking part in the race.' 'She's been invited to take part in a TV quiz programme.'Take place = (of a planned event) happen: 'The next meeting of the Nature Society will take place on Tuesday 3rd March.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The election will take part within the next two years.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The election will take place within the next two years.
