common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Did you take part in Yolanda's party on Saturday?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Did you go to Yolanda's party on Saturday?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go to a party/wedding etc (NOT take part in): 'We can't go to the party if we haven't been invited.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I think you ought to take part in a club.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I think you ought to join a club.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Join a club/society etc (NOT take part in): 'Guy is thinking about joining the drama society.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Teams from all Asian countries will participate the event.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Teams from all Asian countries will participate in the event.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Participate in sth = (formal) take part in: 'Our students are encouraged to participate in extra-curricular activities.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Putting fluoride in the water may solve the problem partly.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
Putting fluoride in the water may solve the problem to some extent.
Putting fluoride in the water may partly solve the problem.
choices: solve the problem to some extent
common_error_corrections.explanation: At the end of a clause use to some extent/to a certain extent or to some degree/to a (certain) degree (NOT partly). Compare: 'I partly agree with him.' 'I agree with him to some extent.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: On Christmas Day we always make a big party.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: On Christmas Day we always have a big party.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Have/hold/throw a party (NOT make/celebrate): 'Let's have a party and invite all our friends.'Celebrate Christmas, the New Year, someone's birthday, retirement, promotion, etc: 'Next month we're having a party to celebrate our sixth wedding anniversary.'A party is held somewhere (NOT made/celebrated): 'Where is the garden party being held?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Next Saturday we're celebrating a small party at John's house.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The party was being made at a friend's house.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We like to pass our holidays near the sea.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We like to spend our holidays near the sea.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You spend your holidays/a period of time somewhere (NOT pass): 'We spent a lazy afternoon down by the river.'When pass is used in connection with time, it is usually intransitive: 'Two weeks passed and there was still no reply.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We passed the night in a cheap hotel.

common_error_corrections.explanation: You spend your holidays/a period of time somewhere (NOT pass): 'We spent a lazy afternoon down by the river.'When pass is used in connection with time, it is usually intransitive: 'Two weeks passed and there was still no reply.'

common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I spent Christmas in London.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It has passed almost a year since we first met each other.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:

'I passed him in the corridor but he didn't say anything.''These remedies have been passed down from one generation to the next.'Past is (1) an adjective: 'For the past week he's been ill in bed.'(2) a preposition: 'She walked past me very quickly.'(3) an adverb: 'She walked past very quickly.'(4) a noun: 'He never speaks about his past.'Past is NOT used as a verb.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was a little past five when the game finished.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It was just after five when the game finished.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use past when you mention exact times: 'eight minutes past three', 'a quarter past two', 'twenty-five past seven'. Otherwise use just after, shortly after, etc: 'Her flight arrived shortly after midnight.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Their daily pattern doesn't include enough exercise.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Their daily routine doesn't include enough exercise.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To refer to the things that you do every day, usually in the same order, use routine: 'The trip to Oslo was quite exhausting, but at least it provided an escape from the same old routine.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Very few office workers get a good pay.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Very few office workers get good pay.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pay is an uncountable noun: 'They've given him a week's leave without pay.'Pay (an amount of money) for sth: 'Let me pay for the meal this time.' 'I can't afford to pay $200 for a suit.' 'How much did she pay for the car?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: 'Who paid the tickets?' I asked.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Dr Schneider charges a high payment but he is very good.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Dr Schneider charges a high fee but he is very good.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Payment = an amount of money that is paid for something: 'I had to get rid of the car because I couldn't keep up the payments.'Fee = an amount of money paid to a doctor, lawyer, or other professional person: 'The fee for one hour's private tuition is $60.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: For the first month the payment by the hour is 650 yen.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: For the first month the hourly rate is 650 yen.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Hourly/daily/weekly rate = the amount that someone charges or is paid for each hour/day/week that they work: 'He charges an hourly rate of $600 plus expenses.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She said she liked the jumper because the colour was very peculiar.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She said she liked the jumper because the colour was very unusual.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Peculiar = strange, especially in a surprising or unpleasant way: 'I'm not sure about this cheese. The taste is a bit peculiar.' common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After a hard day, all people need to relax.

common_error_corrections.explanation: A people (countable) = a race: 'His dream is that the peoples of the world will one day unite.'People (plural noun) = men, women and children: 'He finds it difficult to get along with people.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There was few people at the funeral.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I think people who does these things should be punished.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Only a small percentage of the windmills still works.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I am pleased to say that the tape recorder now works perfect.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I am pleased to say that the tape recorder now works perfectly.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Perfect is an adjective: 'My grandmother enjoys perfect health.'Perfectly is an adverb: 'The baby is perfectly healthy.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In his last film he performed a middle-aged school teacher.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In his last film he played a middle-aged school teacher.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Play a particular part or role in a film, play etc (NOT perform): 'What's the name of that good-looking American actor who played Butch Cassidy?'Compare: 'She has never performed in front of a live audience before.' common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Perhaps I will even decide to get married after all.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I may even decide to get married after all.
common_error_corrections.explanation: May/might usually sounds more natural than perhaps ... will: 'My mother may need to have an operation.' 'You might feel that the course is too difficult.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Perhaps it will be a good chance for you to have a rest.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It may be a good chance for you to have a rest.
common_error_corrections.explanation: May/might usually sounds more natural than perhaps ... will: 'My mother may need to have an operation.' 'You might feel that the course is too difficult.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: These traditions took a long period of time to evolve.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: These traditions took a long time to evolve.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A (long/short) time/while (WITHOUT period): 'You can stay here for a while, if you like.' 'Learning a foreign language can take a very long time.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She needs somewhere to live for a period of time.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She needs somewhere to live for a while.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A (long/short) time/while (WITHOUT period): 'You can stay here for a while, if you like.' 'Learning a foreign language can take a very long time.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: To get a job in Switzerland, foreigners need a special permission.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: To get a job in Switzerland, foreigners need special permission.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Permission is an uncountable noun: 'If you want to put up a tent, you'll have to get the farmer's permission.' 'Nobody is allowed to leave early without permission.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Eventually he gave me the permission to stay at home.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Eventually he gave me his permission to stay at home.
common_error_corrections.explanation: (Their/his mother's/the headmaster's) permission but NOT the permission: 'I'm sure that they'll let you use the library but it's better to have official permission.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Overpopulation doesn't permit these countries to develop.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Overpopulation stops these countries from developing/prevents these countries from developing.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Very soon every person will have a portable computer.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Very soon everyone will have a portable computer.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Any person can vote in the election.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Anyone can vote in the election.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Her husband talked so much that all the other persons in the room had to keep quiet.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Her husband talked so much that all the other people in the room had to keep quiet.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The plural of person is usually people: 'Thousands of people had gathered outside the palace to catch a glimpse of the new princess.'Persons is used mainly in public notices and other formal contexts: 'Seating capacity - 12 persons.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The meals can be improved if the canteen personal agree to cooperate.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The meals can be improved if the canteen personnel agree to cooperate.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He is a man of strong personality who will fight for what is right.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He is a man of strong character who will fight for what is right.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When talking about a person's moral quality, use character (NOT personality). Compare: 'For a career in sales, you need a forceful personality.' 'People of character and integrity never turn their backs on the truth.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Her books deal mainly with personnel relationships, especially marital problems.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Her books deal mainly with personal relationships, especially marital problems.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Personal (adjective) = concerning or belonging to one person in particular; individual or private: 'The novel is based on the author's own personal experience.' 'Our bank manager assured us that she would give the matter her personal attention.'Personnel (noun) = all the people employed in a company, office etc: 'In the event of a fire, all personnel must report to the reception area.' 'The personnel officer wants you to call and arrange an interview.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: This phenomena is called 'culture shock'.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: This phenomenon is called 'culture shock'.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Phenomena is the plural of phenomenon: 'The breakdown of family life is a relatively recent phenomenon.' 'Mathematics explains a wide variety of natural phenomena.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She phoned to the hospital to ask about her husband.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She phoned the hospital to ask about her husband.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Phone/telephone/ring/call a person/place/number (WITHOUT to): 'You must promise to phone me as soon as you get there.'Note that speakers of American English do not use ring for this meaning.In British English the phrase is (talk/speak to sb) on/over the phone (NOT by phone): 'He didn't want to discuss it over the phone.'Note that in American English both by phone and on/over the phone are used, although by phone is not common.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Just phone to 555-879 and I'll come and get you.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Just phone 555-879 and I'll come and get you.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Phone/telephone/ring/call a person/place/number (WITHOUT to): 'You must promise to phone me as soon as you get there.'Note that speakers of American English do not use ring for this meaning.In British English the phrase is (talk/speak to sb) on/over the phone (NOT by phone): 'He didn't want to discuss it over the phone.'Note that in American English both by phone and on/over the phone are used, although by phone is not common.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I talked to him for a long time by phone last night.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I talked to him for a long time on/over the phone last night.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English the phrase is (talk/speak to sb) on/over the phone (NOT by phone): 'He didn't want to discuss it over the phone.'Note that in American English both by phone and on/over the phone are used, although by phone is not common.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We decided to make a picnic in the field opposite the house.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We decided to have a picnic in the field opposite the house.
common_error_corrections.explanation:
Have a picnic (NOT make): 'We decided to have a picnic in the field opposite the house.'DO · HAVE · MAKE · TAKEMany phrases begin with a very common very such as do, make, have, or take: ‘I felt very nervous about taking the test but, after having a long talk with Mrs Fisher, I decided I would just do my best and try not to make too many silly mistakes.’ These verbs can be combined with some nouns but not with others and since they do not have a clear meaning of their own, choosing the right combination can be a problem. Phrases which tend to cause difficulty are shown below.HAVE:Have a bath (or esp. AmE take): ‘She’s probably upstairs having a bath.’Have (your) breakfast: ‘We usually have breakfast in the kitchen.’Have (your) dinner: ‘We had dinner and then went for a walk.’Have a drink: ‘I’ll collapse if I don’t have a drink soon.’Have (an) experience: ‘He has no experience of running a large company.’Have fun: ‘You can’t stop people from having fun.’Have a holiday: ‘It’s almost a year since we had a real holiday.’Have an interview: ‘I’ve had six interviews but no one has offered me a job.’Have a lesson: ‘Every morning we have three fifty-minute lessons.’Have (your) lunch: ‘Isn’t it about time we had lunch?’Have an operation: ‘Before I had the operation I could hardly walk.’Have a party: ‘On Saturday we’re having a party.’Have a picnic: ‘If it’s sunny we could have a picnic.’Have a shower (or esp. AmE take): ‘It only takes me a minute to have a shower.’TAKE:Take/do an examination: ‘Why do we have to take so many tests?’Take (your) medicine: ‘Don’t forget to take your medicine.’Take a pill: ‘He refuses to take sleeping pills.’Take/do a test: ‘The last test I took was a disaster.’MAKE:Make an effort: ‘I had to make a big effort not to laugh.’Make a journey: ‘It was the first journey he’d made all on his own.’Make a mistake: ‘He has made a serious mistake.’Make a noise: ‘How can one small child make so much noise?’Make progress: ‘I made very little progress at the start of the course.’DO:Do (sb) good ‘The holiday has done him a lot of good.’
Do harm ‘A scandal would do his reputation a lot of harm.’Do your homework ‘Have you done your homework yet?’Do a job ‘I’ve got one or two jobs to do this evening.’Do the/some shopping ‘Jake has gone into town to do some shopping.’Do research ‘We need to do a lot more research.’Do things ‘We’ve done lots of different things today.’Do your training ‘Where did you do your training?’Note also: do something/anything etc: ‘I can’t come now – I’m doing something.’ ‘He hasn’t done anything wrong.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: On our day off, we went picnic.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: On our day off, we went on a picnic.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go on / for a picnic (NOT go picnic / go to / on picnic): 'The last time I went on a picnic I was chased by a bull.' 'Lucy loves going on picnics.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The pencils were free and so I took two pieces.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The pencils were free and so I took two.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Piece is NOT used with countable nouns. Compare: 'a piece of cheese', 'a piece of furniture', 'a piece of luck'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The pillows had been removed from the sofa and scattered on the floor.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The cushions had been removed from the sofa and scattered on the floor.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pillow = a bag-like object filled with soft material that you rest your head on when you are in bed: 'No sooner had his head touched the pillow than he was sound asleep.'Cushion = a bag-like object filled with soft material that you put on a chair, sofa etc to make it more comfortable: 'Would you like a cushion for your back?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We both felt pitiful when we saw how lonely she was.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We both felt pity for her when we saw how lonely she was.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When I saw these pity children, my eyes filled with tears.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When I saw these pitiful children, my eyes filled with tears.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pity (noun) = a feeling that you have when you feel sad and sorry for someone because of their situation: 'They don't want out pity. They need our help.'Pitiful (adjective) = causing people to feel sad and sorry: 'The horses were in a pitiful condition, thin and covered with sores.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She expected me to feel pity on her and help her.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
She expected me to take pity on her and help her.
She expected me to feel pity for her and help her.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Take pity on: 'Eventually a kind motorist took pity on us and offered us a lift.'Feel pity for: 'Being a widow, she expects you to feel pity for her.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I hope there's enough place in the wardrobe for all your clothes.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I hope there's enough room in the wardrobe for all your clothes.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Place = an area or a particular part of an area: 'The best place to sit is right in front of the stage.'Room (or space) = an empty part of something that can be used or filled: 'There's room in the back seat for all three of you.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I left the coat in my room but it may not be in that place any longer.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I left the coat in my room but it may not be there any longer.
common_error_corrections.explanation: There = in/to that place: 'It's a long way to New Zealand but I'd love to go there.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When I lived at home, my father did not let me go to any place on my own.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When I lived at home, my father did not let me go anywhere on my own.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Anywhere = in/to any place: 'Have you seen my comb anywhere?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He was looking for a place where to spend the night.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He was looking for somewhere to spend the night.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Somewhere/nowhere/anywhere + to-v: 'She needs somewhere to stay.'Compare: 'He was looking for a place where he could spend the night.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There was no place where to park.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There was nowhere to park.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Somewhere/nowhere/anywhere + to-v: 'She needs somewhere to stay.'Compare: 'He was looking for a place where he could spend the night.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was born in a little planet in outer space.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was born on a little planet in outer space.
common_error_corrections.explanation: On a planet (NOT in): 'Is there life on other planets?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: You'll be able to try some of the local plates.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: You'll be able to try some of the local dishes.
common_error_corrections.explanation: MEAL · MENU · COURSE · DISH · THE DISHES · PLATEMeal. A meal is the food that you eat at about the same time each day: ‘After the meal we went to a discotheque.’ ‘We usually have our main meal in the evening.’Menu. A menu is a list of all the things that you can order in a restaurant: ‘I tried to read the menu but it was all in French.’ ‘Is there any fish on the menu?’Course. A meal may be served in separate stages. Each stage is called a course: ‘The main course was disappointing, but the dessert was excellent.’ ‘I’m not hungry enough to eat a three-course meal.’Dish. A dish is (1) the food prepared in a particular way and served as a meal or part of a meal: ‘My favourite Italian dish is lasagne.’ ‘For the main course there were six different meal dishes to choose from.’(2) a (usually shallow) container that food is placed in and then cooked or served: ‘I hope this dish is ovenproof!’The dishes. The dishes is a collective term for all the plates, bowls, cups, etc, that are used during a meal: ‘Whose turn is it to wash the dishes tonight?’Plate. A plate is (1) a (usually round) flat object that food is placed on, especially just before it is eaten: ‘All the clean plates are still in the dishwasher.’ ‘I’d never seen anyone put so much food on their plate.’(2) (also plateful) the amount of food on a plate: ‘How can you eat two large plates of spaghetti and still feel hungry?’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I've been playing piano since I was eight.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I've been playing the piano since I was eight.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English the phrase is play the piano/guitar/violin etc(WITH the): 'She's learning to play the flute.'In American English the is sometimes omitted.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We would be very pleasant if you could attend.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We would be very pleased if you could attend.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pleasant = (of a person) polite and friendly: 'I've always found Bob very pleasant to work with.'Pleased = happy, satisfied: 'I was very pleased to hear that you're feeling better.' 'She's pleased that the exams are over.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Please, if you cannot come, let me know as soon as possible.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Please let me know as soon as possible if you cannot come.
choices: Please, if you cannot come, let me know as soon as possible
Please let me know as soon as possible if you cannot come
common_error_corrections.explanation: Please does not usually come immediately before a subordinate clause ('if you cannot come').Note the usual positions: 'Please let me know as soon as you can.' 'Will you please let me know as soon as you can?' 'Will you let me know as soon as you can, please?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: As mayor of this town, it gives me a great pleasure to welcome you.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: As mayor of this town, it gives me great pleasure to welcome you.
common_error_corrections.explanation: It gives somebody great pleasure to do something (WITHOUT a): 'It gives me great pleasure to introduce today's guest speaker.'Compare: 'It is a great pleasure for me to introduce ...'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A lot of people work for their pleasure, not because of financial obligations.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A lot of people work for pleasure, not because of financial obligations.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do sth for pleasure (WITHOUT his/our/their etc): 'She used to be in the national team but now she swims just for pleasure.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's the first time that I've had the pleasure to meet her.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It's the first time that I've had the pleasure of meeting her.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be pleased to do sth BUT have the pleasure of doing sth: 'In Java I had the pleasure of attending a traditional wedding ceremony.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I had to spend forty-eight hours listening to him with a gun pointed to my head.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I had to spend forty-eight hours listening to him with a gun pointed at my head.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Point at = hold a weapon, camera etc so that it is in line with someone or something: 'Never point a gun at anyone.' 'With a knife pointed at my chest, I was in no position to argue.'Compare: 'I'd like one of those,' he said, pointing to/at a Mercedes.'There is no/little point (in) doing sth (NOT to do): 'There's no point in going on Sunday - all the shops will be shut.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There's no point to complain about the service.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There's no point (in) complaining about the service.
common_error_corrections.explanation: There is no/little point (in) doing sth (NOT to do): 'There's no point in going on Sunday - all the shops will be shut.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: From my point of view, the war is likely to continue.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In my opinion, the war is likely to continue.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use from ... point of view to introduce the particular position from which a situation is seen and judged: 'From the government's point of view, a June election would make very good sense.' 'From a financial point of view, the proposal has many advantages.'To introduce your opinion about something, use in my opinion: 'In my opinion, the public isn't ready for another election.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: On a cultural point of view, it is always interesting to live in a foreign country.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: From a cultural point of view, it is always interesting to live in a foreign country.
common_error_corrections.explanation: From a particular point of view (NOT on/in/at/to etc): 'From an environmental point of view, the battery-driven car is very attractive.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The police was not able to find anything.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The police were not able to find anything.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Police is always used with a plural verb: 'The police have a very difficult job to do.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He was charged with shooting a police.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He was charged with shooting a police officer.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The police = the police force in general: 'If you get any more of these phone calls, you should contact the police.'Policeman, policewoman, police officer = a member of the police force: 'There are two police officers outside waiting to see you.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The world's most serious ecological problem is the pollution.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The world's most serious ecological problem is pollution.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He gave all his money to the poors.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He gave all his money to the poor.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The poor (WITHOUT -s) = all people that are poor: 'In a recession it is always the poor that suffer the most.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I should like to explain our government's position about nuclear weapons.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I should like to explain our government's position on nuclear weapons.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Position on something (NOT about): 'The President has made his position on taxation perfectly clear.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We are considering the possibility to do the job ourselves.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We are considering the possibility of doing the job ourselves.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Possibility of (doing) sth: 'Is there any possibility of (getting) a refund?'Compare: 'Is it possible to get a refund?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My visit to Tokyo was a good possibility for me to learn some Japanese.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My visit to Tokyo was a good opportunity to learn some Japanese.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use possibility when you are talking about something that may happen: 'There is also a possibility that the peacekeeping forces could themselves come under attack.'To refer to a situation in which it is possible for someone to do something, use opportunity: 'The exchange scheme provides young people with the opportunity to visit a foreign country.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A person who wants to go out to work should be given the possibility to do so.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A person who wants to go out to work should be given the opportunity to do so.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use possibility when you are talking about something that may happen: 'There is also a possibility that the peacekeeping forces could themselves come under attack.'To refer to a situation in which it is possible for someone to do something, use opportunity: 'The exchange scheme provides young people with the opportunity to visit a foreign country.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If you find my book, could you possible return it to me?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If you find my book, could you possibly return it to me?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Possible is an adjective: 'It's quite possible that someone picked up your bag by mistake.' 'There are several possible answers.'Possibly is an adverb: 'I wonder if you could possibly send me some more information.' 'How could you possibly suspect your own brother of doing such a thing?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It could be possible that I left the wallet back at the hotel.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It's possible that I left the wallet back at the hotel.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use can/could before possible. When you are talking about a past event, use it is possible: 'It's quite possible that the letter was sent to the wrong address.' When you are talking about a future event, use it may / might be possible: 'She thinks that it may be possible to get the watch repaired.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was wondering whether it could be possible to arrange another meeting.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was wondering whether it might be possible to arrange another meeting.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use can/could before possible. When you are talking about a past event, use it is possible: 'It's quite possible that the letter was sent to the wrong address.' When you are talking about a future event, use it may/might be possible: 'She thinks that it may be possible to get the watch repaired.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Is it possible that I come and see you tomorrow?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Is it possible for me to come and see you tomorrow?
common_error_corrections.explanation: In enquiries and polite requests, use possible (for sb) to do sth (NOT possible that): 'Would it be possible for me to open a bank account?'Compare: 'It's quite possible that they've got stuck in a traffic jam.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She asked me if it was possible that you ring her back after 5 p.m.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She asked me if it was possible for you to ring her back after 5 p.m.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In enquiries and polite requests, use possible (for sb) to do sth (NOT possible that): 'Would it be possible for me to open a bank account?'Compare: 'It's quite possible that they've got stuck in a traffic jam.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The illness has left her with no power.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The illness has left her with no energy.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A person's power refers to their social, economic or political influence: 'The royal family has very little power these days.' 'The major investors have the power to make or break a company.'When talking about someone's physical condition, use energy or strength (NOT power): 'I don't have the time or energy to go out in the evenings.' 'Her doctor has told her to take things easy until she gets her strength back.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I think it's a great idea and should be put in practice.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I think it's a great idea and should be put into practice.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Put something into practice (NOT in): 'The aim of the project is to give students the opportunity to put what they have learned into practice.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'd prefer to staying at a different hotel this time.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'd prefer to stay at a different hotel this time.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Prefer to do sth (NOT to doing): 'They'd prefer to wait and see what happens.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'd prefer renting a small flat rather than live with a host family.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'd prefer to rent a small flat rather than live with a host family.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about a future or imaginary event, use (would) prefer + to do sth (NOT doing): 'I think I'd prefer to wait a bit longer, just in case the others show up.'Compare: 'I've always preferred eating at home to eating in restaurants.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Why do you prefer the theatre than the cinema?
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Why do you prefer the theatre to the cinema?
common_error_corrections.explanation: Prefer (doing) sth to (doing) sth else (NOT than): 'He normally prefers classical music to rock.' 'Most women prefer breastfeeding to bottle feeding.'Compare: 'I'd rather live in the North than in the South.' 'Most women would rather go out to work than stay at home all day.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I prefer drawing than painting.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I prefer drawing to painting.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Prefer (doing) sth to (doing) sth else (NOT than): 'He normally prefers classical music to rock.' 'Most women prefer breastfeeding to bottle feeding.'Compare: 'I'd rather live in the North than in the South.' 'Most women would rather go out to work than stay at home all day.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Going swimming is more preferable to playing football.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Going swimming is preferable to playing football.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use more with an adjective which contains the sense 'more' as part of its meaning. Preferable means 'better or more suitable': 'As far as I'm concerned, anything would be preferable to spending another night here.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: For most teenagers, living in the countryside is preferable than living in a city.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: For most teenagers, living in the countryside is preferable to living in a city.
common_error_corrections.explanation: One thing is preferable to another thing (NOT than): 'An old computer is preferable to no computer at all.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Our preferences in music are very similar.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Our tastes in music are very similar.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Preference usually refers to what someone prefers on a particular occasion: 'We could eat Chinese, Indian or Italian. Do you have any preference?' 'My own preference is for a hotel with its own swimming pool.'When you are talking about the particular style or styles that someone (always) likes or buys, use taste: 'While in Italy she developed a taste for Renaissance art.' 'When it comes to clothes, he has very expensive taste.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I know Carlos very well and I know his preferences.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I know Carlos very well and so I know his tastes/what he likes.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Preference usually refers to what someone prefers on a particular occasion: 'We could eat Chinese, Indian or Italian. Do you have any preference?' 'My own preference is for a hotel with its own swimming pool.'When you are talking about the particular style or styles that someone (always) likes or buys, use taste: 'While in Italy she developed a taste for Renaissance art.' 'When it comes to clothes, he has very expensive taste.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was preparing to go to bed when the phone rang.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was getting ready to go to bed when the phone rang.
common_error_corrections.explanation: If you prepare yourself (for sth), you get yourself into a suitable mental or physical state for something that you expect to happen: 'Relatives of the victims were told to prepare themselves for a long wait.' 'The villagers are preparing themselves for further flooding.'When you get ready or prepare to do something, you make yourself ready to do it: 'The company is preparing to expand its European network.' 'I had my breakfast and got ready to go to school.'Note that get ready is very common in spoken English and is often used in connection with the simple things that people do as part of their daily routine.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In the present she is involved in a project at the Housing Research Institute.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: At present she is involved in a project at the Housing Research Institute.
common_error_corrections.explanation: At present or at the present time (NOT in the present): 'I'm afraid that we're out of stock at present.'Compare: 'In future, don't keep the customers waiting.'Present (verb) = give something (to someone) during an official ceremony or meeting: 'The company's vice-president will now present the prize for the Best Salesperson of the Year.' 'Before leaving London, Mr Bush was presented with a petition from the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: At present I'm trying to improve my English.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: At the moment I'm trying to improve my English.
common_error_corrections.explanation: At present is used mainly in formal styles: 'At present there is insufficient evidence for the police to press charges.'In other styles use at the moment, just now or right now: 'Alan is in bed with flu at the moment.' 'Mrs Blake is too busy to see anyone just now.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They decided to present a tiny kitten to their son.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They decided to give their son a tiny kitten.
choices: present a tiny kitten to their son
give their son a tiny kitten
common_error_corrections.explanation: Present (verb) = give something (to someone) during an official ceremony or meeting: 'The company's vice-president will now present the prize for the Best Salesperson of the Year.' 'Before leaving London, Mr Bush was presented with a petition from the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Before leaving the examination room we had to present our answer papers.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Before leaving the examination room we had to hand in our answer papers.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Presently, nearly every machine used in the home is made of plastic.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: At present, nearly every machine used in the home is made of plastic.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Presently is used to mean 'soon' in both British and American English: 'The car will arrive presently to take Her Majesty back to the palace.'In American English presently is also used to mean 'now, at present, currently': 'The President is presently undergoing minor surgery.' The American usage is gradually becoming accepted outside the USA, but careful users of British English consider it to be non-standard.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: All these tests put an unnecessary pressure on students.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: All these tests put unnecessary pressure on students.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pressure is an uncountable noun: 'To stem the flow of blood, firm pressure should be applied.' 'They will never agree to the proposal unless there is pressure from above.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: This growing demand for housing gives pressure to the farmland and recreational areas.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: This growing demand for housing puts pressure on the farmland and recreational areas.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Put pressure on sb/sth (NOT give): 'His parents are putting pressure on him to leave school and get a job.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The government pretends to nationalize all the major industries.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The government intends to nationalize all the major industries.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Pretend = behave in a way that aims to give someone a false impression: 'He got into the conference centre by pretending to be a security guard. 'She hurried past, pretending not to see me.'Intend = be planning to do something: 'As soon as the baby can be left with someone, she intends to go back to work.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He pretends that he wasn't informed about the meeting.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He claims that he wasn't informed about the meeting.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Claim = state that something is true, especially when there is no proof or evidence that it is true: 'She claims to have been a close friend of John Lennon.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Stricter punishments would prevent people from doing these things.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Stricter punishments would deter people from doing these things.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Prevent = stop someone from doing something: 'They locked all the doors to prevent him escaping.'Deter = discourage someone from doing something: 'Tougher laws are needed to deter people from drinking and driving.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Stricter punishments may help to prevent society from serious crime.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Stricter punishments may help to protect society from serious crime.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Prevent = stop something from happening: 'Bad weather prevented the plane from taking off.' 'Good tyres help to prevent accidents.'Protect = keep someone or something safe: 'The camera comes with a free leather carrying case to protect it.' 'It is the responsibility of the police and the courts to protect us from these killers and maniacs.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: His parents tried to prevent him to join the army.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: His parents tried to prevent him from joining the army.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Prevent sb (from) doing sth: 'Girls should not be prevented from taking part in these sports.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I decided to take a big stick with me, just as a prevention.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I decided to take a big stick with me, just as a precaution.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Prevention = the act of stopping something from happening: 'The police are also concerned with the prevention of crime.'Precaution = an action taken in an attempt to avoid possible danger, damage, injury, etc: 'Some drivers have had alarms fitted as an extra precaution.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The price of keeping a person in prison for a year is enormous.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The cost of keeping a person in prison for a year is enormous.
common_error_corrections.explanation: PRICE · COST · COSTS · CHARGE · FEE · RATE · RENTAL · FARE · RENTPrice. The price of something is the amount of money that you must pay in order to buy it: ‘I’m interested in the car, but the price is too high.’ ‘Food prices are relatively low at present.’Cost. The cost of something is the amount of money you must pay to buy, do, make or use it: ‘the cost of having the car repaired was £340.’The cost of living (fixed phrase) = the general amount that the people living in a particular area or country have to pay for necessary goods and services: ‘In urban areas the cost of living tends to be higher.’Costs. Your costs are the total amount of money you spend over a period of time in order to make or produce something, or continue an activity: ‘Our costs have doubled over the last five years as a result of the increase in oil prices.’Charge. A charge is the amount of money that you must pay for a service or to be allowed to use something: ‘The waiter explained that the bill included a 10% service charge.’ ‘There is also a small charge for delivery and installation.’If you do not have to pay for something, it is provided free of charge: ‘The company has offered to install the software free of charge.’Fee. A fee is 1 a charge that you must pay to be allowed to do something: ‘Most art galleries charge an entrance fee.’ ‘Every new student has to pay a registration fee.’ 2 (usually fees) a charge that you must pay for professional services such as those provided by doctors, lawyers, consultants, tutors, schools etc: ‘My parents couldn’t afford the school fees.’ ‘Last year alone, the company paid over $12 million in legal fees.’Rate. A rate is the amount of money that you have to pay for a service or for hiring something, especially one that is calculated on an hourly, weekly or monthly basis: ‘His hourly rate is £60.’ ‘For a five-star hotel, the rates are very reasonable.’Fare. A fare is the cost of a journey on a buss, train etc: ‘How much is the train fare from Toronto to Montreal?’ ‘She spends $20 per week on bus fares.’Rent is the money you pay every week or month to live in or use a places that doesn’t belong to you: ‘The rent is £500 inclusive of bills.’

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The magazine is printed every month.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The magazine is published every month.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Print = produce copies of a book, newspaper, etc. by using machines: 'Due to increased demand, another six thousand copies are to be printed.'Publish = produce and distribute (a book, magazine, newspaper, etc) for sale to the public: The first edition was published in 1989.' 'Amateur Photographer is published every Tuesday.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Sending people to the prison is not the way to reduce crime.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Sending people to prison is not the way to reduce crime.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They probably will understand and try to help you.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They will probably understand and try to help you.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I experienced problems to find the right accommodation.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I experienced problems in finding the right accommodation.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Have/experience a problem/problems (in) doing sth (NOT to do): 'You shouldn't have any problems in getting a visa.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Unemployment is a very important problem.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Unemployment is a very serious problem.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A serious problem (NOT important): 'Teenage vandalism is a serious problem in this area.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When population growth is not controlled, serious problems can happen.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When population growth is not controlled, serious problems can arise.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Problem + arise/occur (NOT happen): 'How did the problem first arise?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The main film was proceeded by a short cartoon.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The main film was preceded by a short cartoon.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Proceed = (begin and) continue: 'After a five-minute delay, the lecture proceeded.' 'According to latest reports, negotiations are proceeding smoothly.'Precede = come, go, or happen (immediately) before someone or something: 'Churchill was a much stronger leader than the man who preceded him.' 'The snowfall was preceded by a sudden drop in temperature.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The production of plastic paper clips has seven processes.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The production of plastic paper clips has seven stages.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Process = a series of actions or operations that are performed in order to make or do something: 'The process begins with the gathering of the coffee beans.'Stage = one of the actions or operations in a process: 'During the next stage in the process the beans are dried.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He has applied for a job as a professor in a language school.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He has applied for a job as a teacher in a language school.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In Britain a professor is the most senior teacher in a university: 'My professor was the famous historian A.J.P. Taylor.'In the United States a professor is any university teacher who has a second degree.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The company has gained enormous profits in recent years.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The company has made enormous profits in recent years.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Make a profit (NOT gain): 'Derek would never sell you anything without making a good profit.' 'The company made a profit of $53 million last year.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We have made a great progress in the field of medicine.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We have made great progress in the field of medicine.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Even the teachers were prohibited to walk on the lawn.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Even the teachers were prohibited from walking on the lawn.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Prohibit sb from doing sth: 'The government intends to prohibit shopkeepers from selling cigarettes to children.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In some professions it is still difficult for women to get promotions.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: In some professions it is still difficult for women to get promotion.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In phrases such as get promotion, apply for promotion and chance/s of promotion, the noun promotion is usually uncountable: 'Women should have the same chance of promotion as their male counterparts.'Compare: 'With so many staff leaving, we can expect a few more promotions.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: These bones are a proof that the animals really existed.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: These bones are proof that the animals really existed.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Proof (= evidence) is usually an uncountable noun: 'Investigators now have proof of his involvement in the arms deal.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Today we have scientific proofs that tobacco is harmful.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Today we have scientific proof that tobacco is harmful.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Proof (= evidence) is usually an uncountable noun: 'Investigators now have proof of his involvement in the arms deal.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The television company receives most of its money from propaganda.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The television company receives most of its money from advertising.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Propaganda is used in a political context: 'Roadside hoardings displayed anti-Western propaganda.' 'In times of war the public are bombarded with propaganda.'Advertising is used in a commercial context: 'Car manufacturers spend billions of dollars a year on advertising.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The police eventually found most of the stolen properties.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The police eventually found most of the stolen property.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Property (= things that belong to someone) is an uncountable noun: 'Personal property should not be left unattended.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The country's small food supply is not proportion about the size of the population.

choices: small food supply is not proportion about
food supply is small in proportion to

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The proposal of building a new motorway received little support.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The proposal to build a new motorway received little support.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Proposal to do sth: 'The proposal to close the hospital was rejected.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I propose you to talk to John about it.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I suggest that you talk to John about it.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Propose = formally suggest an idea, plan or course of action, especially to an official person or group that has the power to decide: 'May I propose that we postpone further discussion of this matter until our next meeting.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A friend of mine has proposed me a job in his restaurant.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A friend of mine has offered me a job in his restaurant.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Offer = (1) tell someone that they can have something if they want it: 'He offered me a cup of tea.' 'She was offered a job on a local newspaper.'(2) tell someone that you are willing to do something: 'He offered to drive me back to my hotel.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He proposed to put them up for a few days.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He offered to put them up for a few days.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Offer = (1) tell someone that they can have something if they want it: 'He offered me a cup of tea.' 'She was offered a job on a local newspaper.'(2) tell someone that you are willing to do something: 'He offered to drive me back to my hotel.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I would like to propose to double the number of computers in each office.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
I would like to propose that the number of computers in each office is doubled.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There is little prospect for the situation to improve.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There is little prospect of the situation improving.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Prospect of doing sth/sth happening: 'With all the political unrest, there is little prospect of attracting foreign investment.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She told the shop assistant that she wanted to protest about the cardigan she had bought.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She told the shop assistant that she wanted to complain about the cardigan she had bought.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Protest = say or do something to show that you strongly disagree with something: 'The crowds were protesting against the government's purchase of nuclear weapons.'Complain = say that you are annoyed or unhappy about something: 'He's always complaining about the weather.' common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My job provides me the opportunity to meet new people every day.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The government does not provide enough food to the population.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Provide sth for sb/sth: 'The hotel also provides facilities for business meetings and conferences.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was very pleased with the room you provided to me.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was very pleased with the room you provided for me.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Provide sth for sb/sth: 'The hotel also provides facilities for business meetings and conferences.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In my view, a father should provide his family.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Provide for sb = support someone by paying for all their food, clothes etc: 'How can you provide for your children when you don't have a job?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I think governments should ban the publicity of tobacco.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I think governments should ban the advertising of tobacco.
common_error_corrections.explanation: If something is given publicity, there is an attempt to inform the public about it: 'Scandals involving prominent politicians always receive widespread publicity.'Advertising is the activity of trying to persuade people to buy something: 'The big software companies spend millions each year on advertising.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The police are in favour of stricter punishments.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The police are in favour of harsher punishments.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Severe/harsh punishment (NOT strict/strong): 'A prison sentence seems a very severe punishment for tax evasion.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We opened the window to get some pure air.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We opened the window to get some fresh air.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use pure when you mean 'completely clean': 'The water in the lake is so pure that you can drink it.'The usual word for describing air and water is fresh: 'Her doctor has prescribed a good holiday and lots of fresh air.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I always keep a few bottles of pure water on the boat.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Use pure when you mean 'completely clean': 'The water in the lake is so pure that you can drink it.'The usual word for describing air and water is fresh: 'Her doctor has prescribed a good holiday and lots of fresh air.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The purpose why I have come here is to improve my English.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The reason why I have come here is to improve my English.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Purpose = what you hope to achieve by doing something; aim: 'The main purpose of the trip is to see Helen's parents.' 'Their purpose in coming here is to promote Australian universities.'Reason = the thing that causes someone to do something: 'The reason why she left him was probably to do with his drinking problem.' 'Did they give you a reason for rejecting your application?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The purpose of staying in the United States is to complete my PhD.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My reason for staying in the United States is to complete my PhD.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Purpose = what you hope to achieve by doing something; aim: 'The main purpose of the trip is to see Helen's parents.' common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I am taking another course to improve my qualification.

Speakers of American English use degree, diploma, certificate etc for this meaning.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Switzerland produces goods with a very high quality.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Switzerland produces goods of a very high quality.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Sometimes we quarrel about which programme to watch.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He served his country for over quarter of a century.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He served his country for over a quarter of a century.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A quarter (of something): 'He's had almost a quarter of the cake all to himself.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We are able to exchange information quicker than in the past.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We are able to exchange information more quickly than in the past.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Quicker is sometimes used as an adverb, but only in informal styles. More quickly is always acceptable: 'He spoke more quickly than usual.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I went quickly to the nearest phone booth.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I ran to the nearest phone booth.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Go quickly usually sounds unnatural. The same meaning can be expressed by verbs such as hurry, rush, run, dash, sprint, etc: 'As soon as we saw the rain clouds, we hurried back home.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: This year the work at university is quite harder than last year.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: This year the work at university is rather harder than last year.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Before comparative forms use rather, slightly, somewhat or (especially in informal styles) a bit, a little (NOT quite): 'My new office is rather smaller than my old one.' 'He's slightly older than me.'Note however the common exception: 'Yes, I'm feeling quite better, thank you.' (= completely recovered)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There are quite many foreign students in London.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Quite a lot (of) NOT quite many/much: 'Quite a lot of time has already been wasted.' I've made quite a lot of new friends.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I always listen to the news in the radio.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: On radio there was a current affairs programme.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was heavy rain yesterday.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Two minutes later it started pouring rain.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The afternoon was very rainy.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They offered to raise up my salary.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Raise sth (WITHOUT up): 'If you want to ask a question, just raise your hand.' 'The age of retirement should be lowered, not raised.'
