common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He asked if he could come to your party and take a friend with him.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He asked if he could come to your party and bring a friend with him.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I couldn't talk English in those days.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I couldn't speak English in those days.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Speak English/French/Thai etc (NOT talk): 'Do you speak Italian?' 'I didn't know you could speak Greek.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'd like to talk you about a dream I had last night.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'd like to tell you about a dream I had last night.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When there is something that you want someone to know, you tell them about it: 'She told me about her holiday plans.'When you have a conversation, you talk (to someone) about something: 'We talked about where we could go at the weekend.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There's something I'd like to talk you about.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There's something I'd like to talk to you about.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Talk to sb (about sth): 'The manager would like to talk to you when you have a moment.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I didn't want to talk with him because I was in a hurry.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I didn't want to talk to him because I was in a hurry.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English the usual phrase is talk to someone: 'Who were you talking to just now?'Note that in American English both talk to and talk with are used.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I prefer rooms with tall ceilings.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I prefer rooms with high ceilings.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: During your visit you'll be able to taste some of the local Catalan specialities.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: During your visit you'll be able to try some of the local Catalan specialities.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you taste something, you put a little into your mouth to see what it is like: 'The chef stirred the soup, tasted it, and then added a little salt. When you have something to eat or drink for the first time, you try it. 'I think I'll try the onion soup. What's it like?'Have good/poor/little/no taste (in sth), (WITHOUT a/an): 'She certainly has remarkably good taste in clothes.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I buy all my family's clothes because my husband has such a poor taste.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I buy all my family's clothes because my husband has such poor taste.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Have good/poor/little/no taste (in sth), (WITHOUT a/an): 'She certainly has remarkably good taste in clothes.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We all thought that the joke was of a very bad taste.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We all thought that the joke was in very bad taste.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be in good/poor/bad taste: 'These advertisements are in very bad taste and in my opinion should be banned.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The food was excellent and very tasteful.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The food was excellent and very tasty.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Tasteful = chosen or produced by someone who is able to judge which kinds of art, music, furniture, etc, are attractive: 'The design of the room was very tasteful - pale colours, matching fabrics, and soft corner lighting.'Tasty = (of food) having a pleasant taste: 'These sausages are really tasty - where did you buy them?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: To save time, we decided to go with a taxi.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
To save time, we decided to go by taxi.
To save time, we decided to go in a taxi.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You go somewhere by taxi or in a taxi (NOT with): 'If you go by taxi, you're likely to get stuck in a traffic jam.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: All of a sudden the child burst in tears.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: All of a sudden the child burst into tears.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Burst into tears or break down (in tears): 'Laura burst into tears and ran out of the room.' 'She still can't talk about the war without breaking down in tears.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When the policeman had gone, she broke in tears.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When the policeman had gone, she burst into tears.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Burst into tears or break down (in tears): 'Laura burst into tears and ran out of the room.' 'She still can't talk about the war without breaking down in tears.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The main cause of unemployment is modern technique.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The main cause of unemployment is modern technology.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Technique = a way of doing something, especially one that requires special training: 'Thanks to these new surgical techniques, patients spend far shorter periods in hospital.' 'The purpose of these seminars is to keep our staff up to date with the latest teaching and testing techniques.'Technology = (the study of) the use of scientific theories and methods for practical purposes: 'Can you imagine what the world would be like without science and technology?' 'Space research has produced major advances in computer technology.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The job requires proper technique training.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The job requires proper technical training.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Technical = (1) involving or requiring detailed knowledge, especially of an industrial or scientific subject: 'The flight was cancelled because of a serious technical problem.'(2) requiring special knowledge to be understood: 'Engineering students need a lot of technical English.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He used a lot of technique language that I didn't understand.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He used a lot of technical language that I didn't understand.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Technical = (1) involving or requiring detailed knowledge, especially of an industrial or scientific subject: 'The flight was cancelled because of a serious technical problem.'(2) requiring special knowledge to be understood: 'Engineering students need a lot of technical English.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The modern technology has changed our whole way of life.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Modern technology has changed our whole way of life.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A fine example of modern technologies can be seen in the Indonesian fishing industry.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A fine example of modern technology can be seen in the Indonesian fishing industry.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When technology has a general meaning it is uncountable: 'The country's economic fate depends on access to foreign technology.'Use technology as a countable noun only when you refer to a particular area of activity: 'The system uses advanced computer and satellite technologies.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: High technology requires massive investment.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Advanced technology requires massive investment.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Advanced technology (NOT high): 'The United States government has agreed to provide both capital and advanced technology.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The whole world watched the cup final on televisions.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The whole world watched the cup final on television.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Television (also TV) is usually uncountable: 'The children watch a lot of television.' 'The article explains how television affects family life.'As a countable noun it means 'a television set': 'Some parents buy two televisions - one for the children to watch and one for themselves.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Cigarettes are no longer advertised in television.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Cigarettes are no longer advertised on television.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The article tells about the history of Rome.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The article is about the history of Rome.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You usually say that a book, story, article etc is about a particular subject: 'The novel is about the experiences of a young German soldier during the First World War.'Tell of is used only in literary styles: 'The poem tells of the deeds of a young Greek soldier during the Trojan War.' Tell about does not exist.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The story tells of a princess and a frog.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The story is about a princess and a frog.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You usually say that a book, story, article etc is about a particular subject: 'The novel is about the experiences of a young German soldier during the First World War.'Tell of is used only in literary styles: 'The poem tells of the deeds of a young Greek soldier during the Trojan War.' Tell about does not exist.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He told that he hadn't eaten anything for over a week.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
He told them that he hadn't eaten anything for over a week.
He said that he hadn't eaten anything for over a week.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Tell sb sth (WITH indirect object): 'Jim told me that you've been offered a new job.'Say sth (WITHOUT indirect object): 'Jim said that you've been offered a new job.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: John said that he was trying to get to London. 'That's where I'm going,' told the man.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: John said that he was trying to get to London. 'That's where I'm going,' said the man.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Say is used with both direct and indirect speech: "'I'm not going,"' he said.' 'He said he wasn't going.'Tell is used only with indirect speech: 'He told me he wasn't going.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Kiri was always telling about herself and her problems.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Kiri was always talking about herself and her problems.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Talk about sth (NOT tell about): 'Once she felt more relaxed, she began to talk about her real reasons for coming to see me.'Compare tell sb about sth: 'Did you tell him about the party on Saturday?' 'Don't forget to tell the doctor about your headaches.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have a tendency to agree with the statement.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I tend to agree with the statement.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To introduce an opinion, use tend to (NOT tendency): 'She tends to think that small firms should receive greater government support.'Compare: 'Ann tends/has a tendency to get up late.' (= Ann often gets up late)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The traffic jams are very terrible.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The traffic jams are (absolutely) terrible.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One of the world's greatest problems is the terrorism.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: One of the world's greatest problems is terrorism.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: On my first day at the school, I had to make a test.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: On my first day at the school, I had to take a test.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Take/do a test (NOT make): 'Before they start their courses, all the new students take a placement test.'For actions, the usual verb is do (NOT make): 'Governments are not doing enough to reduce unemployment.' 'I'm so worried I don't know what to do.'DO · HAVE · MAKE · TAKEMany phrases begin with a very common very such as do, make, have, or take: ‘I felt very nervous about taking the test but, after having a long talk with Mrs Fisher, I decided I would just do my best and try not to make too many silly mistakes.’ These verbs can be combined with some nouns but not with others and since they do not have a clear meaning of their own, choosing the right combination can be a problem. Phrases which tend to cause difficulty are shown below.HAVEHave a bath (or esp. AmE take): ‘She’s probably upstairs having a bath.’Have (your) breakfast: ‘We usually have breakfast in the kitchen.’Have (your) dinner: ‘We had dinner and then went for a walk.’Have a drink: ‘I’ll collapse if I don’t have a drink soon.’Have (an) experience: ‘He has no experience of running a large company.’Have fun: ‘You can’t stop people from having fun.’Have a holiday: ‘It’s almost a year since we had a real holiday.’Have an interview: ‘I’ve had six interviews but no one has offered me a job.’Have a lesson: ‘Every morning we have three fifty-minute lessons.’Have (your) lunch: ‘Isn’t it about time we had lunch?’Have an operation: ‘Before I had the operation I could hardly walk.’Have a party: ‘On Saturday we’re having a party.’Have a picnic: ‘If it’s sunny we could have a picnic.’Have a shower (or esp. AmE take): ‘It only takes me a minute to have a shower.’TAKETake/do an examination: ‘Why do we have to take so many tests?’Take (your) medicine: ‘Don’t forget to take your medicine.’Take a pill: ‘He refuses to take sleeping pills.’Take/do a test: ‘The last test I took was a disaster.’MAKEMake an effort: ‘I had to make a big effort not to laugh.’Make a journey: ‘It was the first journey he’d made all on his own.’Make a mistake: ‘He has made a serious mistake.’Make a noise: ‘How can one small child make so much noise?’Make progress: ‘I made very little progress at the start of the course.’DODo your best: ‘Don’t worry, Tim. Just do your best.’Do (or cause) damage: ‘The storm did a lot of damage to the crops.’Do an exercise: ‘Have you done your exercises today?’Do an experiment: ‘To do this experiment, you’ll need two eggs.’Do (sb) good: ‘The holiday has done him a lot of good.’Do harm: ‘A scandal would do his reputation a lot of harm.’Do your homework: ‘Have you done your homework yet?’Do a job: ‘I’ve got one or two jobs to do this evening.’Do the/some shopping: ‘Jake has gone into town to do some shopping.’Do research: ‘We need to do a lot more research.’Do things: ‘We’ve done lots of different things today.’Do your training: ‘Where did you do your training?’Note also: do something/anything etc: ‘I can’t come now – I’m doing something.’ ‘He hasn’t done anything wrong.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She said she was writing a text about France for her local newspaper.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She said she was writing an article about France for her local newspaper.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Text = (1) the words in a book, magazine, etc (as opposed to the illustrations); any written material: 'Alongside each drawing there were several lines of text.' 'A single disk can hold up to 1000 pages of text.'(2) a book or piece of writing on an academic subject: 'The first two texts on the reading list are general introductions.'(3) the written version of a play, speech etc: 'Only 'The Times' printed the full text of the President's speech.'Article = a piece of writing in a newspaper or magazine: 'I've just been reading an interesting article on alternative medicine.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I thank you very much for your last letter.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Thank you very much for your last letter.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use thanks (informal), thank you or (especially in formal styles) I would/should like to thank you (NOT I thank you): 'On behalf of the team, I'd like to thank you for your invaluable advice and support.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: First I thank you for answering my letter so quickly.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: First I'd like to thank you for answering my letter so quickly.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use thanks (informal), thank you or (especially in formal styles) I would/should like to thank you (NOT I thank you): 'On behalf of the team, I'd like to thank you for your invaluable advice and support.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Thank you for agree to listen.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Thank you for agreeing to listen.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Thank sb for doing sth: 'Thank you for being so understanding.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Thank you that you give me a chance to explain the situation.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Thank you for giving me a chance to explain the situation.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Thank sb for doing sth: 'Thank you for being so understanding.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Thank you in advance for your help.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: (Usually better to omit)
choices: Thank you in advance for your help.
common_error_corrections.explanation: You can use thank you in advance if the person you are writing to has already said that they will do something for you: 'It was kind of you to offer to send me a copy. Thank you in advance.' You can also use this phrase if you are in a position of authority and know that the person you are writing to will do what you have asked.Otherwise, thank you in advance should not be used since it can cause offence.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Thank to the microwave, we always have a hot breakfast.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Thanks to the microwave, we always have a hot breakfast.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Thanks to sb/sth (WITH-s): 'Thanks to parents' generosity, the school will soon have its own swimming-pool.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'm very thankful to you for giving me this opportunity.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'm very grateful to you for giving me this opportunity.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Thankful = happy and relieved that something (good) has happened: 'We should all be thankful that nobody was hurt.'Grateful = full of thanks: 'Dr Cameron has received dozens of letters from grateful patients.' 'We'd be grateful if you could let us have your views on this matter.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: First of all, thanks for your most interesting question.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: First of all, thank you for your most interesting question.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is two months now that I left Germany.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It is two months now since I left Germany.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A week/two months etc + since something happened (NOT that): 'It's almost two years since I started my PhD.'When the meaning is 'at/on/in/during which' (referring to time), use when (NOT that): 'These are the times when Dr Roberts will be able to see you.'Compare: 'I shall always remember the two days that I spent in Paris.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was shocked by the sight that I could hardly speak.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was so shocked by the sight that I could hardly speak.
common_error_corrections.explanation: So + adjective/adverb + that clause: 'I'm so tired that I can't keep awake.' 'He spoke so quickly that nobody could understand him.'That is used to introduce an identifying relative clause (one which identifies, defines, or restricts the preceding noun): 'The woman that is sitting behind us is Tom's music teacher.' 'The man that I marry will have lots of money.'That is not used to introduce a non-identifying relative clause (one which simply adds more information about the noun).

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He closed the door quietly that nobody would hear him.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He closed the door quietly so that nobody would hear him.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use so that to express purpose (NOT that): 'The burglars turned off all the lights so that they wouldn't be seen.'To make a precise reference to a previously mentioned action, use do so (NOT do that): 'I asked him politely to take his feet off the seat but he refused to do so.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Children are not as easy to please nowadays that they were in the past.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Children are not as easy to please nowadays as they were in the past.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When making a comparison, use as/so ... as (NOT as/so ... that): 'It's as hard to get into university today as it was ten years ago.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It worried me that the letter had not arrived, especially that it had never happened before.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It worried me that the letter had not arrived, especially since/as it had never happened before.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When giving a reason for something, use since or as (NOT that): 'Instead of cooking, why don't we get a take-away, especially as it's so late.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The weather has been very good, except for two days that it rained.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The weather has been very good, except for two days when it rained.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When the meaning is 'at/on/in/during which' (referring to time), use when (NOT that): 'These are the times when Dr Roberts will be able to see you.'Compare: 'I shall always remember the two days that I spent in Paris.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Sitting next to me was an old lady, that seemed to be sound asleep.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Sitting next to me was an old lady, who seemed to be sound asleep.
common_error_corrections.explanation: That is used to introduce an identifying relative clause (one which identifies, defines, or restricts the preceding noun): 'The woman that is sitting behind us is Tom's music teacher.' 'The man that I marry will have lots of money.'That is not used to introduce a non-identifying relative clause (one which simply adds more information about the noun).

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If you haven't sent it yet, I'd be pleased if you would do that as soon as possible.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If you haven't sent it yet, I'd be pleased if you would do so as soon as possible.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To make a precise reference to a previously mentioned action, use do so (NOT do that): 'I asked him politely to take his feet off the seat but he refused to do so.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She is arriving on March the 25th.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She is arriving on March 25th.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you say the date, use 'March the twenty-fifth' or 'the twenty-fifth of March'.When you write the date, use 'March 25th' or '25th March' (WITHOUT the and of).

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Very few people can speak the English well in Japan.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Very few people can speak English well in Japan.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Speak/learn/know etc + name of a language (WITHOUT the): 'She speaks fluent German.' 'Do you know any Malay?' 'I'd like to learn Mandarin.'Note that the + English/Japanese etc + language may be used when you talk about a language in terms of its history, structure, users etc: 'The English language has evolved over many centuries.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have just seen a new magazine about the computers.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have just seen a new magazine about computers.
common_error_corrections.explanation:
Do not use the with the plural form of a countable noun when it is used in a general sense. Compare: 'She likes cats.' (= cats in general) 
'The cats we saw in Venice looked very hungry.' (= a particular group of cats)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A lot of people are afraid of the death.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A lot of people are afraid of death.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use the with an uncountable noun when it is used in a general sense: 'She hates dishonesty.' 'Power doesn't interest him.'The is used when the sense is restricted: 'She hates the dishonesty of the man.' 'The power enjoyed by politicians doesn't interest him.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nowadays the pollution is a very serious problem.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nowadays pollution is a very serious problem.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use the with an uncountable noun when it is used in a general sense: 'She hates dishonesty.' 'Power doesn't interest him.'The is used when the sense is restricted: 'She hates the dishonesty of the man.' 'The power enjoyed by politicians doesn't interest him.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My main hobby is the photography.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My main hobby is photography.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use the with an uncountable noun when it is used in a general sense: 'She hates dishonesty.' 'Power doesn't interest him.'The is used when the sense is restricted: 'She hates the dishonesty of the man.' 'The power enjoyed by politicians doesn't interest him.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Diseases such as the AIDS and the cancer cause a lot of suffering.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Diseases such as AIDS and cancer cause a lot of suffering.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use the before the name of a disease: 'He caught pneumonia and had to spend three weeks in bed.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Our plane arrived at the Gatwick Airport.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Our plane arrived at Gatwick Airport.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use the before the names of airports and railway stations: 'Charles de Gaulle (Airport)', 'Narita (Airport)', 'Charing Cross (Station)'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The language school is in the Malibu Street.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The language school is in Malibu Street.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The is not usually used in the names of streets and roads: 'Oxford Street', 'Fifth Avenue', 'Fir Tree Avenue', 'Blue Pool Road'.Note that when someone mentions 'the Oxford road' or 'the London road', they mean the road that leads to Oxford/London.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Climbing the Mount Fuji in winter can be very dangerous.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Climbing Mount Fuji in winter can be very dangerous.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not use the with the name of a mountain: 'Mount Everest', 'Mount Fuji', 'Mount Olympus'. Note, however, that the is used with the names of groups of mountains: 'the Alps', 'the Andes', 'the Himalayas'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They were both found guilty and sent to the prison.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They were both found guilty and sent to prison.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Yellow River has caused many terrible floods.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The Yellow River has caused many terrible floods.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Always use the with the names of canals, rivers, seas and oceans: 'the Suez Canal', 'the Ganges', 'the River Thames', 'the Atlantic Ocean', 'the Mediterranean Sea'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is more than ten years since I visited West Indies.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It is more than ten years since I visited the West Indies.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Most plural names begin with the: 'the Bahamas', 'the Himalayas', 'the United States', 'the Philippines'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: This is my second visit to UK.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: This is my second visit to the UK.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use the with any country whose name includes 'state', 'union', 'republic', 'kingdom' etc: 'the UK', 'the United Kingdom', 'the USA', 'the United States', 'the People's Republic of China'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Only very wealthy tourists can afford to stay at Imperial Hotel.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Only very wealthy tourists can afford to stay at the Imperial Hotel.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The names of hotels and restaurants usually begin with the: 'the Hilton', 'the Mandarin', 'the Sheraton'.Note that names which have a possessive form are exceptions: 'Claridge's', 'Salvo's', 'Tiffany's.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: This system was brought to Hong Kong by British.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: This system was brought to Hong Kong by the British.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To refer to the people of a country, use the + adjective: 'the British', 'the French', 'the Portuguese', 'the Swiss'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The hotel is not suitable for disabled.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The hotel is not suitable for the disabled.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The poor, the sick, the deaf, the disabled, etc = all people who are poor/sick/deaf/disabled: 'The rich get richer and the poor get poorer.' 'She devoted her life to looking after the sick.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We took a bus to the city centre then caught a train to London.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We took a bus to the city centre and then caught a train to London.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Then is an adverb (NOT a conjunction). It cannot be used to link clauses.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: After my father retires, then I shall help him financially.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: After my father retires, I shall help him financially.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Then (= at that time) is used after a time clause only when it introduces a result or consequence. Compare: 'When you've seen the trees, then you'll know why I came to live here.' (= as a result of seeing the trees).

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My sister often goes to the indoor pool but I don't like going to there.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My sister often goes to the indoor pool but I don't like going there.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If you aren't busy is something I'd like to ask you about.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If you aren't busy, there's something I'd like to ask you about.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you say that something exists or takes place, the sentence must have a subject. When there is no other subject, use there: 'There's a hair in your soup.' 'Suddenly there was a loud bang.' 'There are two police officers waiting to see you.'Note that in this pattern there has no meaning. It simply fills the subject position.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There was four people in the car.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There were four people in the car.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Use there is/was when the following noun is singular/uncountable: 'There was a letter on the mat.' 'There was smoke all over the house.'Use there are/were when the following noun is plural: 'There were babies crying in every room.' 'There are many times when I would prefer to be alone.'Note that a lot of, plenty of, etc do not affect the number of the verb. Compare: 'There was a lot of traffic on the road.' 'There were a lot of cars on the road.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: In Barcelona there is plenty of things for visitors to do.

'There are many times when I would prefer to be alone.'Note that a lot of, plenty of, etc do not affect the number of the verb. Compare: 'There was a lot of traffic on the road.' common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There was a lot of girls watching the game.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She has lived in New York for many years therefore she regards New York as her home.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The child looked lost and therefore I asked him if I could help.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Therefore is used mainly in formal styles: 'Crops have been badly affected by the drought and therefore food will be in short supply.'In non-formal styles use so: 'It was quite late so I didn't stay long.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The present government doesn't care enough about the poorer sections of our society. Businessmen are encouraged to exploit workers and make huge profits. In spite of all these, I believe in the principles of free enterprise.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The present government doesn't care enough about the poorer sections of our society. Businessmen are encouraged to exploit workers and make huge profits. In spite of all this, I believe in the principles of free enterprise.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To refer back to the points that you have just made, use (all) this (NOT (all) these): 'In spite of all this, we managed to enjoy ourselves.' 'I find all this very confusing.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Being punctual is a very important thing.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Being punctual is very important.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Avoid using thing after an adjective when the adjective can be used on its own: 'To obtain a bank loan when you don't have a job can be very difficult.'Note however the commonly used phrase a/the good thing: 'Most people agree that democracy is a good thing.' 'The good thing about this school is that the teachers are all so enthusiastic.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I have a very important thing to ask you.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have something very important to ask you.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Something + adjective, anything + adjective, somewhere + adjective, nothing + adjective, etc: 'Did you notice anything unusual?' 'Let's go somewhere different tonight.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If you need any special thing, please let me know.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If you need anything special, please let me know.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Something + adjective, anything + adjective, somewhere + adjective, Nothing + adjective, etc: 'Did you notice anything unusual?' 'Let's go somewhere different tonight.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My brother knows many things about England.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: My brother knows a lot about England.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The use of many things often sounds unnatural. Instead, use a lot, a great deal, etc: 'She said that she had a lot to do.' 'In just one or two sessions you can learn a great deal.'Note also the phrase all about: 'The best person to ask is David - he knows all about tropical plants.' (= he knows everything about ...)

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Asian countries have learned many things from western countries.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Asian countries have learned a great deal from western countries.
common_error_corrections.explanation: The use of many things often sounds unnatural. Instead, use a lot, a great deal, etc: 'She said that she had a lot to do.' 'In just one or two sessions you can learn a great deal.'Note also the phrase all about: 'The best person to ask is David - he knows all about tropical plants.' ( = he knows everything about ... )

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was thinking if you would like to have lunch before visiting the museum.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I was wondering if you would like to have lunch before visiting the museum.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We should spend more time thinking why people do such terrible things.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We should spend more time thinking about why people do such terrible things.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Think about sb/sth (= give a lot of thought to): 'She's worried about her father and can't stop thinking about him.' 'Have you ever thought about what you'd like to do for a living?' 'You look serious - what're you thinking about?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: While she was away, he often thought on her.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: While she was away, he often thought about her.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Think about sb/sth (= give a lot of thought to): 'She's worried about her father and can't stop thinking about him.' 'Have you ever thought about what you'd like to do for a living?' 'You look serious - what're you thinking about?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He's thinking to make another trip to Italy next month.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He's thinking about making another trip to Italy next month.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about possible future actions, use think about/of doing sth: 'They're thinking of starting their own health food business.' 'We're thinking about going to Disneyworld again next year.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We're thinking on going to the beach after lunch.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We're thinking of going to the beach after lunch.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about possible future actions, use think about/of doing sth: 'They're thinking of starting their own health food business.' 'We're thinking about going to Disneyworld again next year.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He advised me to think deeply about it before making a decision.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He advised me to think seriously about it before making a decision.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Think seriously/carefully (NOT deeply) (about sth), especially before making a decision: 'The job has a lot of attractions and in my opinion you should think seriously about it.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Some foreigners are thinking the Japanese are rich.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I think she didn't understand what you said.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I don't think she understood what you said.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Do not think (that) is more usual than think (that) ... not . This applies to believe, imagine, suppose, feel etc: 'I don't imagine they'll be coming after all.' 'I don't suppose you could give me a lift?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Will you be at home on this Sunday afternoon?

Will you be at home this Sunday afternoon?

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: People's attitudes and thoughts don't change overnight.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They are prepared to kill in order to defend their thoughts.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Belief = a strong feeling that something is true or untrue, good or bad etc: 'In the old days people were persecuted for their religious beliefs.' 'The poet's belief in life after death is not evident in these early poems.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They used to threat each other with atomic bombs.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He picked up a small stone and threw it to Sally's window.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He picked up a small stone and threw it at Sally's window.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Some smokers just throw their cigarette ends.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I heard a terribly loud noise, like a thunder.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We waited for the thunders and lightning to stop.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: We waited for the thunder and lightning to stop.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: My house is near Greenwich Park and thus we'll be able to visit the famous Observatory.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The journey takes long time.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: People tell me many times that America is a dangerous country.

common_error_corrections.explanation: If you do something repeatedly, you keep doing it or you are always doing it: 'Why does she keep writing to you?' 'At school I was always getting into trouble.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Last time Singapore used to be a fishing village.

'This is the last time I'm coming here!'To refer to a period in the (distant) past, use previously, formerly, many years ago, in the old days, etc: 'The new road changed people's lives enormously - previously the only way of reaching the village was on foot.' common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The fire brigade arrived just on time, before the fire could spread.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They had to rush to get to work in time.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It didn't take a long time before we were back home again.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Medical science is developing every time.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We went to the cinema to spend the time until the train arrived.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: We spent a very good time in New York.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The manager's timetable next week is very busy.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The flight from Hong Kong to London was very tiresome.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The newspaper titles were all about the earthquake.

There's been another car bomb in London.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He was reading a short story by Saki titled 'The Open Window'.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He was reading a short story by Saki called 'The Open Window'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She sent me an article from Life Magazine titled 'A Soldier's Anguish'.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She sent me an article from Life Magazine entitled 'A Soldier's Anguish'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: At that moment he noticed a man running to him.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I usually have a cup of coffee and a toast for breakfast.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: One of the children wanted to go to toilet.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I was too happy when I received your letter today.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Too = more than is good, reasonable or acceptable: 'He was driving too fast and couldn't stop in time.' 'The meat was too tough to eat.'Compare: 'I was very tired but not too tired to go out.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Bearing in mind that it is too far from here, we should make an early start.

common_error_corrections.explanation: Too = more than is good, reasonable or acceptable: 'He was driving too fast and couldn't stop in time.' 'The meat was too tough to eat.'Compare: 'I was very tired but not too tired to go out.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's an interesting magazine with too many good ideas.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: For some reason they didn't receive the fax and your letter hasn't arrived too.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It is one of the most popular touristic resorts in Spain.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I made my training with the Swiss Bank in London.

common_error_corrections.explanation: DO · HAVE · MAKE · TAKEMany phrases begin with a very common very such as do, make, have, or take: ‘I felt very nervous about taking the test but, after having a long talk with Mrs Fisher, I decided I would just do my best and try not to make too many silly mistakes.’ These verbs can be combined with some nouns but not with others and since they do not have a clear meaning of their own, choosing the right combination can be a problem. common_error_corrections.explanation: In formal styles, when you are talking about an unreal situation, use were (NOT was): 'If the motorway were extended, farming would be severely disrupted.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I wash my body and then get dressed.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I have a bath/shower and then get dressed.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you talk about someone washing themselves, you usually use have a wash/bath/shower: 'I always feel better after I've had a good wash.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He's gone upstairs to wash.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He's gone upstairs to have a wash.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you talk about someone washing themselves, you usually use have a wash/bath/shower: 'I always feel better after I've had a good wash.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The report deals with the problem of nuclear wastes.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The report deals with the problem of nuclear waste.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He explained the ways how we can help to protect the sea.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He explained how we can help to protect the sea.

'In this morning's talk I'll be looking at how smaller companies are dealing with these problems.'Note the alternative: 'He explained the ways in which we can help to protect the sea.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: She loves the farm and refuses to change her way of living.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: She loves the farm and refuses to change her way of life.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Then I wore some clothes and went downstairs.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Then I put on some clothes and went downstairs.
common_error_corrections.explanation: GET DRESSED · DRESS ONESELF · PUT ON · TAKE OFF · DRESS · DRESS UP · WEAR · HAVE ON · BE + ADV · DRESSEDACTIONSGet dressed. When you get dressed you put on your clothes or a different set of clothes: ‘I had a shower, got dressed and went downstairs.’ ‘I was still getting dressed for the party when the taxi arrived.’Dress oneself is not common. It is mainly used when you are thinking about the special skill or ability that is required to put on clothes: ‘Sally isn’t old enough to dress herself yet.’Put on. When you put on a piece of clothing or a watch, necklace etc, you put it into position on your body: ‘Wait a minute! I haven’t put my coat on yet.’ ‘Put your gloves on or your hands will get cold.’Take off is the opposite of put on: ‘I can’t wait to take off these new shoes.’ ‘Why don’t you take your coat off and come and sit down?’Dress up. If you dress up you put on: (1) a special costume: ‘When the children were young, George used to dress up as Father Christmas.’(2) formal or smart clothes: ‘We won’t be going to an expensive restaurant so there’s no need to dress up.’STATESWear. When you wear something, it is on a part of your body: ‘Did you notice the jacket she was wearing at Alan’s party?’ ‘He always wears smart clothes.’Have on. If you have something on, you are wearing it: ‘The trousers he had on were too big for him.’ ‘You won’t get cold as long as you have a coat on.’Be dressed in/be in. If you are dressed in or are in something, you are wearing it: ‘She arrived at the theatre dressed in a long white gown.’ ‘Everyone was in their best clothes, but Alex turned up in an old T-shirt and jeans.’Be + adverb + dressed. When you are talking about someone’s appearance, you can say that they are smartly/neatly/well etc dressed. ‘Make sure you’re smartly dressed for the interview.’ ‘He’s always very well dressed – smart jackets, silk ties and so on.’

common_error_corrections.explanation: Using numbersDay, month, minute, mile, kilo etc are always SINGULAR when used (with a number) immediately before a noun: ‘a six-minute wait’, ‘a ten-second silence’, ‘a five-mile race’.My travel agent had arranged a 6-day coach tour.The company provides a three-month training course.Compare: ‘We waited for thirty minutes: ‘We had a thirty-minute wait.’When you say 100, 1000 etc , or write these numbers in words, use a hundred, a thousand (WITH a):The palace was build a thousand years ago.Compare: ‘The palace was built 1000 years ago.’For emphasis or to be exact, it is possible to use one instead of a:I am one hundred percent against the idea.After a/one/five/twelve etc, the words hundred, thousand, etc are always SINGULAR and are NOT followed by of:Five hundred children are born in the city every day.More than three thousand people were there.Similarly, of is NOT used after 100, 250, 3000 etc:If you kill 200 whales a year, they will soon disappear.Hundreds (of), thousands (of) etc are used only when you give a general idea of how many or how much: ‘There were hundreds of stars in the sky.’ ‘They’ve spent thousands (of pounds) on improvements to the house.’Use and between hundred and the next number. (In American English, and is often omitted, especially in formal styles.)BrE The club has about a hundred and thirty members.AmE The club has about a hundred (and) thirty members.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Most of the people whom I met were very kind.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Most of the people (that) I met were very kind.

In non-identifying clauses, however, only who is possible: 'Both girls - who you may remember from Helen's party - have got places at Oxford.'

common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The magazine gives broad descriptions of market trends.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: When capital punishment was abolished, people thought that murders will become more numerous.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: When capital punishment was abolished, people thought that murders would become more numerous.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If a developing country will become a developed country, it has to attract foreign investors.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Without a full-time work, some people think it's not worth living.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
Without a full-time job, some people think it's not worthliving.
Without full-time work, some people think it's not worth living.
choices: a full-time work, some people think it's not worth living
full-time work, some people think it's not worth living
a full-time job, some people think it's not worthliving
common_error_corrections.explanation: JOB · DO · OCCUPATION · POST/POSITION · CAREER · TRADE · PROFESSIONJob. Your job is what you do to earn your living: ‘You’ll never get a job if you don’t have any qualifications.’ ‘She’d like to change her job but can’t find anything better.’ Your job is also the particular type of work that you do: ‘John’s new job sounds really interesting.’ ‘I know she works for the BBC but I’m not sure what job she does.’A job may be full-time or part-time (NOT half-time or half-day): ‘All she could get was a part-time job at a petrol station.’Do (for a living). When you want to know about the type of work that someone does, the usual questions are What do you do? What does she do for a living? etc ‘What does your father do?’ - ‘He’s a police inspector.’Occupation and job have similar meanings. However, occupation is far less common than job and is used mainly in formal and official styles: ‘Please give brief details of your employment history and present occupation.’ ‘People in manual occupations seem to suffer less from stress.’Post/position. The particular job that you have in a company or organization is your post or position: ‘She’s been appointed to the post of deputy principal.’ ‘He’s applied for the position of sales manager.’ Post and position are used mainly in formal styles and often refer to jobs which have a lot of responsibility.Career. Your career is your working life, or the series of jobs that you have during your working life: ‘The scandal brought his career in politics to a sudden end.’ ‘Later on in his career, he became first secretary at the British Embassy in Washington.’Your career is also the particular kind of work for which you are trained and that you intend to do for a long time: ‘I wanted to find out more about careers in publishing.’Trade. A trade is a type of work in which you do or make things with your hands: ‘Most of the men had worked in skilled trades such as carpentry or printing.’ ‘My grandfather was a bricklayer by trade.’Profession. A profession is a type of work such as medicine, teaching, or law which requires a high level of training or education: ‘Until recently, medicine has been a male-dominated profession.’ ‘She entered the teaching profession in 1987.’
