common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Nepal has one of the highest mountains in all over the world.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Nepal has one of the highest mountains in the world.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Superlative + noun + in the world: 'At that time China was the richest and most powerful country in the world.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The sewing machine is one of the most widely used products of the world.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The sewing machine is one of the most widely used products in the world.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Superlative + noun + in the world: 'At that time China was the richest and most powerful country in the world.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Pollution is a serious problem in all of the world.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Pollution is a serious problem all over the world.
common_error_corrections.explanation: All over the world = everywhere in the world: 'Since joining the newspaper, she's travelled all over the world.' 'There will be teams from all over the world.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Their music is played in every part of the world.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Their music is played all over the world.
common_error_corrections.explanation: All over the world = everywhere in the world: 'Since joining the newspaper, she's travelled all over the world.' 'There will be teams from all over the world.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It was the worse journey I had ever made.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It was the worst journey I had ever made.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Bad, worse, (the) worst: 'The medicine just made me feel worse.' 'It's the worst film I've ever seen.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: People's lack of responsibility makes the problem even more worse.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: People's lack of responsibility makes the problem even worse.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Bad, worse, (the) worst: 'The medicine just made me feel worse.' 'It's the worst film I've ever seen.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The next time I saw her she looked even worst.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The next time I saw her she looked even worse.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The day finished worst than it began.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The day finished worse than it began.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The ring has great sentimental worth.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The ring has great sentimental value.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Worth is usually used as a preposition: 'A four-bedroomed house in the middle of town is probably worth about £200,000.'The noun related to worth is value: 'The current value of property is very low compared with this time last year.'Compare: 'That watch is worth fifty pounds.' 'That watch has a value of fifty pounds.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: They do not appreciate the worth of life.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: They do not appreciate the value of life.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Worth is usually used as a preposition: 'A four-bedroomed house in the middle of town is probably worth about £200,000.'The noun related to worth is value: 'The current value of property is very low compared with this time last year.'Compare: 'That watch is worth fifty pounds.' 'That watch has a value of fifty pounds.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The missing ring worths about two thousand pounds.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The missing ring is worth about two thousand pounds.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be worth £20/very little/a fortune etc: 'These old computers aren't worth much nowadays.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: A holiday doesn't worth all the effort it takes preparing for it.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: A holiday isn't worth all the effort it takes preparing for it.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Be worth £20/very little/a fortune etc: 'These old computers aren't worth much nowadays.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's also worth to visit the north of England if you have time.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It's also worth visiting the north of England if you have time.
common_error_corrections.explanation: It's worth doing sth; sth is worth doing (NOT to do): 'It's worth remembering that these old cars can be very expensive to run.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The museum was certainly worth to see.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The museum was certainly worth seeing.
common_error_corrections.explanation: It's worth doing sth; sth is worth doing (NOT to do): 'It's worth remembering that these old cars can be very expensive to run.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The film reviews are always worthwhile looking at.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The film reviews are always worth looking at.
common_error_corrections.explanation: It's worth/worthwhile doing sth: 'It might be worth having one or two copies made.' 'Is it worthwhile talking about it now, or shall we leave it until our next meeting?'Something is worth doing (NOT worthwhile): 'Some of these so-called professional teams aren't worth watching.'Compare: 'Was the long drive up to Scotland really worthwhile?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: It's not worthy taking your own car.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: It's not worth taking your own car.
common_error_corrections.explanation: It's worth doing sth; sth is worth doing (NOT worthy): 'Do you think it's worth having the engine tuned?' 'The letter isn't worth worrying about.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The cathedral is certainly worthy to be visited.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The cathedral is certainly worth visiting.
common_error_corrections.explanation: It's worth doing sth; sth is worth doing (NOT worthy): 'Do you think it's worth having the engine tuned?' 'The letter isn't worth worrying about.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If I would live in the countryside, I would be much healthier.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If I lived in the countryside, I would be much healthier.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about the present or the future and you imagine something that is untrue or unlikely, use the past tense ('lived') in the if clause (NOT would): 'If I knew her address, I'd send her a postcard.' 'If I won a lot of money, I'd buy a new car.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If you would have caught the earlier train, we could have travelled together.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If you had caught the earlier train, we could have travelled together.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about the past and you imagine something that is impossible, use the past perfect tense ('had caught') in the if clause (NOT would have): 'If he hadn't got on the plane, he would still be alive.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: If you would have any more questions, I'll do my best to answer them.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: If you should have any more questions, I'll do my best to answer them.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When you are talking about the present or the future and you imagine something that is possible but unlikely, use if ... should (NOT if ... would): 'If anyone should need me, I'll be back in half an hour.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Only the driver was wounded in the accident.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Only the driver was injured/hurt in the accident.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Manufacturers should dispense with all unnecessary wrapping.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Manufacturers should dispense with all unnecessary packaging.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Wrapping (also wrappings) = paper or paper-like material that is put round something: 'I wanted to tear off the wrapping and see what was inside.'Packaging = the container or material that something is placed in by a manufacturer, especially to protect it or make it look attractive: 'Packaging should be biodegradable and kept to a minimum.'Note that both wrapping and packaging are used in connection with food: 'Somewhere on the packaging/wrapping there should be a date stamp.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I'd like to apologize for not having written you before.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I'd like to apologize for not having written to you before.
common_error_corrections.explanation: In British English you write to a person or place (WITH to): 'Wingate wrote to his father, asking for more money.'In American English to is optional: 'I'll write (to) you and give you all the latest news.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Dear ... I write to you to ask for your advice.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Dear ... I am writing to you to ask for your advice.
common_error_corrections.explanation: For actions which are happening at the time when they are mentioned, use the present progressive tense (NOT the present simple): 'I'm writing to tell you that I'll be coming to London next Thursday.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: The belief that Spanish is easy to learn is wrong.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: The belief that Spanish is easy to learn is mistaken.
common_error_corrections.explanation: To describe a belief or idea that is wrong although people do not know it is wrong, use mistaken: 'Some people have the mistaken idea that cats need to drink milk.' 'I'm afraid you must be mistaken.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I've been playing the piano since I was seven years.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence:
I've been playing the piano since I was seven.
I've been playing the piano since I was seven years old.
I've been playing the piano since I was seven years of age.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When stating someone's age, use just a number on its own OR a number + years old/years of age (NOT years): 'I'm almost eighteen.' 'My sister is fifteen years old.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Robert was a little boy of ten years.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Robert was a little boy of ten.
common_error_corrections.explanation: A boy/girl/son etc + of + number (WITHOUT years): 'a child of six', 'a man of fifty'.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: More houses are built yearly.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: More houses are built every year.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Yearly usually means that something is done or takes place once a year: 'The interest is paid yearly or, if you prefer, every six months.' 'The front of the house was getting its yearly coat of white paint.'Yearly is also used to connect a total number or amount with a period of one year: 'We were manufacturing and selling about 20,000 tonnes yearly.' 'The yearly catch rose to a peak of 52,000 tonnes.'When you simply want to say that something happens 'all the time', use every year or each year (NOT yearly): 'The country's tourist industry is growing every year.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Thousands of people die from cancer yearly.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Thousands of people die from cancer every year.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Yearly usually means that something is done or takes place once a year: 'The interest is paid yearly or, if you prefer, every six months.' 'The front of the house was getting its yearly coat of white paint.'Yearly is also used to connect a total number or amount with a period of one year: 'We were manufacturing and selling about 20,000 tonnes yearly.' 'The yearly catch rose to a peak of 52,000 tonnes.'When you simply want to say that something happens 'all the time', use every year or each year (NOT yearly): 'The country's tourist industry is growing every year.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: He left the house at five in the morning, when the family was yet asleep.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: He left the house at five in the morning, when the family was still asleep.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Yet means 'up to the moment of speaking' and is used mainly in questions and negative sentences: 'Do you feel any better yet?' 'The post office isn't open yet.'When you want to say that an earlier state or situation has not changed, use still: 'I've taken the medicine but I still feel terrible.' 'Does Hilary still go to the same school?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I've only been here two weeks and everything is strange yet.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I've only been here two weeks and everything is still strange.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Yet means 'up to the moment of speaking' and is used mainly in questions and negative sentences: 'Do you feel any better yet?' 'The post office isn't open yet.'When you want to say that an earlier state or situation has not changed, use still: 'I've taken the medicine but I still feel terrible.' 'Does Hilary still go to the same school?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: I didn't finish my thesis yet.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: I haven't finished my thesis yet.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Yet (= up to the moment of speaking) is usually used with the present or present perfect tense (NOT the past tense): 'Has the taxi arrived yet?' 'Is the taxi here yet?'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Dear Mary ... Yours faithfully ...
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Dear Mary ... Yours/With love/With best wishes ...
common_error_corrections.explanation: Yours faithfully and Yours sincerely are used only in formal letters.At the end of a letter to a friend or relative, use Yours, With love, With best wishes, etc.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Dear John, ... Yours sincerely ...
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Dear John, ... Yours/With love/With best wishes ...
common_error_corrections.explanation: Yours faithfully and Yours sincerely are used only in formal letters.At the end of a letter to a friend or relative, use Yours, With love, With best wishes, etc.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Dear Sir, ... Yours,
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Dear Sir, ... Yours faithfully.
common_error_corrections.explanation: When a formal letter begins with Dear Sir or Dear Madam, it usually ends with Yours faithfully.

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: There'll be a lot of youths at the party and so you should be able to enjoy yourself.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: There'll be a lot of young people at the party and so you should be able to enjoy yourself.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Youth (countable) is used, often in a disapproving way, to refer to a boy/young man between the ages of about fifteen and twenty: 'He was attacked and robbed by a gang of youths.'Youth (uncountable) is used mainly in formal styles to refer to all young people considered as a group in society: 'The youth of industrialized nations need to be made aware of global problems.'The usual phrase for 'people between the ages of about fifteen and twenty' is young people: 'These holidays are designed for young people like yourselves.'

common_error_corrections.error_sentence: Life in a city is more interesting for the youth because there are more things to do.
common_error_corrections.correct_sentence: Life in a city is more interesting for young people because there are more things to do.
common_error_corrections.explanation: Youth (countable) is used, often in a disapproving way, to refer to a boy/young man between the ages of about fifteen and twenty: 'He was attacked and robbed by a gang of youths.'Youth (uncountable) is used mainly in formal styles to refer to all young people considered as a group in society: 'The youth of industrialized nations need to be made aware of global problems.'The usual phrase for 'people between the ages of about fifteen and twenty' is young people: 'These holidays are designed for young people like yourselves.'

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Carl's ambition, to become a goalie in professional soccer, is within his reach.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Carl's ambition, to become a goalie in professional soccer, is within his reach.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Generally appositives should use bracketing commas since they are parenthetical statements.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: It tastes good like a cigarette should.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: It tastes good as a cigarette should.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Like cannot be used as a conjunction.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: They give me the most unique present.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: They give me the most unusual present.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: There are no degrees of uniqueness - it's either unique or not. Try special, or unusual instead.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Neither my brothers nor my father is going to sell the house.
Are either my brothers or my father responsible?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Neither my brothers nor my father is going to sell the house.
Are either my brothers or my father responsible?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When nor or or is used, the subject closer to the verb determines the number of the verb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: My brothers and my father is going.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: My father and my brothers are going.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Switch the places of "my father" with "my brothers" so that my brothers is closer to the verb and the verb must become are going. That is, force the plural.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Some of the beads are missing.
Some of the water is gone.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Some of the beads are missing.
Some of the water is gone.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Subject-verb agreement for some depends on what is referred to.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Everyone have done their homework
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Everyone has done their homework
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Subject-verb agreement for everyone, anyone, no one, someone, nobody (the ONES and BODIES): always singular.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Each of the students are responsible for doing his or her work in the library.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
No, each ... is responsible.
Each is always singular (don't let "students" distract).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The mayor as well as his brothers are going to prison.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The mayor as well as his brothers is going to prison.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Together with, as well as, along with do not make compound subjects.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Neither of the two traffic lights are working.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Neither of the two traffic lights is working.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Neither usually takes singular (even though seems to refer to two things).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: A pair of plaid trousers are in the closet.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: A pair of plaid trousers is in the closet.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: A pair of x is always singular, trousers/glasses and so on are always plural.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The department members but not the chair has decided not to teach on Valentine's Day.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The department members but not the chair have decided not to teach on Valentine's Day.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If your sentence compounds a positive and a negative subject and one is plural, the other singular, the verb should agree with the positive subject.

grammar_rules_find_error.prompt: What 3 forms does an adjective have?
grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: big - bigger - biggest.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Positive (big) - Comparative (bigger) - Superlative (biggest).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The plant grew only .07 of a foot this year because of the drought.

The plant grew only 0.07 of a foot this year because of the drought.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Leave out the zero if the decimal begins with a zero.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Forty three persons were injured in the train wreck.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Hypenate all compound numbers from twenty-one through ninety-nine:
Forty-three persons were injured in the train wreck.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
1. Pacific Ocean
2. Pacific ocean
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Common nouns used as an essential part of a proper noun are capitalized: Vine Street, Fifth Avenue, Pacific Ocean, Lake Huron.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: the torah
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: the Torah
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Terms with religious or sacred signifiance must be capitalized.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Birds fly south in the winter. (compass)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Yes, north, south etc. are not capitalized unless referring to a specific place: 
She lives in the western part of the Old South.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He is not unwilling to help.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He is willing to help

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I have some pound cake Mollie baked in my lunch bag.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: In my lunch bag, I have some pound cake that Mollie baked.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The modifier for "have" is placed on the opposite side of the sentence. Also it suggests that Mollie baked the cake using the lunch bag as the furnace.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: There are some revisions which must be made.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Some revisions must be made.
Please make some revisions.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: 'There is/there are' sounds crap. The problem with there is is that the author has thrown away the subject.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Did she say, "May I go"?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Did she say, "May I go?"
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When you have a question outside quoted material AND inside quoted material, use only one question mark and place it inside the quotation mark, there's no need for an additional full stop.

grammar_rules_find_error.prompt: How to indicate that the original material quoted contained an error?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
She wrote, "I would rather die then [sic] be seen wearing the same outfit as my sister."
Note the square brackets, placement after the mistake and italics.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I asked if he would go with me?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
No - question marks should only be used after direct questions.



I asked if he would go with me.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You may be required to bring many items namely: sleeping bags, pans, and warm clothing.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You may be required to bring many items namely sleeping bags, pans, and warm clothing.
You may be required to bring many items: sleeping bags, pans, and warm clothing.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: A colon is not used to introduce a list of items when introductory words such as namely, for example, or that is are used.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Unamerican.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Un-American.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Prefixes are hyphenated when they come before proper nouns.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Ultra-ambitious and semi-invalid.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Ultra-ambitious and semi-invalid.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: You should hypenate prefixes ending in an 'a' or an 'i' when their root word begins with the same letter. However: when a prefix ends in one vowel and a root word begins with a different vowel, generally attach them without a hyphen: antiaircraft.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I have re-covered the sofa twice.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I have re-covered the sofa twice.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: 'Re' means again AND omitting the hyphen would cause confusion with another word, recovered.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: My brother-in-law's hat.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: My two brothers-in-law's hats.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Ted couldn't distinguish between his 6's and 0's.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Ted couldn't distinguish between his 6's and 0's.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: You need to use the apostrophe to indicate the plural of zero or it will look like the word Os. To be consistent within a sentence, you would also use the apostrophe to indicate the plural of 6's.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I appreciated John working with me to resolve the conflict.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I appreciated John's working with me to resolve the conflict.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Use the possessive case with gerunds.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: My $10 million estate is to be split among my husband, daughter, son, and nephew.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: My $10 million estate is to be split among my husband, daughter, son, and nephew.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Omitting the comma after son would indicate that the son and nephew would have to split one-third of the estate.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Stan is more single.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Stan is single.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Adjectives that should not have comparative or superlative forms, because their meanings already express the qualities to the highest possible degree: instantaneous, unique, dead, single.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The manager of your Company confirmed the booking in writing on 15 August.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The Manager of your Company confirmed the booking in writing on 15 August.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Good practice in polite business wrtiting to capitalise titles of important people: The Director will cast the final vote.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The company staff are adverse to change.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The company staff are averse to change.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Should be averse (averse means strongly disinclined and usually refers to people).
Adverse usually means hostile or unfavourable, e.g. adverse conditions including rain, snow, ice and fog affect your visibility.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Inform the clerk if Mark needs a seat.
Inform the clerk whether Mark needs a seat.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Both are correct.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. The clerk is only to be informed if Mark needs a seat.
2. The clerk is to be informed of Mark's preference regardless.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The parade will go ahead whether it rains.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The parade will go ahead whether it rains or not.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
"Or not" can be ditched all of the time, except when it means 'regardless of whether'. 
It also shows that the placement of "or not" need not be directly after "whether".

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Mice need advise.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Mice need advice.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: "Advice" means suggestion for a beneficial course of action.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The principal objective is to make a profit.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Principal is an adjective here. The word principle, on the other hand, is never an adjective. It is a noun. Principal can also be noun when it means head or chief.

grammar_rules_find_error.prompt: Why doesn't doctor have a full stop but prof does:
grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Dr Ingols and Prof. Munro.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Only use a full stop at the end of a contraction if its last letter is different to the last letter of the whole word.



Doctor ends in r - no full stop required.
Professor ends in r, but Prof ends in f - full stop required.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I have never seen these kind of things before.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I have never seen these kinds of things before.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: No. These / those must always take a plural: I have never seen these kinds of things before. Sarah is not used to those types of situations.

grammar_rules_find_error.prompt: Is this correct for number agreement?
grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The evacuation of the offices is the floor manager's responsibility.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Yes, a phrase like 'of the offices' or 'of nails' (called a 'prepositional phrase') does not affect whether the main word is singular or plural. The subject in question is "the evaluation", singular.
Similarly, the following is wrong: a combination of factors were the cause of the crash => was the cause.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: What are you inferring?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: What are you implying?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: "Inferring? I don't understand. Oh, I see. I was implying...." When you imply, you transmit an indirect message. When you infer, you receive the indirect message.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: There are less pigeons in Trafalgar Square than there used to be.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: There are fewer pigeons in Trafalgar Square than there used to be.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
The word 'less' should be used for a single item (e.g., less time, less space); whereas, 'fewer' should be used when there is more than one item (e.g., fewer mice, fewer omissions).
Fewer people will vote in the forthcoming elections. There is less cheese on this plate.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Being born in Texas, it is understandable that I miss the sea so much.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: As I was born in Texas, it is understandable why I miss the sea so much.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Dangling modifier. Not placing the noun being modified next to its modifier (or failing to use the noun being modified in the sentence) ("As I was born in Texas" is not a modifier).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Do you like being so ignorant?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: It's a gerund.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The jury ___ to convene at 4 o'clock.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The jury is to convene at 4 o'clock.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If you're unsure which verb to use, add an additional word: The members of the jury are to convene at 4 o'clock.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Forget-me-not
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Forget-me-nots
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
To form the plural of a compound noun, pluralize the principal word in the compound. When there is no obvious principal word, add 's' (or 'es') to the end of the compound, as done here.
Compare: Mothers-in-law (pluralize the principal word "mother").

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Two and a half thousand.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Two-and-a-half-thousand.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Technically that means 502. You should hyphenate compound adjectives: two-and-a-half thousand.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Provided that the weather is fine, we'll have a picnic on Saturday.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Provided the weather is fine, we'll have a picnic on Saturday.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: That is unnecessary with provided.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Forty-four thousand one hundred and twenty.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: No matter where they appear in the whole number, numbers between 21 and 99 should be hypenated(except, obviously, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She turned everything she touched in to gold.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: She turned everything she touched into gold.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The word into is a preposition. It's written as one word: She turned everything she touched into gold. The confusion arises because the words in and to appear next to each other in a sentence when a verb includes the preposition: Paul wanted to hand the purse in to the police.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Put the fruit in to the basket.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Put the fruit into the basket.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: No, the verbs are 'put into, drive into (drive in) and fall into (fall in)'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: After seeing the sheep, we moved onto the cows.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: After seeing the sheep, we moved on to the cows.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Moved on: is the verb.
Onto means "on top of".

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I would like to ___ about the toilet facilities in the hotel.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I would like to enquire about the toilet facilities in the hotel.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Inquiry is being used in relation to a formal inquest (i.e., an investigation); whereas, enquiry is being used to denote the act of questioning.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The ___ deceleration will likely cause a further fall in unemployment.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The economic deceleration will likely cause a further fall in unemployment.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
The adjective 'economic' pertains to the economy, finances or wealth.


The adjective 'economical' denotes that something saves money or resources or is not wasteful of money or resources.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Altogether / All together Mark earns more than his cousin.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Altogether Mark earns more than his cousin.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
The adverb 'altogether' means 'wholly', 'to the full extent' or 'with everything considered'.

The term 'all together' pertains to when a group acts or is acted upon collectively.

The soldiers stood all together waiting for the plane.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The water molecule comprises of two atoms of hydrogen and one atom of oxygen.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The water molecule comprises two atoms of hydrogen and one atom of oxygen.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Do not use the word of with comprise.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Electioneers canvas twice as many votes as painters.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Electioneers canvass twice as many votes as painters.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Canvass: electioneer, collect opinions.
Canvas: heavy woven cloth of hemp, flax or cotton.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He was touched by Winter's icy breath.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He was touched by Winter's icy breath.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The four seasons are not normally written with capital letters. However, if a season is given a human trait (i.e., personified), then it can be given a capital letter: The leaves had been subjected to Autumn's touch.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The amount of women in London who flirt with their own husbands is perfectly scandalous. It looks so bad. It is simply washing one's clean linen in public.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The number of women in London who flirt with their own husbands is perfectly scandalous. It looks so bad. It is simply washing one's clean linen in public.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Women - plural and can be counted: 'The number of women...'

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The disease affected a large amount of camels in the town.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The disease affected a large number of camels in the town.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Amount is for things you cannot measure; number is for plural of things you can measure.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Anya is the one that rescued the bird.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Anya is the one who rescued the bird.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
'Who" is for people, "that" is for things.
Lokua is on the team that won first place. "That" is used even if it's a thing made up of people, such as a team or organisation.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: That is a decision which you must live with for the rest of your life.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: That is a decision you must live with for the rest of your life.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Streamline by leaving out which.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Nurses work 12-hour shifts.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Nurses work 12-hour shifts.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: 12-hour is a single idea adjective that comes before a noun. Twelve hours later, she was exhausted. - Correct, because twelves hours is not used as an adjective above.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Debbie, pregnant, will be due in September.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Debbie, pregnant, will give birth in September.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Reword to replace state (be due) with a verb (give birth).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The customer was being helped by the salesman when the thief came into the store.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The salesman was helping the customer when the thief came into the store.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Note the double be in 'was being'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The work will be finished by 5:00 PM.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Someone will finish the work by 5:00 PM

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Shaggy throws as a raccoon. 
Shaggy throws like he were a raccoon.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Shaggy throws like a raccoon. 
Shaggy throws as if he were a raccoon.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Use like when no verb follows: Shaggy throws like a raccoon. It acted just like my computer.
If the clause that comes next includes a verb, then you should use as: Shaggy throws as if he were a raccoon. It acted just as I would expect my computer to behave.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Imagine a grown woman acting as a child.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Imagine a grown woman acting like a child.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We’re comparing two things (the woman and the child), so like should be used.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He stood up.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He stood.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: States the obvious: people rarely stand sideways.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You should practise more.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Yes, practise is a verb and practice is a noun. You need more practice.
If you are unsure then try using the word 'preparation' (or 'lessons') instead of 'practice'.
Memo: both practice and ice are nouns.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He prophecies a great war between East and West.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
No, the word prophesy is a verb (predict the future) (pronounced sigh) and the word prophecy is a noun. (sea).
He prophesies a great war between East and West.
On the second day of the course, we will study the prophecies of Nostradamus.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
It happened in August, e.g., two months ago.
All amphibians are thriving in the new pond; i.e., two bullfrogs were spotted yesterday.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
It happened in August, e.g., two months ago.
All amphibians are thriving in the new pond; i.e., two bullfrogs were spotted yesterday.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The abbreviation i.e. (id est) means 'in other words' or 'that is to say'; whereas e.g. (exempli gratia) means 'for example'. Do not confuse the two.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The well was collapsed in 2001 AD.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Write AD before the year: AD 2001;
 BC comes after the year: Caesar reigned from 63 BC to AD 14.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The new hall will breath new life into the town.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: No. The word 'breath' is a noun. 'Breathe' is a verb. The new hall will breathe new life into the town.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: There are three other Latvian families on the cruise beside us.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: There are three other Latvian families on the cruise besides us.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When you want to say "apart from us" use besides.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The cashew nuts were an excellent compliment for the soup.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The cashew nuts were an excellent complement for the soup.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: No. Compliment: expression of praise, complement (with an 'e') is something that enhances something else or goes well with it.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You can trust my aide - he is very discrete.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: You can trust my aide - he is very discreet.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Discrete is separate, discreet is respecting secrecy.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: All embassy staff and their dependants must be at the airport by 6 o'clock.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: All embassy staff and their dependants must be at the airport by 6 o'clock.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Dependant: NOUN person who is dependent on someone else.
Dependent: ADJECTIVE meaning 'contingent on', 'relying on'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: In the climatic scene of the movie, the aliens emerge from the capsule and start zapping the onlookers.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: In the climactic scene of the movie, the aliens emerge from the capsule and start zapping the onlookers.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Climatic derives from the noun climate, climactic refers to a decisive moment.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The reprimand which you received was justified.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The reprimand you received was justified.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Which introduces a restrictive clause, and often you can get rid of the 'which' or 'that': the reprimand you received was justified.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Heat the soup up.
Where are you going to?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Heat the soup.
Where are you going?

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: It is a present from my wife and I.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: It is a present from my wife and me.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: This is as wrong as saying "from I". Put "me" – objective case of "I" after the preposition "from". In fact, you should only use 'I' in an expression like 'you and I' when it is the subject of the verb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: This approach is an improvement on Smith’s design.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: This approach improves Smith’s design.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: We have their teeth; we have their bones; we have their pictures.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Anaphora.

grammar_rules_find_error.prompt: What writing technique is shown below?
grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Their teeth, we have; their bones, we have, their pictures we have.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Epistrophe: repeating words at the end of sentences.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
1. Jerome bought flowers not only for his mother but also for Yolanda, his wife.
2. Jerome bought flowers for not only his mother but also Yolanda, his wife.
3. Both.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: 3. Both
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The point is to show that parallelism is required when using not only ... but also, either .... or, neither ... nor.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: For the convenience of the reader.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: For the reader's convenience.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Resolve into possessive.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: ___ the government ___ increase taxes, it would have more money. (If the government increased....)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Were the government to increase taxes, it would have more money.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Were + subject + to + verb ...... would:
I wouldn't need to use these flashcards were I to know English perfectly.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You should continue to build-up your pension.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: You should continue to build up your pension.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: You should NOT put a hyphen within phrasal verbs - verbs made up of a main verb and an adverb or preposition. For example: stop off, break in. However, if phrasal verb is in a noun function then you should hyphenate: There was a build-up of traffic on the ring road.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Mailman, businessman, salesman, man-hours.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Businessperson, executive, salesperson, labour hours.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Use gender neutral nouns.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
A thirty-three-year-old man rather liberally.
The man was thirty-three years old.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Thirty-three-year-old is a compound modifier BEFORE man in 1st example => all hyphenated.
Thirty-three years is a compound of YEARS, but whole structure is not hyphenated because it is after the verb.


There would be no hyphen in "He lived to be one hundred." (nothing modified by adjective)

but there is one in "a hunred-year-old man".

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Non English speaking countries.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Non-English-speaking countries.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He's going to Sri Lanka alongside his school class.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He's going to Sri Lanka along with his school class.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Alongside is more a physical relationship and sounds off.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
If the next two nights are sellouts, the play will be extended.
The play's run will be extended, if the next two nights are sellouts.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
If the next two nights are sellouts, the play will be extended.
The play's run will be extended if the next two nights are sellouts.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Adverb claues that start sentences must be set off by a comma, but not ones that end sentences.
This is wrong: The play's run will be extended, if the next two nights are sellouts.

grammar_rules_find_error.prompt: What do you call the bolded?
grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Looking for help, the man fell on his knees to beg.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: A participial phrase... it contains a verb used as an adjective.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Present Participle => ends in 'ing' (e.g. boiling water). 
Past Participle => ends in 'ed' or 'en' (e.g. cooked ham, broken record).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He helped to write the program.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He helped write the program.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When the infinitive follows some verbs (helped here) as the direct object, the 'to' may be dropped.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Twelve dollars are less than what I want to sell it for.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Twelve dollars is less than what I want to sell it for.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
A noun expressing an amount or measurement is normally singular: twelve spoons of sugar is less than what I usually take.
But contrast where the unit of measurement refers to a number of individual items, then it treated as a plural: twelve cubes of sugar are less than what I usually take.
Reasoning: the sugar, despite being more than one mg, was added at the same time, as a single unit. It would not be helpful (semantically or grammatically) to think of each mg of sugar as being added separately. Instead, treat the mass noun as the group it is, and use the singular.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Four-fifths of the country is satisfied with its health insurance.
Four-fifths of the people are satisfied with their health insurance.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Four-fifths of the country is satisfied with its health insurance.
Four-fifths of the people are satisfied with their health insurance.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
One part of a whole - of the country.
Four-fifths refers to many individuals - of the people.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Baked beans are one of my favorite dishes.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Baked beans is one of my favorite dishes.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Some foods, like some diseases (e.g. measles, mumps), or branches of knowledge (e.g. physics) end in -s but are really singular. Also note the 'one' which suggests singular.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: 10 g of tissue were tested.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: 10 g of tissue was tested
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When a measurement is being described in a sentence, that quantity takes a singular verb form, but: Ten mice underwent surgery. A plural verb is appropriate when items should be considered individually.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: It's like my cousin thinks he is Batman.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: It's as if my cousin thinks he is Batman.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: First option is used mostly in conversation. Grammarians want the following: It's as if my cousin thinks he is Batman. You cannot use like as a conjunction (i.e. with a phrase).

grammar_rules_find_error.prompt: What part of speech is 'before' acting:
grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: It will be some time before summer.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
A preposition. A preposition is a word placed before a noun or noun phrase and somehow indicates the noun or noun phrase's relationship to another verb, adjective or noun (phrase). These are words like 'over, by, in, to, with, etc.'
But here it's a conjunction: It will be some time before the seasons change.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You should have a spare wheel in case you have a puncher.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: You should have a spare wheel in case you have a puncher. (Present tense for future)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You can't turn right here. You ___ turn left.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: You can't turn right here. You have to turn left.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: I have to do something: it's necessary to do it, I am obliged to do. Use have to with will and may/might. You'll have to go to doctor. You can say have got to instead of have to. I've got to work tomorrow.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You ___ keep it a secret. You ___ tell anyone. You ___ tell him, but you can if you want to.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You must keep it a secret. You mustn't tell anyone. 
You don't have to tell him, but you can if you want to.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
You mustn't do it: it's necessary that you don't do it. (so don't do it)
You don't have to do it: you don't need to do it. (but you can if you want to)

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: We've got plenty of time. We _____ hurry.(needn't)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
We've got plenty of time. We needn't hurry.
We've got plenty of time. We don't need to hurry.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: You needn't do it: you don't need to do it(but you can if you like).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Everything was ok. You ___ worried. (needn't have).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Everything was ok. You needn't have worried.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Everything was ok. You needn't have worried. (You worried, but it wasn't necessary).
Everything will be ok. You needn't worry. (It's not necessary).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I ___ get up early, so I didn't / but I did.
I ___ got up early, I could have stayed in bed longer. (meeting cancelled).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I didn't need to get up early, so I didn't / but I did.
I needn't have got up early, I could have stayed in bed longer.(meeting cancelled).
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Didn't need to: it wasn't necessay for me to .... (I knew this at that time).


Needn't have: I did it but now I know it wasn't necessary.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You look tired. You ___ go to bed.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: You look tired. You should go to bed.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. Should: It's a good/right thing to (advice/opinion), use when something is not right or what you expect.
2. Should is not as stronger as must or have to.
3. should == ought to. Ann ought not to go to bed so late.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You missed a great party last night. You ___ come. (should have)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: You missed a great party last night. You should have come.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. You should have done something: you didn't do it, but it would have been the right thing to do it.

2. You shouldn't have done something = you did it, but it was the wrong thing to do.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I insisted that something ___ be done about the problem.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I insisted that something should be done about the problem.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
We can use should after a number of words:
- demand: I demanded that he should apologise.
- propose: He proposes that we should watch a movie.
- insist: They insisted that we should have dinner with him.


Similarly recommend, suggest, it's improtant, vital, necessary, essential, strange, odd, funny, typical, interesting, suprised, suprising: It's strange that he should be late, he's usually on time. I was suprised that he should say such a thing.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: We _______ stop for petrol soon, the tank is almost empty.(better)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: We'd better stop for petrol soon, the tank is almost empty.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
I'd better(had better) do something: it's advisable to do it. If you don't do it, there will be a problem or a danger. 
Negative: I'd better not.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
It's a great film. You ___ go and see it.
The film starts at 8.30. You ___ go now or you'll be late.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
It's a great film. You should go and see it.
The film starts at 8.30. You'd better go now or you'll be late.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
'd better: there is always a danger or a problem if you don't follow the advise.
should: Its a good thing to do, no problem if don't do it.


'd better - for specific situation, should also possible.

Should for general and specific situations: It's late, You should / you'd better go home. (specific). / You're always at home. You should go out nore often. (general).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
___ to go home.
___ for us to go home.

___ we went home.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
It's time to go home.
It's time for us to go home.

It's time we went home.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
In last sentence meaning is present.
It's time you did something = You should have already done it or started it (use to complain or to criticise): It's time children were in bed. It's long after their bed time.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Whenever Richard was angry, he ___ walk out of room.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Whenever Richard was angry, he would walk out of room.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Use 'would' when you talk about thing that happened regularly in the past: would === used to.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Lisa: I have lost my wallet. Have you seen it anywhere?
Sue: No, but If I find it, I'll tell you.
Joy: If I found a wallet in the street, I would take it to the police station.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Lisa: I have lost my wallet. Have you seen it anywhere?
Sue: No, but If I find it, I'll tell you.
Joy: If I found a wallet in the street, I would take it to the police station.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Sue feels there is a real possibility that she'll find the wallet. Joy doesn't expect to find a wallet, he is imagining a situation/situation is different. We don't use would in if-part. Could/might also possible instead of would. I wish I + past tense, same way: If I ... but this time you regret it, something is not as we would like it to be. Eg: I wish I knew his number, I would phone him.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I would be greatful if you ___ let me know your decision asap.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I would be greatful if you would let me know your decision asap.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We can use "would" in if-part: when you ask somebody do something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Rachel: If I knew you were in hospital, I would have gone to see you.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Rachel: If I had known you were in hospital, I would have gone to see you.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Here Rachel didn't know that he was in hospital.


Use 'I + had .......' to talk about past.


I wish I had known that Gary was in hospital. I would have gone to see him.
I wish something had happen: I'm sorry it didn't happen, this time I also regret it.



I'm not hungry. If I was hungry, I would eat something. [now]
I wasn't hungry. If I had been hungry, I would have eaten something. [past]

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I ___ you every sucess in future. (wish)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I wish you every sucess in future.
I saw tim before the exam and he wished me luck.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Wish somebody something: luck, a happy birthday, etc.
But you can't wish something happens, use hope: I hope you get this letter before you go away.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I'm sorry I have to go. I ___ I could stay longer.(wish)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I'm sorry I have to go. I wish I could stay longer.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
I wish I could(do something): I regret that I can't do it.
I wish I could have (done something): I regret that I couldn't do it. I hear the party was great. I wish I could have gone.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I ___ it would stop raining. (wish)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I wish it would stop raining.
I wish you would do something instead of just sitting and doing nothing.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
I wish ..... would....: to complain about actions and changes, not situations - I wish Sarah would come but I wish Sarah was here now.
I wish ..... wouldn't ....: to complain about things that people do repeatedly - I wish you wouldn't keep interrupting me.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Lisa ____ the roof _____ yesterday. (have, repair)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Lisa had the roof rapaired yesterday.
I think you should have your coat cleaned.
I don't like having my photograph taken.
Our neighbours has just had a garage built.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Have something done: somebody else do it for subject./subject arrange for somebody else to do something.
Get something done: I think you should get you hair cut really short.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Gary ____ his nose _____ in a fight. (have, break).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Gary had his nose broken in a fight.
Have you ever had your passport stolen.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Have something done (different meaning): something happens to somebody or their belongings.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Who did Emma telephone?
Who telephoned Emma?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
1. 'Who' is the object: Emma telephone somebody.
2. 'Who' is the subject: somebody telephoned Emma.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We do not use do/does/did if who/what etc. is the subject of the sentence: What happened to you last night? How many people came to the meeting?

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Who do you want to speak to?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
We do not ignore preposition as well as don't change position:
Who do you want to speak to?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Special case: Preposition + whom in formal style: To whom do you want to speak? = With whom do you wish to speak?
Always use whom after preposition(not who): You have a child by whom? (by – preposition)

What was the weather like yesterday? Where are you from?

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: ___ you hear the doorbell? I rang it three times.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Didn't you hear the doorbell? I rang it three times. (suprise)
Haven't we met somewhere before? (agree)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Negative questions (isn't it?, didn't you? ...):
1. to show surprise.
2. when we expect listener to agree with us.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Do you know where _?_ Tom _?_ gone? (has)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Do you know where Tom has gone?
Please explain what you mean?
I wonder why she left early?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
When question is a part of longer sentence (do you know.... / I don't know.... / etc), the word order changes. Police asked us where we were going?
Use if/whether when there is no question word (what, why, etc): Did anybody see you? Do you know if/whether anybody saw you?

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Have you locked the door? 'Yes, I ___.' (guess).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Have you locked the door? 'Yes, I have.'
She could lend me money, but she won't.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Use auxiliary verbs(do, does, has, other helping verbs) when you don't want to repeat something.
Use do/does/did for present, past simple.
Do you like onions? 'Yes I did but I don't anymore.'

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Jim and Nora are getting married. Surprise? Really?'
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Jim and Nora are getting married. 'Are they? Really?'
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Have you? / Isn't she? / Do they? etc: to show interest in what other said or to show surprise. I have seen Jim. 'Oh, have you? How is he?'

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
It's a nice day, is it?(voice goes down)
You haven't seen Lisa today, have you?(voice goes up)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
It's a nice day, isn't it? (inviting listener to agree with him)
You haven't seen Lisa today, have you? (asking question)
- Tom doesn't look well today, does he? (inviting listener to agree with him) 
- 'No, he looks tired'
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
If voice goes down: inviting listener to agree with him.
If voice goes up: asking question.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You ___ got a pen, ___ ? (have)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You haven't got a pen, have you?
You couldn't do me a favour, could you?
You don't know where Karen is, do you?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: -VE sentence + question tag: to ask for things/information or somebody to do something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Don't be late, ___ you?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Don't be late, will you? (voice goes DOWN).
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Negative imperative have a question tag 'Will you'.
Positive imperative: Stop dreaming, will/won't you?
An imperative sentence gives a direct command. It can end in a full stop or an exclamation mark, depending on the forcefulness of the command.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I wouldn't ___ to tell him. (dare)
I ___ tell him what happened. (dare + not)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I wouldn't dare to tell him.
I daren't tell him what happened.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: After 'dare' you can use infinitive with or without to, but after 'daren't (dare not)', you must use infinitive without to.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Would you ____ go now? (like)
Would you ______ to go now? (like + object)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Would you like to go now?
Would you like me to go now?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Verb + to...., Verb + Object + to.......
Don't say '....want that.... ': Do you want me to come with you?
Help + Object + Infinitive: Can you help me to move the sofa?

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I wouldn't advise/recommend ___ in the hotel. (stay)
I wouldn't advise/recommend anybody ___ in the hotel. (stay)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I wouldn't advise/recommend staying in that hotel.
I wouldn't advise/recommend anybody to stay in that hotel.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
After advise, allow, recommend two structures are possible:
verb + -ing, verb + object + to.
Passive:
Parking isn't allowed in front of the building. You aren't allowed to park in front of building.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Hot weather ___ me feel tired.
___ me carry your bag for you.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Hot weather makes me feel tired.
Let me carry your bag for you.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: With let and make: verb + object + infinitive. We say 'make somebody do', (not to do), but the passive is 'be made to do' (with to). We were made to wait for two hours. (they made us wait).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I know I locked the door. I clearly remember  ___ it. (lock)
I remember ___ the door, but I forgot to shut the windows. (lock)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I know I locked the door. I clearly remember locking it.
I remember to lock the door, but I forgot to shut the windows.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
I remember doing something: I did it and now I remember it. You remember doing something after you have done it.
I remember to do something: I remembered that I had to do it, so I did it. You remember to do something before you do it.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I now regret ___ what I said. I shouldn't have said it. (say)
We regret ___ you that we can't offer you the job. (inform)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I now regret saying what I said. I shouldn't have said it.
We regret to inform you that we can't offer you the job.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
I regret doing something: I did it and now I'm sorry about it.
I regret to say/to tell you/to inform you: I'm sorry that I have to say it.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The president paused for a moment and the went on ___. (talk)


After discussing the economy, the president went on ___ about foreign policy. (talk)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The president paused for a moment and the went on talking.


After discussing the economy, the president went on to talk about foreign policy.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. Go on doing something: continue with the something.
2. Go on to do something: do or say something new.


- ing or to ...... also possible with these verb: begin, start, contbinue, intend, bother:
It has started raining or It has started to rain.
- but normally we don't use -ing after -ing (It's starting to rain).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I tried ___ the table, but it was too heavy. (move)
The photocopier doesn't seem to be working. Try ___ the green button. (press)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I tried to move the table, but it was too heavy.
The photocopier doesn't seem to be working. Try pressing the green button.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Try to do: attempt to do it, make an attempt to do it. Try also means 'do something as an experiment or test'. 
Try + participle: perhaps this will help to solve the problem.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I need ___ more exercise. (take).
This room needs ___. (tide).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I need to take more exercise.


This room needs tidying. (room needs to be cleaned)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
I need to do something: its necessary for me to do something so as to achieve something.
Something needs doing: It's need to be done.
The batteries in the radio need changing. (They need to be changed).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Everybody helped ___ after the party. (clean up).
I'm sorry I'm nervous. I can't ___ it. (help).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Everybody helped to clean up after the party || Everybody helped clean up.



I'm sorry I'm nervous. I can't help it.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Help to do or help do (both are possible).

I can't help doing: I can't stop myself doing it.
She tried to be serious, but she couldn't help laughing. (She couldn't stop herself laughing).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Do you like ___ early?
Do you like ___ early? (get up)
Do you like ___ a student. (be)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Do you like getting up early?
Do you like to get up early?
Do you like being a student.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Love: I love mating or to mate.
Like: I like meeting people or to meet people.
Hate: Stephens hates flying or Stephens hates to fly.
Love / like / hate + -ing or to...: when we talk about repeated action. We use -ing (not to...) when we talk about a situation that already exists (or existed): I hated being working here.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I like ___ the kitchen. (clean).
It's not my favourite job, but I like ___ the kitchen as often as possible. (clean)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I like cleaning the kitchen.
It's not my favourite job, but I like to clean the kitchen as often as possible.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. l like doing something: I do it and I enjoy it.
2. I like to do something: l think it's a good thing to do, but l don't necessarily enjoy it.
3. Note: enjoy and mind are always followed by -ing (not to.....).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I like ___ tennis. (play)
I'd like ___ play tennis today. (play)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I like playing tennis. (I like it in general)
I'd like to play tennis today. (I want to paly today)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. Would like / would love / would hate / would prefer are usually followed by  to ... 
2. Would mind is always followed by -ing (not to .....)
Would you mind closing the door, please.
3. (redo) I would like / would love / would hate / would prefer to have done something: I would have regret it / I regret it now if I didn't or couldn't do it.
We'd like to have gone away, but we were too busy at home.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I don't like cites. I prefer ___ in the country. or I prefer ___ in the country. (live).
I prefer ___ to ___ you were wearing yesterday. (coat).
I prefer ___ to ___ by train. (drive, travel).
I prefer ___ rather than ___ by train. (drive, travel).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
1. I don't like cites. I prefer to live in the country. or I prefer living in the country.
2. I prefer this coat to the coat you were wearing yesterday.
3. I prefer driving to travelling by train.
4. I prefer to drive rather than travel by train.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Use prefer to or prefer -ing to say what you prefer in general.
I prefer something to something else or I prefer doing something to doing something else or I prefer to do something rather than (do) something else.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
___ you ___ tea or coffee? 'Coffee, please.  (would prefer)
Shall we go by train? 'I'd prefer ___.' (drive).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Would you prefer tea or coffee? 'Coffee, please.'
Shall we go by train? 'I'd prefer to drive.'
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Would prefer to say what somebody wants in a specific situation.
We say 'would prefer to do something' (not doing).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Shall we go by train? 'I'd rather drive.'
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Shall we go by train? 'I'd rather drive.'
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. Would rather (do) = would prefer (to do).
2. Negative: I'd rather not (do something): I'm tired. I'd rather not go out this evening, if you don't mind.
3. We say 'I'd rather do something than do something else: I'd rather stay at home than go to cinema.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Shall I stay here? 'I'd rather you ___ with us.' (come)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Shall I stay here? 'I'd rather you came with us.' (I would prefer this)
I'll repair your car tomorrow, OK? 'I'd rather you did it today.'
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone what I said.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. I'd rather you did something: we want/prefer him to do that thing.
2. I'd rather you didn't (do something): I'd prefer you not to do it.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Are you looking forward ___ the weekend?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Are you looking forward to the weekend?
Are you looking forward to going on holiday?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: To + Noun/Gerund: I prefer driving to travelling by train.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Let's go to the cinema tonight, ___ we?
Let me use your car, ___ you?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Let's go to the cinema tonight, shall we?
Let me use your car, will you?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Let's has tag 'shall we?'
'Let me/him' has tag 'will/won't you?'

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I'm on time, ___ I?
I'm not late, ___ I?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I'm on time, aren't I?
I'm not late, am I?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Question tags exceptions:
I'm: aren't I?
I'm not: am I?

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Are you Interested ___ working __ us?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Are you Interested in working for us?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Preposition + gerund/noun: intrested + in.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I'm good ___ learning languages.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I'm good at learning languages.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Preposition + gerund/noun: good + at.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She must be fed up ___ studying.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: She must be fed up with studying.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Preposition + gerund/noun:
fed up + with, also 'fed up with people doing something'.
I'm fed up with people telling me what to do.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: How ___ meeting ___ lunch tomorrow?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: How about meeting for lunch tomorrow?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Preposition + gerund/noun: How + about.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: What did you do after ___ school? (leave)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
What did you do after leaving school?
What did you do after you left school?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Before/after + -ing or other form as shown above.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You can improve your English by ___ more. (read)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You can improve your english by reading more.
She made herself ill by not eating properly.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: By + -ing: how something happens.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Are you looking forward to ___ on a holiday? (go)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Are you looking forward to going on a holiday?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Look forward to + -ing.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Frank is used to ___ alone. (live)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Frank is used to living alone.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
I'm used to something: it's not new or strange for me. 
I'm used to do something: I did it regularly in the past but no longer do it.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: You must apologise ___ not telling the truth.(preposition)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You must apologise for not telling the truth.
I apologised to them for keeping them waiting.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Apologise + for + noun/gerund.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Have you suceeded ___ finding a job yet?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Have you suceeded in finding a job yet?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Suceed + in + noun/gerund.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Theu insisted ___ paying ___ the meal.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Theu insisted on paying for the meal.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Insist + on + noun/gerund.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He doesn't approve ___ swearing.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He doesn't approve of swearing.
I don't approve of people killing animals for fun.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Approve + of + noun/gerund.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: We have decided ____ moving to London.(prep.)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: We have decided against moving to London.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Decide + against + noun/gerund.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Do you feel ___ going out tonight.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Please forgive me ___ not writing to you.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I live only a short walk from here, so it's not worth ___ a taxi.

I live only a short walk from here, so it's not worth taking a taxi.
Our flight was very early in the morning, so it wasn't worth going to bed.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I had no difficulty / trouble ___ a place to live (find).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
It was a waste of time ___ that book. It was rubbish. (read)
It's a waste of money ___ things you don't need. (buy)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
It was a waste of time reading that book. It was rubbish.


It's a waste of money buying things you don't need.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Do you have much opportunity ___ your English? (practice)

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Money/time/opportunity/energy/courage etc. to (do something).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Let's go to the pool ___ a swim.
Let's go to the pool ___ have a swim.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Let's go to the pool for a swim.
Let's go to the pool to have a swim.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: What is this switch ___?

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
It's ___ you to take me to the airport.
(nice of / stupid of)

It's nice of you to take me to the airport.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Was Patrick _____ to see me? (surprise)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
