I'm sorry to hear that your father is ill.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
'I'm sorry to/I'm suprised to' etc to say how somebody reacts to something.
(happy, glad, pleased, sad, disappointed, amazed, astonished, relieved)

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: This part of town is dangerous kid, aren't you afraid ___ around here. (roam)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: This part of town is dangerous kid, aren't you afraid to roam around here.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: I'm afraid to do something = I don't want to do it cause it's dangerous or result could be bad.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Let me know if you are interested ___ the club. (join)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Let me know if you are interested in joining the club.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I was interested ___ that Tanya has left the job. (hear)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I was interested to hear that Tanya has left the job.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: I'm interesting to ...: to say how somebody reacts to what they hear/see/read/learn/know/find.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I'm sorry for/about ___ at you yesterday. (shout)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I'm sorry for/about shouting at you yesterday.
I'm sorry I shouted at you.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
I'm sorry for/about(doing something) = to apologise for something you did before.
Sorry to ... = regret something that happens.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: 'Do you want _______ to eat?' 'No, I don't want ________ to eat.'
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: 'Do you want something to eat?' 'No, I don't want anything to eat.'
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Some (also somebody/someone/something): in positive sentences.
Any (also anybody etc.): in -ve sentences, or if meaning is negative - He refused to eat anything.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Can I have _______ sugar, please? (asking for things)
Are you waiting for ___ ?
Have you got _____ luggage? 'No, I haven't.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Can I have some sugar, please?(asking for things)
Are you waiting for somebody? I think you are waiting for somebody.
Have you got any luggage? 'No, I haven't.'
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: In questions some(also somebody/someone/something): talk about a person or thing that we know exists or we think exists, offer or ask for things, any(also anybody etc.): we dont know if person or think exists.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
If ___ has any questions, I'll be pleased to answer them.
I'm sorry for ___ trouble I've caused.
'Sing a song' 'Which song shall I sing?' '___ song. I don't mind.'
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
If any has any questions, I'll be pleased to answer them.
I'm sorry for any trouble I've caused.
'Sing a song' 'Which song shall I sing?' 'Any song. I don't mind.'
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Any: after if or when sentence or have idea of if, it doesn't matter which.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
1. quite
2. pretty
3. rather
4. fairly
5. 1, 2, 3, 4
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Quite/pretty/rather/fairly > a little < very + adjectives or adverb.
Fairly is weaker then the rest of the siblings.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Sally has ______ good job(quite).
Sally has ______ good job(pretty).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Sally has quite a good job.
Sally has a pretty good job.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Pretty: used as an informal word in spoken English. We say 'quite + a/an' but 'a pretty'. We can say 'quite a/an + noun' (without adjective): I didn't expect to see you. It was quite a surprise.
Quite a lot of .....: There was quite a lot of people at the meeting.
Quite + verb, especially 'like' and 'enjoy': I quite like tennis, but it's not my favourite sport.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: My teacher ___ me apologize for what I had said.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: My teacher made me apologize for what I had said.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Make + person + verb: to force someone to do something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Please ___ your secretary fax me the information.
Dr. Smith ___ his nurse take the patient's temperature.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Please have your secretary fax me the information.
Dr. Smith had his nurse take the patient's temperature.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: [Have + person + verb]: to give someone the responsibility to do something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Everyone was late except me. I was ______ one to arrive on time.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Everyone was late except me. I was the only one to arrive on time.
The next train to arrive at platform 4 will be the 10:50 to London.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The first/the next/the last/the only/the second etc + to + .....

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I am ___ to be late home this evening.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I am likely to be late home this evening. (I'll probably be late home)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Something is sure/certain/likely/bound to happen.

grammar_rules_find_error.prompt: See somebody do VS see somebody doing:
grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I saw Kate ___ in taxi and left for holidays.
I saw Kate ___ for bus.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I saw Kate get in taxi and left for holidays.
I saw Kate waiting for bus.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
I saw somebody do something: he did something and I saw it (complete action).



I saw somebody doing something: he was doing something and I saw it.


Same structure with other verbs: hear, listen, find, notice, smell etc.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: ___ tired, I went to bed early. (feel)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Feeling tired, I went to bed early.
Not having a car, she finds it difficult to get around.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
If -ing clause is at beginning we write a comma(,) after it.
-ing clause to explain something / why somebody does something.
Can also use -ing after while or when.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: ___ a hotel, we looked for somewhere to eat. (find)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Having found a hotel, we looked for somewhere to eat.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
If -ing clause is at begining we write a comma(,) after it.
When one action happens after another action, we can use having/after done for first action.
When both action are short, we can omit having: Taking key out of pocket, he opened the door.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
All tickets have been sold, there are ___ left.
All tickets have been sold, there are ___ tickets left.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
All tickets have been sold, there are none left.
All tickets have been sold, there are no tickets left.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
No + noun = not a (when noun is singular) or not any (when noun is pularal), can be used at the begining of sentence.
None: without noun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: None ___ were (was) open. (shop)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: None of shops were (was) open.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: None of + plural, auxiliary verb can be singular or plural but plural is more common.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I didn't said ___.
I said ___.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I didn't said anything.
I said nothing.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Nothing / nobody: not + anything/anybody.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Everyone ___ done his or her homework.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Everyone has done his or her homework.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Anyone, everyone, someone, no one, nobody are always singular, but we often use they/them/their or her/him/his after these words.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Turn on ___.
I turn ___ on.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I turn on the light.
I turn the light/it on.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. If object is noun two positions is possible 
2. If object is pronoun only one position is possible.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: His parents don't ___ what he does, but they can't stop him.

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Approve/disapprove of something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Everybody ___ me ___ the accident. (blame).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Everybody blamed me for the accident.
Everybody said that I was to blame for the accident.
Everybody blamed the accident on me.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Blame somebody/something for ...
Somebody is to blame for ...
Blame (a problem etc.) on somebody/something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Do you ___ being rich and famous? (dream)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Do you dreamed of/about being rich and famous?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:

Wouldn't dream of doing something: I would never do it.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: My sister ___ moving to Canada. (thinking)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: My sister's thinking of / about moving to Canada.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: You can say think of or think about doing something (for possible future actions).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
We had ___ about what we should do.
We ___ a lot of things at the meeting. (discussed/discussion)

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Have a discussion ABOUT something, but discuss something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He's very selfish. He doesn't ________ other people.

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:

But: care what/where/how etc. (without about).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Would you _______ a cup of coffee?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Would you care for a cup of coffee?
I don't care for very hot weather.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Care for somebody/something: like something (usually in questions and negative sentences).

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I haven't seen her since she ___ the office this morning.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The tray of ice cubes ___ fallen on the kitchen floor.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: A few of us wants to go camping this weekend.

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Few: a plural indefinite pronoun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Both was watching her as if she had something earth-shattering to say.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Both were watching her as if she had something earth-shattering to say.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Both takes plural.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Everybody ___ here, so we can get started on the trip.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I don't think either of them are at home.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The Matrix is one of the best films has ever been made.

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: One, other, somebody, someone, something: singular pronoun but the given example is a case of relative clause (that omitted), that refer to films, there subject is plural.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Some of the money ___ missing.

Some of the money is missing.
Some of the people in the bank are the suspects.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Most of my coworkers is cleared of any suspicion.
Most of my jewelry are still missing.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Most of my coworkers are cleared of any suspicion.
Most of my jewelry is still missing.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Most ...: look at the object of the preposition to decide whether to use a singular or plural verb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
All of the water ___  evaporated. (to have)
All of suspects ___ dead. (to be)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
All of the water has evaporated.
All of suspects are dead.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: All ...: look at the object of the preposition to decide whether to use a singular or plural verb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
None of them is/are good enough for the job.

grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
None of them are good enough for the job.
None of it is better than that.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Any ...: look at the object of the preposition to decide whether to use a singular or plural verb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The only one of those people I feel comfortable with ___ Prince. He is one of those people who always ___ when I have a problem.(listen)

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Many a good man is/are trying to please his wife.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Many a good man is trying to please his wife.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Many a ...: takes singular

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The number of people who came to the concert is/are disappointing.

A number of people are upset about the outcome of the election.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
The number ...: takes singular.
A number ...: takes plural.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: More than one person is/are upset about the outcome of the election.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: More than one person is upset about the outcome of the election.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: More than one ...: takes singular.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Ten dollars to see this movie is/are highway robbery!

grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Ten dollars to see this movie is highway robbery!
I would estimate that two thirds of the snow has melted.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Expression of measurement or quantity: singular expression.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The United States ___ defending its title against the United Kingdom.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The United States is defending its title against the United Kingdom
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Some nouns look plural but actually name one person, place, or thing.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Mr. and Mrs. Claxton ___ joining us for an informal dinner tonight.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Mr. and Mrs. Claxton are joining us for an informal dinner tonight.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Subject joined by 'and' take a plural verbs. When 'and' is used in common phrases, connecting two things or people that are closely linked, the determiner is not usually repeated before the second: a knife and fork, my father and mother, but a knife and a spoon, my father and my uncle.
When numbers (but not dates) are spoken,and is used between the hundreds and the figures that follow: 2 264 — two thousand, two hundred 
and sixty-four, but 1964 — nineteen sixty-four.
Go, come, try, stay, etc. and used before a verb instead of 'to', to show purpose: Go and get me a pen please. I'll come and see you soon. We stopped and bought some bread.
In this structure 'try' can only be used in the infinitive or to tell somebody what to do: Try and finish quickly.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
My cat or my three dogs are coming with me on the trip.
My three dogs or my cat is making me itch all the time.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
My cat or my three dogs are coming with me on the trip.
My three dogs or my cat is making me itch all the time.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Singular subject or plural subject: takes plural.
Plural subject or singular subject: takes singular.
If one subject is sungular and one is plural and connected by or then verb must agree with the subject closer to it.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Who was that man you were talking ___?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Who was that man you were talking to?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Talk/speak to somebody ('with' is also possible but less usual).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I wrote ___ the hotel complaining about the poor service we had received.

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Write (a letter) + to.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
You're ___ than me. (old)
Last night I went to bed ___ than usual. (early)
You're ___ than me. (patient)
Can you walk a bit ___? (slow)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You're older than me.
Last night I went to bed earlier than usual.
You're more patient than me.
Can you walk a bit more slowly?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Comparison: -er vs more.
We use -er for short words(one syllable): cheap - cheaper, large - larger. We also use -er for two-syllable words that end in -y: lucky - luckier, early - earlier.
We use more for larger words: more serious, more often, more expensive. We also use more ... for adverbs that end in -ly: more slowly, more quietly.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The garden looks ______ since you tidied it up?

The garden looks better since you tidied it up?
I know him well - probably better than anybody else knows him.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
How is your headache? Better? 'No, it's ___' (bad).
He did very badly in the exam, ___ than expected. (bad)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
How is your headache? Better? 'No, it's worse.'
He did very badly in the exam - worse than expected.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Bad/badly -> worse: irregular comparative forms.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I've waited long enough. I'm not waiting ___ longer.

I've waited long enough. I'm not waiting any longer. (not even a bit longer).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Your English is improving. it's getting ___. (better, improving)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Your English is improving. It's getting better and better.
The city is growing fast. It's getting bigger and bigger.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
- What time shall we leave?
- The ___ the better.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
- What time shall we leave?
- The sooner the better (as soon as possible).
When you're travelling, the less luggage you have the better.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We say the (sooner/bigger/more etc) the better.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The _____ we leave, the _______ we will arrive.
The ___ expensive the hotel, the ___ the service.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:

Complex sentence: principal clause + sub-ordinate clause.
Adjective clause: qualifies an antecedent (noun or pronoun).

Who, whose, whom: for living beings.

Why is used: after reason as an antecedent.
When is used: after time as a antecedent

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Investors who are averse to ___ risks. (take)

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We say averse to + gerund: strongly ​disliking or ​opposed to.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: These ​measures have been taken with a view to ​___ the company's ​profits. (increase)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: These ​measures have been taken with a view to ​increasing the company's ​profits.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: With a view to doing something: with the ​aim of doing something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He devoted his ​life to ___ his ​family, ​friends, and ​neighbors. (serve)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He devoted his ​life to ​serving his ​family, ​friends, and ​neighbors.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Devote something/yourself to something/someone: to give ​your ​time or ​effort ​completely to something you ​believe in or to a ​person, or to use a ​particular ​amount of ​time or ​energy doing something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Members of the academic community are given to ___ meetings and conferences. (attend).
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Members of the academic community are given to attending meetings and conferences.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Given to doing something: to be likely to do something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She couldn't resist ​___ at him in those ​clothes. (laugh)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: She couldn't resist ​laughing at him in those ​clothes.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Resist + gerund: to ​stop yourself from doing something that you ​want to do.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: My sister is prone to ______ because of her allergies.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: My sister is prone to sneezing because of her allergies.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Prone to something: likely to [do] something; apt to have something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I don't like him wasting time.
Geel insisted on Ronal going with her.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I don't like his wasting time.
Geel insisted on Ronal's going with her.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The noun or pronoun before a gerund should be in possessive case.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The director as well as the the dancers ___ honoured by the public
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The director as well as the the dancers was honoured by the public.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Subject-verb agreement: as well as, with, together with, along with - according to first subject.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The mother, and not her children ___ been arrested for committing theft.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The mother, and not her children has been arrested for committing theft.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Subject-verb agreement and not: according to first subject.
Other example: rather than.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: More men than one ___ absent yesterday.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: More men than one were absent yesterday.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Subject-verb agreement: more (men) than one - according to first subject.
Other example: except.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Nothing but the truth ____ immortal.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Nothing but the truth is immortal.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Subject-verb agreement: nothing - according to first subject.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: My mother no less than my father ___ strict.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: My mother no less than my father is strict.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Subject-verb agreement: no less - according to first subject.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She like John ___ Madonna. (hate)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: She like John hates Madonna.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Subject-verb agreement: like, unlike - according to first subject.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: His real love, besides his guitar playing, ___ untlimately songwriting
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: His real love, besides his guitar playing, is untlimately songwriting.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Besides = in addition to: according to first subject.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: None but the leaders of our country ___ responsible for this state of affairs.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: None but the leaders of our country are responsible for this state of affairs.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Subject-verb agreement, none-but: verb according to nearest subject.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Every boy and every girl ___ been invited.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Every boy and every girl has been invited.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
We each ___ taken our bags. (have)
They each ___ honest. (be)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
We each have taken our bags.
They each are honest.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When 'each' is used after subject the verb is plural.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Many accidents ___ recently taken place.
Many an accident ___ recently taken place.
More than one man ___ absent.
More men than one ___ burnt.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Many accidents have recently taken place.
Many an accident has recently taken place.
More than one man was absent.
More men than one were burnt.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: 'Many a/an', 'more than one' should be followed by a singular noun and singular verb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
He surrendered before the court and sent to jail.
She is intelligent but her sister is dull.
I did not and will not go there.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He surrendered before the court and was sent to jail.
She is intelligent but her sister dull.
I did not and will not go there.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: In a compound sentence both auxiliary verbs and principal verbs should be mentioned separately if they differ in number, form or voice. In such cases one verb cannot act for both the clauses.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
So quickly she finished her work that we were surprised.
May you succeed in life.
Hardly/scarcely I had reached the airport than the plane arrived.
No sooner did she arrive when she started laughing.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
So quickly did she finish her work that we were surprised.
May you succeed in life.
Hardly/scarcely had I reached the airport when the plane arrived.
No sooner did she arrive than she started laughing.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Inverted form of the verb is used in the following cases:
- when the sentence is introduced by adverb.
- when the verb is meant to express a wish or prayer.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: It’s high ​time you ___ that ​bad ​knee ​looked at by a ​doctor! (get)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: It’s high ​time you got that ​bad ​knee ​looked at by a ​doctor!
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: (It’s) high time: (it's) past the ​time when something should have ​happened.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The government's ​campaign is ​aimed ___ influencing ​public ​opinion.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The government's ​campaign is ​aimed at influencing ​public ​opinion.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Aim at gerund/sth: to plan, hope, or intend to achieve something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She was forbidden ___ move out with friends.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: She was  forbidden to move out with friends.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We say forbid to + infinitive.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Cow is a useful animal.
Rose is a beautiful flower.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
A cow is a useful animal.
A rose is a beautiful flower.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: A/An: before a singular countable noun which is use to single out some person / something as representative of a class of things, animals and persons.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: What the hot day!
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
What a hot day!
What a naughty child!
What a fool he is.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
A/An: In exclamations with 'what' or 'how' before singular countable nouns but with some exception.


Exceptions: How fine a day. What kind of a teacher.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He is much hated character.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He is a much hated character.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She is as intelligent student as her brother is. (a)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: She is as intelligent a student as her brother is.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She is too weak student to pass.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: She is too weak a student to pass.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She is so weak student that she can't pass.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: She is so weak a student that she can't pass.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The times of England.
The Himalayas.
The Persian Gulf.
The USA.
The Tower of London.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The times of England.
The Himalayas.
The Persian Gulf.
The USA.
The Tower of London.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The: before proper nouns (unique objects) when they refer to the names of historical buildings, mountain ranges, planets, rivers, oceans, gulfs, groups of islands, holy books, ordinals, descriptive names of countries, states, newspapers, magazines, deserts, superlative degree, names of trains, hotels, shops trains... Note: The is not used before Everest because it's not a mountain range.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: ___ son should be obedient.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: A son should be obedient.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The: when a singular noun expresses a class of animal or things. But 'the' is avoided with their plural forms and persons to express a class.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: A Man is mortal.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Man is mortal.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: No article: Man/Woman/Mankind used in general sense to represent human race are used without article.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
A rich shoud help a poor.
The old are respected by a young.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The rich shoud help the poor.
The old are respected by the young.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The: before an adjective when it represents a class of persons.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
He can play flute.
She is fond of playing the harmonium.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He can play the flute.
She is fond of playing the harmonium.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The: before musical instruments.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Homer is Shakespeare of Greece.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Homer is the Shakespeare of Greece.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The: before the proper noun for the sake of comparision.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: France won Singer Cup last year.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: France won the Singer Cup last year.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The: before sports cups and trophies.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Vikings are brave people.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The Vikings are brave people.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The: before caste and communities.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
This is same book that you gave me.
The whole class was absent.
Both the brother were honest.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
This is the same book that you gave me.
The whole class was absent.
Both the brothers were honest.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The: before the adjectives 'same and whole' and after the adjectives 'all and both with plural nouns'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The telephone.
Television.
He was watching the television.
He was listening to radio.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The telephone.
The television.
He was watching television.
He was listening to the radio.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The: before the inventions, before the dates, political parties, organs of government(the Judiciary, the legislature), before armed forces.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Chinese are hard working.
Japanese are patriots out and out.
Greeks are in trouble.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The Chinese are hard working.
The Japanese are patriots out and out.
The Greeks are in trouble.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
The: before language to signify nationality, before nationality (plural).
The little = some but all, the few = some but all.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
We go to the temple on Mondays.
I go to the bed early.
He went to the sea in his early youth.
He went to the Sea alone.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
We go to temple on Mondays.
I go to bed early.
He went to sea in his early youth.
He went to the Sea alone. (travel or other purposes)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The omission of articles: before school, college, home, church, temple, sea, work, bed, table, hospital, market, prison, court -  when their purpose is thought of something rather than the actual building/place, but 'the' is used before: office, cinema, movie, theatre, circus, picture, station, bus, stop etc.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Cancer is a dreaded disease.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Cancer is a dreaded disease.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The omission of articles: before names of diseases, but we can say the Measles, the mumps, the rickets, the Plague, the Flu.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I take the breakfast at 8 a.m.
They gave us a good breakfast.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I take breakfast at 8 a.m.
They gave us a good breakfast.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The omission of articles: before regular meals except when preceded by an adjective.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I will see you in the summer.
It always rains in summer season.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I will see you in summer.
It always rains in the summer season.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We say in summer, winter but in the summer season.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I watch the whole movie from beginning to end.
He does the same thing from the beginning of the day to the end of the day.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I watch the whole movie from beginning to end.
He does the same thing from the beginning of the day to the end of the day.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We say from beginning to end but from the beginning of something to the end of something.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
We go for walk at the night.
It's silent in the night.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
We go for walk at night.
It's silent in the night.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We say at dust, at dawn, at midday, at noon, at night and during the day, in the afternoon, in the evening, in the night.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I met her last week.
This is the final step to success.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I met her last week.
This is the final step to success.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We say next week, last week when we mean time and we say the next question, the last question when we mean number.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The Prime Minister and the President are visiting the town today.
The Prime Minister and the president of the party is on a visit to the town today.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The Prime Minister and the President are visiting the town today.
The Prime Minister and president of the party is on a visit to the town today.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When two or more connected nouns refer to the same person or thing, the article should be used before the first noun. However, the article is used before each noun if they refer to two different persons or objects.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She is wearing a black and a white saree.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: She is wearing a black and white saree.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Similarly, one article before the first adjective is used when two or more adjectives qualify the same noun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The first and second chapter is very difficult.
The first and second chapters are very difficult.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The first and the second chapter are very difficult.
The first and second chapters are very difficult.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If there are two articles before ordinals(number), use singular noun. In the case of article before one ordinals, noun should be used in plural form.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
You should be true to your words.
He was punished for committing many mischiefs.
Young persons dislike the advices of the elderly people.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You should be true to your word. (word = promise, mesage, discussion)
He was punished for committing many much mischief.
Young persons dislike the advice of the elderly people.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
- Uncountable nouns are used in the singular forms only.
- They are not used with plural verbs.
- 'Much' or 'some' are used in place of 'Many' for denoting plurality.
- other similar nouns: hair,  work, scenery, abuse, vacation, evidence, alphabet, furniture, fuel, paper, equipment, material etc.
- to denote singularity using these nouns we use: a piece / a word of advice, a word of abuse, an act of mischief, a piece of work, a piece / loaf of bread, an article of luggage.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Cattles are grazing in the field.
Majority is in favour of this proposal.
The peoples of all the countries should work for piece.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Cattle are grazing in the field.
Majority are in favour of this proposal.
The peoples of all the countries should work for piece(peoples of different countries).
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Some collective noun are used with plurals: cattle, gentry(people of good social position), peasantry, clergy, people, majority, folk.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The committee is unanimous on this issue.
The committee is divided and there is bitterness among the members.
The average family consist of four members.
His family is not agreed on this point.
The police has become insensitive.
The police were posted all over the route.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The committee is unanimous on this issue.
The committee are divided and there is bitterness among the members.
The average family consists of four members.
His family are not agreed on this point.
The police has become insensitive.
The police were posted all over the route.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The nouns 'committee, jury, house, ministry, family, mob, crowd, audience, police, team, number, board, staff, public' are used with singular verbs when they are used as a body or group and not as members.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Sheeps are economically useful.
A sheep is grazing in the field.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Sheep are economically useful.
A sheep is grazing in the field.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: 'Offspring, deer, fish, sheep' both in singular and the plural have the same form.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Politics are a dirty game.
Summons have been served on him.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Politics is a dirty game.
A summons has been served on him.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Words that are used with singular verb: innings, series, news, summons, politics, billiards, bowls, cards, darts, diabetes, measles, mumps, rabies, draughts, skittles, rickets, shingles.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I gave him two hundreds horses.
I gave him five dozens pencils.
There are hundreds of partially built houses.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I gave him two hundred horses.
I gave him five dozen pencils.
There are hundreds of partially built houses. (correct)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Nouns expressing number are used in singular with numerical adjectives.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The table's wood.
Time's march.
A dollar's worth.
A one-kilometer's journey.
Nature's law.
A week's holiday.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The table's wood.
Time's march
A dollar's worth
A one-kilometer's journey.
Nature's law
A week's holiday.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Apostrophe is restricted only to living things, time, weight, distance, amount, or personified nouns.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Mari and Romeo's father is coming for the meeting.
Mari's and Romeo's fathers are meeting today.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Mari and Romeo's father is coming for the meeting.
Mari's and Romeo's fathers are meeting today.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When apostrophe is used with one noun, it expresses singular form.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Mother's-in-law behaviour.
Maid-servant's absence.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Mother-in-law's behaviour.
Maid-servant's absence.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: With compound nouns apostrophe should be added only with the last word.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
This is not my book, this is somebody's else.
Who else is coming?
Who else book is this?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
This is not my book, this is somebody else's.
Who else is coming?
Whose else book is this?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
'Else' combined with indefinite pronous is expressed in possessive case as somebody else's in place of somebody's else.
Correct expression 'whose else' should be used in place of the wrong expression 'who else's'. However 'who else' is correct.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Cultural and social life in the world is changing.
Summer and winter vacation is coumpulsory in our school.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Cultural and social life in the world are changing.
Summer and winter vacation are coumpulsory in our school.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Two adjectives denoting different meanings and qualifying the same noun are considered plural and are used with plural verbs.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Word for word.
Hour after hour.
Door to door.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Word for word.
Hour after hour.
Door to door.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Noun after preposition is repeated in singular form.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
One and a half years is wasted.
One and a half hours are wasted.
A year and a half are wasted.
An hour and a half are wasted.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
One and a half years are wasted.
One and a half hours are wasted.
A year and a half is wasted.
An hour and a half is wasted.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The use of fractions: according to position and number of a noun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Attorney general.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Attorneys general.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The use of fractions: accoding to postion and number of noun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Man servant or woman servant.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Men servants.
Women servants.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
1. M.A
2. M.A's
3. M's.A's
Mouse, Ox.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Mice, Oxen.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: stadium
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: stadia or stadiums

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Formula
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Formulae

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Lacuna
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Lacunae
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Lacuna: an unfilled space; a gap.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Both the brothers love one another.
People should not fight with each other.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Both the brothers love each other.
People should not fight with one another.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: One another: for more than two people. Each other: for two people.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
You should avail yourself, of every chance in life.
They enjoyed picture last evening.
They enjoyed during summer vacation.
He resigned himself to his failure.
The former DM acquitted very efficiently.
He was determined to avenge the death of his wife.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You should avail yourself, of every chance in life.
They enjoyed picture last evening. (correct)
They enjoyed themselves during summer vacation.
He resigned himself to his failure.
The former DM acquitted himself very efficiently.
He was determined to avenge the death of his wife. (correct)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When the subject of the verb is the receiver of the action, the action is said to be reflected. Such verbs are used reflexively: acquit, absent, avail, reconcile, amuse, resign, avenge, enjoy, exert, apply, adapt, pride, overreach etc

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
You should keep yourself from the bad boys.
He has qualified himself for the post.
He hid himself in the room.
The thief hid money under the carpet.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You should keep from the bad boys.
He has qualified for the post.
He hid in the room.
The thief hid money under the carpet.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The following verbs are not used reflexively: keep, stop, turn, qualify, bathe, rest, hide.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
It is me who have brought you home.
Was it her who did it for you?
It will be us who will buy a new house.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
It is I who have brought you home.
Was it she who did it for you?
It will be we who will buy a new house.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The verb 'to be' should be followed by subjective form when the complement is pronoun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Between you and I Sus is intelligent.
She is teaching Ronald and she.
Let us go.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Between you and me Sus is intelligent.
She is teaching Ronald and her.
Let us go.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Verbs and prepositions are followed by objective case of a pronoun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I and you will attend her wedding tomorrow.
He and you will share the mangoes.
You, Mike and I will watch movie tonight. We, you and they are leaving for Paris tomorrow.
You and I will be punished.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You and I will attend her wedding tomorrow.
You and he will share the mangoes.
You, Mike and I will watch movie tonight.
We, you and they are leaving for Paris tomorrow.
I and you will be punished.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The order of singular pronouns should be second person, third person and first person (231). But in plural or when refering to unpleasant acts: 'we' is used before 'you' and 'they' after 'you' (123).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Your separation is very painful to me.
At his sight the robbers fled.
I beg your favour, please.
She did make mention of you.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Separation from you is very painful to me.
At sight of her the robbers fled.
I beg favour of/from you, please.
She did make mention of you.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: A noun or pronoun in possessive case should not be used with the nouns such as: separation, leave, excuse, mention, report, pardon, sight, favour.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Both you as well as my brother are going to attend her marriage tomorrow.
Both of them are not going there.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

I don't believe in the words that/which she uttered. (adj clause)
I don't believe in what you say. (noun clause)

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

We bought neither of the bikes.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

Taste, sound, look, feel, smell, seem.

Happiness is the chief aim of mankind.
How can divided Kingdom become the supreme power?

Lemon juice is preferable to tea.

She is comparatively smarter than her husband. (correct)
She is senior to her boss in service.
Milk preferable to tea.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

There is less passengers in the compartment today.

There is fewer passengers in the compartment today.
There are five students less in the class. (correct)

Few: plural countable noun - hardly anyone/anything(negative sense).
A few: not many(some) - affirmative meaning.
Other means the second of the two.
Another means additional one.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

She was some angry.

She was somewhat angry.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Some is used in affirmative and while making request.
Any is used for negative and interrogative sentences and in the sense of every.
Somewhat: is used as an adverb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
My friend is older than I.
She came latter than I.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
My friend is older than I. (correct)
She came later than I.

Later: refer to time.
Latter: refers to position.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

She is the most active and most energetic social worker in our club.
She is both cleverer and more intelligent than her sister.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

I will not do this kind/sort of acts.

The expression 'these' and 'those' should not be used with the singular nouns 'kind', 'type' and 'sort'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
All students were present.
Both the boys left soon.
Whole country is suffering from drought.
All the sugar is wasted.
My all efforts ended in vain.
Both my friends are honest.

All the students were present.
Both the boys left soon.
The whole country is suffering from drought.
All the sugar is wasted. (uncountable noun)
All my efforts ended in vain.
Both my friends are honest.
He is a fortunate person all whose efforts succeed.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Place 'the' after 'all' and 'both' when used as adjectives for plural nouns. But 'the' is used before 'whole'. Place possessive case after 'all' and 'both'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
She is as honest, if not more honest than her brother.
I am as strong or even stronger than my foe.

She is as honest as, if not more honest than her brother.
I am as strong as or even stronger than my foe.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: 'As' is used in the positive degree to denote equality while 'than' is used in the comparative degree.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
He is senior and older than I.
His dress is different and cheaper than mine.
She is stronger and younger than her sister.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He is senior to and older than I.
His dress is different from and cheaper than mine.
She is stronger and younger than her sister.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When two adjectives require different prepositions, appropriate prepositions should be used with both adjectives.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The subject is a matter worthy of note.
He is a man suitable for any post.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

A small Indian stadium.
A big round black Swedish plastic table.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Twenty year old black American Negro.
A small Indian stadium.
A big round black Swedish plastic table.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: The order of adjectives qualifying a noun, OSASCOMP: Opinion -> Size -> Age -> Shape -> Colour -> Origin(nationality) -> Material -> Purpose -> Noun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

Your income is many times as high as Tisha's.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

My brother often comes every Sunday.

He never talks ill of friends.
He is always satisfied.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

He returned immediately. (correct)
He briefly narrated the incident to me. (correct)
He narrated to me the incident briefly. (correct)
He slept soundly last night.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

No sooner did she reach the station than she met her friend. (correct)
She had hardly reached the station when the train arrived. (correct)
Hardly/scarcely had she reached the station when the train arrived.(correct)
So quickly did she ran that she overtook her rivals.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

It is nothing else but sheer madness.

She has no one else to look after her but me.

'Else' should be followed by 'but'.
'Other' and 'otherwise' are followed by 'than'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: We seldom or ever meet our relatives these days.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:

'That' is used with 'the same' when: noun is present (1st sentence: perfume (noun), 4th sentence: girl (noun)).

We say "All that" not "all what" or "all which":

grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When there is more than one of the three types of adverb together, they usually go in the order: manner, place, time.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She plays really well the piano.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
She plays the piano really well.
I don’t watch the TV very often.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: We don’t put adverbs between the verb and the object.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Can you ___ my house over the cliff?
___ at me while I am speaking.
I like ___ the spectacular sunset every day.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Can you see my house over the cliff?
Look at me while I am speaking.
I like watching the spectacular sunset every day.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
See: We start to see unintentionally when we open our eyes, It may not be deliberate, we just see without any effort.
Can you see my house over the cliff?
Bats can see very well in the dark.
See you tomorrow.
You may not see much in dim light.
Look: Different from the action “see” we make a special effort when we try to see something. It's an active verb.
Don't look at the sun with naked eye.
Look at me while I am speaking.
He looked at his watch and told me the time.
Don’t look at me like that, I didn't do anything wrong.
Watch: The verb “watch” is used when we look at something that moves or changes for a period of time. It's a continuous action of looking and observing.
All day long I just watched TV yesterday.
I like watching the spectacular sun set every day.
Please be quiet, I am trying to watch the world cup series.
Do you like watching talk shows?
Watch a Movie vs See a Movie. 
We watched a movie yesterday. This would imply we watched a movie at home (TV/DVD...). 
We saw a movie yesterday. This would imply that we did so by going to a movie theatre. We can also explicitly say that we went to the movie theatre and watched Ice Age.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I can’t see very ___ without my glasses on.
San Francisco is ___ from New York.
Where we live is ___ enough away from the city. I don’t want to move any further away.
From here, you can see as ___ as the ocean.
Food costs ___ more in the UK.
With more than seven million people, London is ___ the biggest city in England.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I can’t see very far without my glasses on.
San Francisco is a long way from New York.
Where we live is far enough away from the city. I don’t want to move any further away.
From here, you can see as far as the ocean.
Food costs far more in the UK.
With more than seven million people, London is by far the biggest city in England
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Far and a long way both describe something at a great distance:



- far is used mostly in negatives and questions.
- far is used in affirmative statements with words such as so, too, enough and as. These expressions can refer to time as well as distance.

- far is also used in comparatives to mean ‘much’.

- we can use by far before a superlative adjective to add emphasis.



- a long way is used mostly in affirmative statements but we also use it in questions and negatives.
- we use the phrase has come a long way to mean ‘has improved or developed': Our team has come such a long way. We lost our first game 5-0!

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Luxury gifts are out this Christmas – with practicable presents now topping most people's wish lists.

Health Amendment Act 2007 required councils to take all practical steps to ensure drinking water complied with drinking water standards.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Luxury gifts are out this Christmas – with practical presents now topping most people's wish lists.

Health Amendment Act 2007 required councils to take all practicable steps to ensure drinking water complied with drinking water standards.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When faced with a choice between practical and practicable, look at the context around the word. Do you mean to say that a thing is sensible? Choose practical. Do you want to say it is possible? Choose practicable. Out of context, sometimes either word will do.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
A £100 _____ has been offered for the return of the necklace.
An _____ of £600 000 in libel damages.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
A £100 reward has been offered for the return of the necklace.
An award of £600 000 in libel damages.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
An award is 
- a prize, medal, grant or other item given in recognition of an achievement
- the action of giving a prize, medal, grant or other item in recognition of an achievement
- compensation bestowed because of a legal judgement
- the action of bestowing compensation because of a legal judgement.
Award may be used as a noun or as a transitive verb, which is a verb that takes an object. Awards are often sought.

A reward is 
- a prize, bonus or token of appreciation given in recognition of one’s service or effort
- the just return on one’s good or bad actions
- monetary compensation for the apprehension of a criminal or the return of missing goods, or information leading to the apprehension of a criminal or the return of missing goods
- the action of bestowing compensation for any of the preceding situations. 
Reward may be used as a noun or as a transitive verb, which is a verb that takes an object. Rewards are given regardless of whether they are sought.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I cannot be able to come tomorrow.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I cannot come tomorrow or I will not be able to come tomorrow.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Both 'able to' and 'can/could' show capacity. Hence they are never used together.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He may possibly come tomorrow.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He may come tomorrow.
He will possibly come tomorrow.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Possibly/likely is never used with may.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
You will leave the room at once.
You shall be awarded.
Trespassers will be prosecuted.
I will work hard and score good marks.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You shall leave the room at once. (command)
You shall be awarded. (promise)
Trespassers shall be prosecuted. (threat)
I will work hard and score good marks. (determination)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Shall is used with second person, third person, to denote command, promise, threat, determination, compulsion and advice.
Will is used with I and we in similar cases.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
He ran fast, lest he should miss the train.
Take care lest he falls.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He ran fast, lest he should miss the train.
Take care lest you/he fall.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. If should is used after lest, it shows negative purpose.
2. Lest can also take 'V1' but plural form even with singular subjects.
3. 'Lest' doesn't take 'not' after it: He doesn't take risk lest he should lose all his money.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He uses to study till 10 P.M. and then goes to bed.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He studies till 10 P.M. and then goes to bed.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
'Use to' to 'Uses to' does not show present routine action. Instead simple present tense is used for such purpose.
Negative use of 'used to': He used not to come here. (He did not use to come here.)
Interrogative: Did he use to come here? (Used he to come here?)

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Help the needy woman.
Love a beautiful woman.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The needy woman should be helped. You are advised to help the needy woman.

A beartiful woman should be loved.
You are advised to love a beautiful woman.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
He is to do it.
She is to buy a car.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
It is to be done by him.
A car is to be bought by her.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Active: is/am/are/was/were + to + V1.
Passive: is/am/are/was/were/has/have/had + to be +V3.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
There are five books to write.
There is a piece of work to do.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
There are five books to be written.
There is a piece of work to be done.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Active: There + is/am/are/was/were/ + Noun/Pronoun + infinitive.
Passive: There+ is/am/was/were + Noun/Pronoun + to be + V3.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Tommy knows Mikey very well.
The idea interests me.
You pleased me.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Mikey is known to Tommy very well.
I am interested in this idea.
I am pleased with you.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Addicted to
annoyed at/with
compared with/to
disgusted with
displeased with
invited to
known to
pleased with
prepared for
satisfied with
amazed at
astonished at
dependent on
disinterested in
interested in 
knocked at 
listen to 
prefer to
quarreled with

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The surface feels smooth.
A mango tastes delicious.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The surface is smooth when felt.
A mango is delicious when tasted.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Active: sub + feel/taste + adj.
Passive: sub + is/am/are/was/were + adj + when + felt/tasted or 
Passive: sub + is/am/are/was/were + adj + when + it/they + is/are/was/were + tasted/felt.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
It is time to cook food now.
It is time to meet her.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
It is time for food to be cooked now.
It is time for her to be met.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Active: It + to be verb + time + to + V1 + object.
Passive: It + to be verb + time + for + object + to be + V3.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
It is your duty to make tea now.
It is our duty to help the poor.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
You are supposed to make tea now.
We are supposed to help the poor.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Active: It is your/my/his.... duty + to + V1.
Passive: You/I/he + to be verb + supposed + to + V1.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: She will have finished her work by the time her boss reaches his office.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The work will have been finished by her by the time her boss reaches his office.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If there are more than one clause in a sentence, see whether passive of both the clauses possible.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He did makes a mistake.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He did make a mistake.
You do come here everyday.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Usually in a sentence, 'do', 'does' and 'did' are not used in positive sentences as a helping verb. But to emphasise the main verb, we use 'do, 'does' and 'did' before the main verb. In such sentences main verb should be in 'v1' form.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I saw him before he stopped his car.
I met him after I finished my work.
By the time I reached the theater, the show started.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I had seen him before he stopped his car.
I met him after I had finished my work.
By the time I reached the threatre, the show had started.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He says to me, "You work hard".
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He tells me that I work hard.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Say/said remains unchanged in indirect speech. 'Say to' changes into 'tell' and 'said to' changes into 'told'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He said to me, "When will the train arrive?"
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He enquired of me when the train would arrive.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Interrogative sentences: change 'said to' into 'asked, questioned, inquired or interrogated.'

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He said to me, "Madam, can I help you?" She said, "No."
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He asked her respectfully if he could help her. She answered in the negative.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. If we use 'Sir/Madam/Your Honour' or any other word of respect in the Direct speech, such word should be replaced by word 'respectfully' in the Indirect Speech.
2. If we use 'Darling/Dear/My beloved' or any other word of affection in the Direct Speech, such word should be replaced by word 'lovingly/affectionately' in the Indirect speech.
3. If the answer is in 'yes' or 'no', they must be changed into 'answered in the affirmative/answered in the negative' respectively.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
She said, "How beautiful is the rain!"
He said, "Bravo! You have done well."
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
She exclaimed with joy that the rain was very beautiful.
He applauded him saying that he had done well.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
He said, "I shall come tomorrow."
She said to me, "What shall I do after the exam?"
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He said that he would come the next day.
She asked me what she should do after the exam.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Will/shall is changed into would/should but the statement will/shall should be changed into 'should' if the statement is suggestive.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Everyone has come, haven't ___?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Everyone has come, haven't they?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Each, every, everyone, everybody, no one, nobody, none are singular and hence will take singular verb / singular pronoun / singular adjective with them but their question tag will take plural verb and plural pronoun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The jury has taken its decision, hasn't ___?
The committee are divided in their opinion, aren't ____?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The jury has taken its decision, hasn't it?
The committee are divided in their opinion, aren't they?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Collective noun takes singular verb and singular pronoun in question tag.
If we talk about the individual members of the collective noun or if there is a difference in opinion among the members of the collective noun, plural verb and plural pronoun are used.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: There is no water, is ___?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
There is no water, is there?
There were no good schools in the town, were there?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If a sentence starts with 'There', the question tag will have 'there' in the place of pronoun.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Open the door, ___?
Have some more tea, ___?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Open the door, would you?
Have some more tea, would you?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If in an imperative sentence, somebody is being offered anything or if someone is being asked to do something, 'will you / would' is used in the question tag.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Slow and steady win the race.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Slow and steady wins the race.
Fish and chips is my favorite dish.
My friend, philosopher and guide, has come.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If two or more than two nouns or adjectives are joined by 'and' but only person or thing or idea is discussed, singular verb is used.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: One of the boys have done their work.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: One of the boys/them has done his work.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If 'of' is used after each, every, one etc, the noun or pronoun that comes immediately after 'of' will be plural in form. However, the verb, pronoun, adjective etc that comes in the latter part of the sentence will be singular in form.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: We each has a duty towards our nation.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: We each have a duty towards our nation.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If 'each' is used after plural noun or plural pronoun, plural verb is used.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Long lives the Queen.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Long live the Queen.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: In optative sentences, singular subject takes plural verb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The amount of money ___ not sufficient. (is/are)
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The amount of money is not sufficient.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: With uncountable nouns we use 'amount of/quantity of' followed by a singular verb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Monies has been collected and handed to the women's welfare society.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Monies have been collected and handed to the women's welfare society.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Monies is the plural of money which means amounts of money.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Wages ___ paid in cash.
Wages of hard work ___ sweet.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Wages are paid in cash.
Wages of hard work is sweet.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Wages (labour): plural, wages (result): singular.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Our team is the best.
Our team are trying their new uniform.
There are two fish in the pond.
There are many fishes in the aquarium.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Our team is the best.
Our team are trying their new uniform.
There are two fish in the pond.
There are many fishes in the aquarium. (Here the word 'fishes' refers to different species of fish.)
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Deer, sheep, series, species, fish, crew, team, jury, air craft, counsel are certain nouns that are used in both singular and plural form. If they are used in singular sense, they take singular verb and if they are used in plural sense, they take plural verb.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Suppose she does not agree what could we do?
Supposing if you do not reach the station in time, what will you do?
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Suppose she does not agree what can we do?
Supposing if you do not reach the station in time, what will you do?
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. Change 'could' into 'can'. The sentence is not of past ability.
2. Remove 'if'. 'Suppose' and 'if' mean the same, when used together, they make the sentence superfluous.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Police has arrested the thieves.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Police have arrested the thieves.
Cattle are grazing in the field.
Our infantry have marched forward.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Cattle, cavalry, infantry, poultry, peasantry, gentry, police are certain nouns that are plural in form but singular in meaning.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
He gave me two hundred-dollars notes.
He stays in five-stars hotels.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He gave me two hundred-dollar notes.
He stays in five-star hotel.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Hyphenated noun does not have plural form.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Watch out for pickpocketers, especially at the train station.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Watch out for pickpockets, especially at the train station.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
For peace's sake.
For Ganesh's Idol.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
For peace' sake.
For conscience' sake.
For Ganesh' idol.
For Jesus' sake.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When noun ends in hissing sound, 's' is not added after apostrophe. Note: God's sake.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: My wife's secretary's mother has expired.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The mother of my wife's secretary has expired.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Do not use double apostrophe.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: If you have a way with words/a good sense of design and administration ability, you may enjoy working in high pressure world of advertising.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: If you have a way with words/a good sense of design and administrative ability, you may enjoy working in high pressure world of advertising.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Administation is a noun. We need an adjective form here which is administrative.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The ticket window remained closed throughout the day.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The ticket counter remained closed throughout the day.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: When we reached the fair, we found that there was no place to stand.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: When we reached the fair, we found that there was no room to stand.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Use 'no room'. 'Room' means 'enough empty space for people or things to be fitted in'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Everybody but he was present for the meeting.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Everybody but him was present for the meeting.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: An objective pronoun comes after 'let, 'like', 'between...and', 'but', 'except' and 'all prepositions'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
I know you as much as him.
He is as fast as me.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
I know you as much as him.(I know you as much as I know him).
He is as fast as I.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If there's a comparison between two nominative cases, the pronoun of the nominative case is used after as/than.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: The man and his dog who I saw yesterday have been kidnapped.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: The man and his dog that I saw yesterday have been kidnapped.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If two antecedents are joined by 'and' one being a human and the other being a non living thing / animal, a relative pronoun 'that' is used.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: All that are interested to do this work can start now.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: All who/that are interested to do this work can start now.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If 'all' denotes people and is used as a subject, 'who' or 'that' is used and not 'whom/which'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: All which glitters is not gold.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: All that glitters is not gold.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: If 'all' denotes non living things, 'that' is used and not 'who' or 'whom'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: All the money which I gave her has been spent.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: All the money that I gave her has been spent.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: All + uncountable noun is followed by 'that'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Little quantity of food was wasted.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Small quantity of food was wasted.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Little or few cannot be used with quantity and number. Instead 'small' used with them.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
She is the best of two sisters.
He is the best of the three.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
She is the better of two sisters.
He is the best of the three.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. When one is chosen out of two, we use a comparative degree preceded by 'the' and followed by 'of'.
2. If one is chosen out of 'more than two' or 'all', superlative degree is used preceded by 'the' and followed by 'of'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He is wiser than intelligent.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: He is more wise than intelligent.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: When two qualities of a noun or a pronoun are compared with each other, more + positive degree is used instead of a comparative degree.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: I am sure that all my monthly expenses would exceed the income if I do not economise.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: I am sure that my monthly expenses would exceed the income if I do not economise.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Do not use 'all. 'Monthly expenses' includes 'all the expenses'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: He is so good as you.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He is as good as you.
He is not so good as you.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. So ..... as/as ...... as is used to make a comparison between two person or things.
2. So .... as is used in negative sentences.
3. But as..... as is used in both affirmative and negative sentences.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
He doubts that she will help him.
I have no doubt if/whether he will cheat me.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
He doubts if/whether she will help him (affirmative).
I have no doubt that he will cheat me (negative).
I am doubtful if/whether he will allow me to go to the party (affirmative).
He is not doubtful that I will finish his work in time (negative).
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: In affirmative sentences 'doubt' and 'doubtful' are followed by 'if/whether'. In negative or interrogative sentences 'doubt' and 'doubtful' are followed by 'that'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Never tell a lie.
Do not make noise.
Twelve inches make a foot.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Never tell a lie.
Do not make a noise.
Twelve inches make a foot.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: In a few phrases 'a/an' are used, some of these phrases are: in a fix, in a hurry, in a nutshell, make a noise, make a foot, keep a secret, as a rule, at a stone's throw, a short while ago, at a loss, take a fancy to, take an interest in, take a liking, a pity, tell a lie...

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: What sort of a man he is!
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: What sort of man he is!
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Articles are not used before the nouns, in sentences, starting with 'What kind of', What sort of', 'What type of' and 'What variety of'.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
Honesty is the best policy.
Honesty of this boy is liked by all.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
Honesty is the best policy.
The honesty of this boy is liked by all.
The cotton of Egypt is known for its superior quality.
God is precious.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
1. Article is generally used with abstract nouns. They are uncountable nouns hence 'a/an' cannot be used with them.
2. If nouns are followed by 'of', an article proceeds the noun i.e. article + noun + of.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: There are ten millimetres between each centimetre.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: There are ten millimetres between centimetre.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: Each / Every cannot be used after between.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Put a blanket on the baby.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Put a blanket over the baby.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation:
Over is used:
1. Motion or position higher than but no physical contact.
2. So as to cover the whole surface no matter whether there is physical contact or not.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence:
The warehouse has been badly damaged in fire.
Five people died in a house fire last night.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version:
The warehouse has been badly damaged by fire. (passive).
Five people died in a house fire last night. (active).

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: A member shall be required to pay interest at such rate as is fixed by the committee.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: A member shall be required to pay interest at such a rate as is fixed by the committee.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Sudoku was first designed in the 1970s by a retired architect and freelance puzzle constructor.
grammar_rules_find_error.correct_version: Sudoku was first designed in the 1970s by a retired architect and freelance puzzle constructor.
grammar_rules_find_error.explanation: No error: 'the' before 1970s is correct.

grammar_rules_find_error.sentence: Many overseas students attend colleges in the Great Britain.
